title: Torque Specifications for Tandem Axle Hanger Kit Spring and Equalizer Bolts
body: What are the torque specifications for the spring bolts and equalizer bolts on a tandem axle hanger kit with 2-inch wide slipper springs?
summary: For tandem hanger kits with 2-inch slipper springs, equalizer and spring eye bolts should be torqued to 30-50 ft-lbs, while U-bolts range from 35-90 ft-lbs depending on diameter.

comments.body: For a tandem hanger kit with 2-inch wide slipper springs (typically 3,500-8,000 lb axles), the primary pivot bolts should be torqued to 30-50 ft-lbs. Equalizer/center bolts (7/8 inch or 1 inch bolts): 30-50 ft-lbs, ensure components do not bind. Spring eye/shackle bolts (9/16 inch bolts): 30-50 ft-lbs. U-bolts (axle to springs): 35-90 ft-lbs depending on diameter. If using wet bolts or standard nuts, ensure they are tight but allow for suspension movement. If using locking nuts, they should be tight against the hanger. Use a wrench to hold the bolt head to prevent rotation while tightening. Ensure the equalizer moves freely after tightening. Check torque annually.

One thing worth adding — those 30-50 ft-lb values assume you're using Grade 5 hardware, which is what most hanger kits ship with. If you upgraded to Grade 8 bolts (which some guys do for peace of mind), the torque spec stays the same for this application because you're not supposed to clamp the equalizer tight. You want it snug but still pivoting freely. Over-torquing Grade 8 bolts on an equalizer is actually worse because they won't give you any warning before something binds.

Learned this the hard way on my 7K tandem car hauler. Cranked the equalizer bolts to about 75 ft-lbs because I figured tighter = better. Took it on a 200 mile trip and the trailer was riding rough as hell. Got home and realized the equalizer wasn't pivoting at all — basically locked solid. Backed off to about 40 ft-lbs and it was night and day difference. The suspension actually needs to move.

Can confirm the 30-50 range. I build about 10-12 trailers a year in my shop and that's what I torque every tandem hanger kit to. One small addition: I always put a dab of anti-seize on the equalizer and spring eye bolts before assembly. Makes it a lot easier when you need to pull things apart 3 years down the road. Without it, those bolts rust in place and you're reaching for the torch.

Quick question — if I'm using nylock nuts instead of regular nuts with cotter pins, does that change the torque spec at all? I've heard nylocks need a bit more initial torque to seat the nylon insert.

Nylocks don't really change the target torque for this application. The nylon insert adds maybe 5-10 ft-lbs of prevailing torque (the resistance you feel before the nut contacts the hanger), but you're still torquing to the same final clamping value. The advantage of nylocks is you don't need cotter pins and they're less likely to back off from vibration. Just don't reuse nylocks — once they've been run on, the nylon is deformed and won't hold as well the second time.

Something that gets overlooked: re-torque your U-bolts after the first 100 miles and again at 500 miles. New springs settle and the U-bolt clamp load drops. I've seen axles shift on springs because someone installed them, torqued everything to spec, and never went back to check. On a tandem setup that shift throws your axle alignment off and you'll eat tires.

If you don't already have a decent torque wrench, get a click-type (like a 1/2" drive that goes to 150 ft-lbs). The beam-type wrenches are fine for engine work where you can see the scale, but crawling under a trailer trying to read a beam wrench upside down is miserable. I keep a cheap 3/8" drive click wrench just for spring bolts — the 30-50 range is right in its sweet spot.

Had my spring bolts back off on a trip from Memphis to Dallas pulling a skid steer. Started hearing a clunk over every bump. Pulled over at a truck stop and the front spring eye bolt on the driver side was finger loose. The cotter pin had sheared off at some point. Now I do a walk-around and wiggle test on every bolt before any trip over 50 miles. Takes 5 minutes and it's cheap insurance.

One more detail on the torque specs — wet vs dry makes a difference. If you're applying anti-seize or grease to the threads (which Steve mentioned above), the effective clamping force at the same torque reading is higher than dry threads. Some people compensate by reducing torque about 15-20% on lubricated bolts. For these spring bolts at 30-50 ft-lbs it's a narrow range, so if you're using anti-seize I'd stay at the lower end, around 30-35 ft-lbs, and verify the equalizer pivots freely.

Good info in this thread. I'll just add — check your bolts for signs of stretching or necking once a year. If the shank diameter under the bolt head looks narrower than the threads, that bolt has been overloaded and needs replacing. On a 2" slipper spring setup, the bolts see a lot of cyclical loading, especially if you're running heavy loads on rough roads. I swap all my hanger hardware every 3-4 years as preventative maintenance. Bolts are cheap, axle failures aren't.

title: How to Find the Right 6-Lug Brake Drum for an Older Trailer
body: I'm looking for a 6-lug brake drum for my trailer. It has a 12" diameter and 2" deep drum. It's an older trailer and I can't find the exact one. The last one I purchased had races that were too big. My spindle is 1" outer and 1-1/2" on the inner.
summary: Finding the correct 6-lug brake drum requires matching your spindle bearing sizes exactly. Non-standard spindle sizes may require a specialty drum or swapping to a more common hub/drum assembly.

comments.body: It sounds like you're looking for a 6-lug, 12" x 2" brake drum that fits a spindle with a 1" outer bearing and 1-1/2" inner bearing. Based on your spindle size, you'll likely need a drum that takes the following bearing set: Inner Bearing 25580 (1.750" inner diameter) and Outer Bearing 15123 (1.250" inner diameter). However, your spindle measurements (1" outer and 1-1/2" inner) don't match the typical 6-lug brake drums commonly found. Standard 6-lug drums use bearings that fit 3.5K, 5.2K, and 6K axles. Possible solutions: 1) Confirm your bearings by checking the old drum or spindle for bearing numbers. 2) Check if you need an older or specialty drum. 3) Consider switching to a different hub/drum assembly to match more common bearing sizes.

What year and make is the trailer? Some of the older Calkins and EZ Loader boat trailers used oddball spindle sizes that don't match anything standard anymore. If it's pre-1995 there's a decent chance the spindle is a proprietary size from a manufacturer that either changed specs or went out of business.

Before you buy another drum, pull the old bearings out (or what's left of them) and look for a number stamped on the bearing cone — it's usually on the flat face of the inner race. Common trailer bearings have numbers like L44649, L68149, 25580, 15123, etc. Those numbers will tell you exactly what drum you need. If the numbers are worn off, measure the inner diameter of the cone with a caliper. That'll narrow it down fast.

I ran into almost this exact problem on a 1992 boat trailer I bought at auction. Turned out the spindles were Fulton brand with non-standard bearing sizes. I went through two drums that didn't fit before I figured it out. What finally solved it was taking the old drum and spindle to my local NAPA and having them cross-reference the bearing numbers right there. They pulled the correct bearings off the shelf and we confirmed it in 10 minutes.

Your spindle at 1" outer and 1-1/2" inner — that actually sounds like it could be an L44649 outer bearing (1.0" bore) and L68149 inner bearing (1.3775" bore). The L68149 is close to 1-3/8" not 1-1/2" though. Are you measuring the spindle shaft diameter or the bearing bore? Because if it's the shaft you're measuring, 1-1/2" inner could actually be a bearing with a 1.500" bore, which would be a different series entirely. Worth double checking with a set of calipers.

Here's what I'd do: get a set of cheap digital calipers (Harbor Freight sells them for $15) and measure three things — (1) the outer spindle diameter where the outer bearing sits, (2) the inner spindle diameter where the inner bearing sits, and (3) the outer diameter of the hub bore where each race/cup is pressed in. Write those numbers down and you can match the correct bearing set from any bearing catalog. The races that were "too big" in your last drum just means the cups in that drum were for a larger bearing set than your spindle takes.

Have you considered just swapping the spindles to a standard 3,500 lb straight spindle? They're like $30-40 each, and then you can use any standard 6-lug 12x2 brake drum that's meant for a 3.5K axle. You'd need to press off the old spindles and press on the new ones (or have a shop do it), but it means you'll never have a sourcing problem for drums or bearings again. Standard 3.5K parts are everywhere.

This happened to me three separate times on the same trailer. Bought drums that looked right, got them home, races wouldn't seat on the spindle. Turned out I had been pressing the new races into the drum but the cup outer diameters were slightly wrong — the races would drop in loose instead of press-fitting tight. If your races are going in too easy or wobbling, that's a red flag that you have the wrong bearing set for that drum casting.

If you can take the old drum off and bring it to any trailer parts shop, they can usually identify it by the casting markings. Most drums have a cast-in number somewhere on the outside of the cup. Even just a photo of the hub face showing the bolt pattern and inner bore would help narrow things down. Also measure the bolt circle — 6 lug at what spacing? 6 on 5.5" is the most common trailer pattern, but some older ones ran 6 on 5.25" or even 6 on 6".

Agree with the accepted answer — if you can't match the bearings, the most hassle-free path is switching to a standard hub/drum assembly. A 6-lug 5.2K or 6K hub and drum with standard bearings (25580 inner / 15123 outer) is readily available and reasonably priced. You'd need to confirm the spindle fits, but if you're already buying a drum, spending a little more for the correct matched assembly saves a lot of headache.

One more thing to watch for on older trailers — some of them came with metric bearings rather than standard inch-series Timken-style bearings. If your trailer was imported or built by a manufacturer that sourced overseas axles, the bearing designations will look completely different (like 30205 or 32008 instead of L44649). Metric bearings and inch-series bearings are NOT interchangeable even if they look similar in size.

Don't forget to measure your bolt circle diameter too. On a 6-lug drum, the bolt circle (center to center across the hub face) tells you a lot. 6 on 5.5" is the standard for 5.2K-7K trailer axles. If yours measures 6 on 5.25" or something else, that confirms you have a non-standard hub and you'll need to factor that into whatever replacement you choose. Bolt pattern plus bearing sizes together will give you a definitive match.

title: Triple Axle Hanger Kit for Double Eye Leaf Springs
body: I'm looking for a triple axle hanger kit for double eye leaf springs. Do you have this available?
summary: Triple axle hanger kits can be assembled by purchasing two tandem hanger kits, which is often the cheaper route and provides spare hangers.

comments.body: Yes, we sell triple axle hanger kits, however it's not currently in a single kit form on our website. We can piece together a triple axle hanger kit for you, or you could also buy 2 of the tandem hanger kits like SKU# THK175DBI or APT5. This will also make a triple axle hanger kit with a few extra hangers you will not need. This option is also the cheaper route to go. It will also give you a couple extra hangers just in case you mess up on welding a hanger in place.

Can confirm the two-tandem-kit approach. I did this on my 21-foot triple axle flatbed last year. Bought two APT5 kits, used 6 of the 8 hangers and both equalizer sets. Had two spare hangers left over which I kept as backups. Total install took about 4 hours including welding the hangers in place.

If you go the two-tandem-kit route, pay close attention to your hanger spacing. On a triple axle, you have four hanger brackets and two equalizers. The spacing between hangers needs to match your axle-to-axle distance. Measure center-to-center of your axles and that's your equalizer spacing. I like to tack weld the hangers first, roll the trailer to check alignment, then finish the welds once everything tracks straight.

Does the equalizer on a triple axle sit in between axle 1 and 2, and then another between 2 and 3? Or is there a different arrangement? I've only ever done tandems so I'm not sure how the load transfer works with three axles and double eye springs.

Built a triple axle gooseneck about 6 years ago using this same method. Two tandem hanger kits bolted to slipper springs. One thing I'll say — triple axle trailers with leaf spring suspension are harder on tires in tight turns because the middle axle scrubs. Not a suspension kit issue per se, but something to keep in mind if you're doing a lot of parking lot maneuvering. I ended up lifting my middle axle slightly to reduce tire wear.

If you're building a triple axle from scratch rather than replacing existing suspension, you might want to look into Torflex (rubber torsion) independent axles instead of leaf springs. They're more expensive up front but there's no inter-axle load transfer to worry about, each axle is independent. Downside is if one goes bad you replace the whole axle instead of just a spring. For leaf springs though, the two-tandem-kit solution is the most cost-effective route by far.

Just a heads up — double eye springs on a triple axle work differently than slipper springs. With double eye springs, both ends of the spring are fixed, so the equalizer geometry is more critical. Make sure the equalizer is positioned exactly at the midpoint between axles, and that the spring eye bolts allow the spring to pivot without binding. If the hangers are even slightly off-center, you'll get uneven tire wear across the three axles. I'd recommend a string line or laser level when positioning the hangers before welding.

title: Carry-On Trailer 504T Leaf Spring Cross Reference Replacement
body: I have a Carry-On trailer and need new suspension springs. I have a part number for the springs — it's 504T. Do you have a replacement?
summary: The Carry-On 504T is a 25-1/4" double eye leaf spring with 3 leaves. A direct replacement with upgraded 4-leaf construction is available under part number TPU-212.

comments.body: The part number you provided is a Carry-On 25-1/4" double eye leaf spring with 3 leaves, part #504. We have a 4-leaf double eye spring that has the same specs, and our part number is TPU-212. The extra leaf actually gives you a little more capacity and durability compared to the original 3-leaf spring, while still being a direct bolt-on replacement.

I put the TPU-212 on my Carry-On 5x10 utility trailer about 8 months ago. Bolted right in, no modifications needed. The ride is slightly stiffer than the original 3-leaf spring, which makes sense since you're adding a leaf. But it's a good kind of stiff — less sag when I load up 2,000 lbs of mulch. I'd do it again.

My 5x8 Carry-On had the original 3-leaf springs and they were sagging noticeably after about 2 years of hauling a 14-foot aluminum boat. One spring actually cracked at the eye. The 504 series springs on those little Carry-Ons are just light duty. Upgrading to a 4-leaf made a real difference in how the trailer sits loaded and unloaded.

Before you order, grab a tape measure and confirm the eye-to-eye length is actually 25-1/4 inches. Carry-On used a few different spring lengths across their models, and I've seen guys order the wrong size because they assumed all Carry-Ons are the same. Takes 30 seconds to measure and saves you a return shipping hassle.

Heads up — some Carry-On models actually used slipper springs on one end instead of double eye. If your spring has a curved end that sits in a hanger cradle (no bolt through it), you've got a slipper spring and the 504T/TPU-212 double eye replacement won't work. Just double-check both ends before ordering. Double eye means a bolt goes through a loop at both ends of the spring.
Should I replace both springs at the same time even if only one looks bad? One of mine is cracked but the other looks fine. Trying to save a few bucks if I can get away with just doing one side.

Always replace springs in pairs — even if only one is visibly bad, the other one has the same age and fatigue. If you put a new spring on one side and keep the old one, the trailer will sit uneven and the new spring will carry more of the load than it should. Springs are cheap enough that doing both sides at once is worth it. Plus you only have to crawl under there once.

Worth noting that the 504T part number shows up on more than just Carry-On trailers. I've seen the same spring on some Big Tex utility trailers and a few PJ models in the light-duty range. So if you're searching for a cross-reference for any 25-1/4" double eye 3-leaf spring, the TPU-212 four-leaf upgrade is a solid option regardless of brand.

title: 10K Brake Assemblies for Quality and Rockwell American Axles
body: Do you have brake assemblies for the 10K Quality axles? I need electric brakes and want to make sure they're compatible with Rockwell American.
summary: Carter brake assemblies are fully compatible with Quality (Rockwell American) 10K axles. Part numbers 4738-L (left) and 4738-R (right) are the correct electric brake assemblies.

comments.body: Yes, we carry the brake assemblies for the Quality axles, also known as Rockwell American. The 10K electric brake assembly part numbers are as follows: 4738-L for the left hand electric brake assembly and 4738-R for the right hand electric brake assembly. These are direct replacements for your 10K Quality or Rockwell American trailer axles.
testing
test2
testing 3

Important note on the 4738-L and 4738-R: make sure you install them on the correct sides. The L (left) goes on the driver side and the R (right) goes on the passenger side when you're standing behind the trailer looking forward. The magnet arm orientation is different between left and right — if you swap them, the brakes will still work but they'll apply unevenly and you'll get a pull to one side under braking.

Ask me how I know the left/right thing matters. Installed a set on my tandem 10K and accidentally swapped them. First time I hit the brakes at highway speed the trailer tried to swap ends on me. Pulled over, checked everything, realized my mistake. Swapped them to the correct sides and it was fine. Scared the life out of me though.

Are these self-adjusting brakes or do you need to manually adjust them after install? Also what size brake controller do I need for 10K electric brakes — is a 2-channel proportional controller enough?

These are manually adjusted — you set the star adjuster through the slot in the backing plate until you get light drag on the drum, then back off a couple clicks. For brake controllers, a proportional (inertia-based) controller is what you want for 10K axles. Something like a Tekonsha P3 or Curt Assure handles up to 4 brakes easily. If you're running tandem 10K axles that's 4 brake assemblies drawing about 3 amps each, so 12 amps total — make sure your controller and wiring can handle that. 10-gauge wire minimum from the controller to the trailer plug.

I've got the same Quality/Rockwell American 10K axles on my car hauler and the Carter 4738 assemblies bolted right on. Backing plate bolt pattern matches perfectly. One tip — when you mount them, put a thin layer of grease on the brake shoe contact points on the backing plate (the raised pads where the shoes rest). It helps the shoes slide smoothly and prevents squealing.

If your 10K axles see heavy use or you haul in mountainous terrain, you might want to consider upgrading to hydraulic disc brakes instead of electric drums. The disc brake conversion kits for 10K axles run about $350-400 per axle but you get way better stopping power, no fade on long downhill grades, and they're virtually maintenance free compared to drums. Tradeoff is cost and you need a hydraulic actuator instead of an electric brake controller. For flat-land hauling though, the electric drums are perfectly adequate.

When you install new brake assemblies, don't forget the burnish-in procedure. You need about 20-30 light-to-moderate stops from around 30 mph to seat the shoes to the drum properly. Until the shoes are burnished in, braking performance will feel weak. Also, after about 200 miles, go back and re-adjust the brakes — the shoes wear into the drum and the gap opens up. I see guys complain about weak brakes on new assemblies and 9 times out of 10 they just didn't adjust them after break-in.

Did a full brake job on my tandem 10K equipment hauler last spring with the Carter assemblies. Whole job took about 3 hours per axle including cleaning up the old mounting surface and running new wires. One thing I'll mention — check your brake drums for scoring while you've got everything apart. If there are deep grooves in the drum surface, the new shoes won't seat properly and you'll be disappointed in the braking. Drums for 10K axles aren't that expensive and it's the right time to replace them if they're worn.

For anyone reading this thread down the road — the wire connections on 10K electric brakes are pretty simple. White wire is ground, and the colored wire (usually blue) is the hot lead from your brake controller. Left and right assemblies share the same wiring, just make sure your grounds are solid. A bad ground is the number one cause of weak or no trailer brakes. I always run a dedicated ground wire back to the frame rather than relying on the ball/coupler connection for ground.

title: How to Determine Hub Face From Backing Plate Measurement
body: I measured 86 inches from backing plate to backing plate and 80 inches spring center on my 7K axle. Would that be a 95" hub face?
summary: On a 7K brake axle, an 86" backing plate to backing plate measurement corresponds to a 95" hub face.

comments.body: I went and measured a 7,000 lb brake axle and yes, the measurement from backing plate to backing plate (or brake flange to brake flange) is 86" on a 95" hub face axle. So yes, you have a 95" hub face with 80" spring center. This is a useful trick — if you can't easily measure hub face directly, you can measure backing plate to backing plate and use that to confirm your hub face dimension.
That checks out. On a 7K axle with standard brake flanges, the difference from backing plate face to hub face is about 4.5 inches per side, so 9 inches total. 86 + 9 = 95. Good rule of thumb.

Here's a quick reference for those who want to use the backing plate method on different axle sizes:

- 3.5K axle: hub face ≈ backing plate measurement + 7 to 8 inches total
- 5.2K/6K axle: hub face ≈ backing plate measurement + 8 to 9 inches total
- 7K axle: hub face ≈ backing plate measurement + 9 inches total
- 8K+ axle: hub face ≈ backing plate measurement + 9 to 10 inches total

These are approximate because different manufacturers have slightly different flange thicknesses and spindle lengths. Always verify with the actual axle if you can.

Does this offset number change if it's a 5.2K or 3.5K axle? I need to order a replacement axle for my enclosed cargo trailer and I can only get to the backing plates easily — the hub face is buried behind the wheels and I'd rather not pull them off if I can avoid it.

Yes, smaller axles have a smaller offset. A 3.5K axle has a shorter spindle and smaller brake assembly, so the difference is more like 7-8 inches total (about 3.5-4" per side). On a 5.2K or 6K it's around 8-9 inches. Just measure backing plate to backing plate and add the appropriate offset for your axle weight rating.

Careful with this measurement — I messed it up the first time because I was measuring to the outside face of the backing plate instead of the mounting flange where the plate bolts to the axle tube. The backing plate itself sticks out a bit past the flange. You want to measure to the flange face (where the flat of the backing plate contacts the axle), not the outer rim of the plate. It's only about a half inch difference per side but that's a full inch on hub face, which could give you the wrong axle.

Another approach if you don't have brakes (like on an idler axle) — measure from the inboard face of the hub at each end, then add for the distance from hub face to hub mounting surface. But honestly, backing plate to backing plate is the easiest proxy when you have brake axles. If you have the axle tube exposed somewhere, you can also measure spring seat to spring seat to get your spring center directly, which is the other measurement you'll need when ordering.

Good thread. One more tip — on older trailers, take your measurements at a couple of different points because things shift over time. I've seen axles that were slightly bent or frames that were tweaked from overloading. If your backing plate measurements differ by more than about 1/4 inch from one method to another, something is off and you should investigate before ordering a replacement axle.

For anyone searching for this info later: the 80" spring center with a 95" hub face is one of the most common configurations for 7K trailer axles. If you're getting those numbers, you're dealing with a very standard setup and replacement axles should be easy to source in that size.

title: Dexter 12K Hub Assembly Cost vs Buying a Complete Axle
body: I need a Dexter 12K hub assembly. I have the part number 8-214-5-UC1. Do you have this in stock and what's a reasonable price?
summary: Individual 10K/12K Dexter hub assemblies can cost $450+ each. A complete 10K electric brake axle fully assembled sells for around $1,000, making full axle replacement a cost-effective alternative.

comments.body: The part number 8-214-5-UC1 is actually for a 10K heavy duty Dexter trailer hub. Unfortunately, as of this time we do not stock these individually. I see them online ranging from $450 and up per hub. We do, however, sell a whole 10K electric brake axle fully assembled and ready to install with electric brakes and hub drums on them for only $1,000 each. So that might be another option to consider — in many cases, it makes more financial sense to replace the entire axle.

Went through this same decision on my 14-foot dump trailer last year. Two bad hubs on a Dexter 10K axle. By the time I priced out hubs ($450 each), new bearings, seals, and races for both sides, I was looking at over $1,000 just for the hub rebuild. Bought a complete 10K axle with electric brakes already mounted for about the same money and got essentially a brand new everything. No brainer.

The accepted answer is right on the money. The math almost always favors a complete axle at the 10K and 12K level. But one thing to keep in mind — if you go with a complete replacement axle, you'll need to cut off the old spring perches and weld new ones in the correct position to match your spring center. That's a couple extra hours of work and you need a decent welder. If you're not comfortable welding load-bearing structural components, have a shop do it.

Does the replacement axle need to be Dexter specifically, or can you put a different brand (like Lippert) on the same trailer? My concern is whether the spindle diameter and flange pattern would match my existing drums and brakes if I keep any of those parts.

For 10K axles, the spindle size is pretty much standardized across manufacturers — typically 2-1/4" diameter with a 3.38" seal. Dexter, Lippert, and most aftermarket 10K axles use the same spindle spec, so your hubs, drums, and brakes will swap right over. The key measurements are spindle diameter, flange bolt pattern (usually 5 bolts), hub face, and spring center. Match those and you're good regardless of brand.

If your hubs are damaged but the spindle, brakes, and axle tube are fine, you might be able to get away with just replacing bearings, seals, and races. A bearing kit for a 10K hub runs about $40-60 per side, and the inner and outer races press into the drum. That's a LOT cheaper than $450 per hub. It depends on what actually failed — if the spindle is scored or the hub bore is out of round, then yeah, you need hubs or a full axle. But if it's just bearing failure from running dry, new bearings and seals might be all you need.

Just want to clarify something from the thread title — the part number 8-214-5-UC1 is actually for a 10K Dexter hub, not a 12K. The 12K Dexter hubs use a different, larger hub and bearing set. So if you're actually running a 12K axle, make sure you get the correct part number. The 10K and 12K are NOT interchangeable.

Bought a complete 10K axle from TPU for my equipment trailer when I had a hub failure. Came assembled with electric brakes, hubs, drums, even had the spring perches welded on at the right spacing. Total out-the-door was around $1,000 and I had it swapped in a Saturday afternoon. When you factor in the cost of individual Dexter hubs plus your time chasing parts, the complete axle is hard to beat.

If you do go the full axle replacement route, here's a tip from experience: before you cut off the old spring perches, mark their position on the new axle tube with a soapstone marker and double-check the spring center measurement. Measure twice, weld once. I use a fish scale to set the perch — tack it, measure spring center and verify it matches the opposite perch, then do a full weld. Use at least a 3/16" fillet weld all the way around the perch.

Another thing people don't think about — when you replace the whole axle, you also get a new axle tube that isn't fatigued or corroded. On a heavy-use trailer, the axle tube itself can develop micro-cracks over time, especially near the spring perch welds. So you're not just getting new hubs, you're getting structural peace of mind too. At the $1,000 price point for a fully assembled 10K electric brake axle, that's honestly a bargain.

At $450 per hub, the axle practically pays for itself with the brakes included as a bonus. My only regret when I did this swap was not ordering two axles at once for my tandem — I replaced one, then the other side failed six months later and I had to do the whole job again. If one hub is shot on a tandem, the other side has the same miles on it. Just saying.

title: What Is the Minimum Overhang for 10K Trailer Axles?
body: What's the minimum overhang for the 10K trailer axles? I'm trying to figure out the maximum spring center I can use for my hub face measurement.
summary: The minimum overhang for Lippert 10K trailer axles is 19.75 inches per side. For example, a 92" hub face axle could use a maximum spring center of about 72.25 inches.

comments.body: The minimum overhang for the Lippert 10K trailer axles is 19.75 inches — that comes straight from our sales rep. So for example, if you have a 92" hub face axle, then you could use a spring center up to about 72.25 inches. This is important to keep in mind so that you don't de-rate your axle by spreading the spring centers too far apart.

Can confirm the 19.75" overhang. I'm running Lippert 10K axles on a 20-foot car hauler with a 95" hub face and 72" spring center. That gives me exactly the minimum overhang and the axles are rated at full capacity. Been hauling loaded at 10K for two seasons with no issues.

The reason minimum overhang matters is structural — the unsupported length of the spindle beyond the spring seat is a cantilever. If you make that cantilever too long (by spreading the spring centers too far apart), the bending moment at the spring seat increases and the axle tube or spindle weld can fail below the rated capacity. Lippert's 19.75" is their tested limit. Going wider than that doesn't mean it'll break tomorrow, but the axle is effectively de-rated and you won't be covered under warranty.

Is the 19.75" overhang figure specific to Lippert, or is it the same for Dexter and other 10K axle manufacturers? I've got Dexter 10K axles and I want to make sure I'm not running too wide on my spring centers.

Dexter's minimum overhang for their 10K axles is in the same ballpark — roughly 18 to 20 inches depending on the specific model. I've seen Dexter spec sheets that call out 19" minimum on some and 20" on others. If you don't have the spec sheet for your exact axle, contacting the manufacturer with your axle model number is the safest bet. But 19-20" per side is a good rule of thumb across the industry for 10K rated axles.

Important clarification: the minimum overhang is measured from the CENTER of the spring seat pad to the outboard end of the spindle, not to the hub face. Hub face is measured from the mounting surface of the hub/drum on each side. The spindle extends inboard of the hub face by a few inches. So don't confuse hub face measurement with overhang — they're related but not the same reference points. If you're calculating spring center from hub face, subtract overhang from each side: spring center = hub face - (2 × overhang).

Found out the hard way about overhang when I rebuilt a flatbed and set the spring centers too wide. Was trying to get wider spring centers for stability, ended up at about 78" on a 95" hub face 10K axle. That's only about 8.5" overhang per side. The axles sagged noticeably under full load after about a year. Had to cut off the perches and reweld them at the correct spacing. Expensive lesson in not ignoring the manufacturer's specs.

If you find yourself needing wider spring centers than the minimum overhang allows on a 10K, consider stepping up to a 12K axle. The 12K has a heavier tube and longer spindles, which allows for wider spring center spacing while maintaining adequate overhang. You'll have more capacity headroom too. The cost difference between a 10K and 12K axle isn't that much — maybe $100-150 — and it gives you more flexibility in your frame design.

title: Complete 10K Trailer Axle Kits With Tires and Wheels
body: I have a trailer with 10K axles and need to get them replaced. Do you have a whole 10K axle kit that comes complete with tires and wheels?
summary: Complete 10K trailer axle kits are available with everything needed for installation, including optional tire and wheel combos. Hub face and spring center measurements are required to order.

comments.body: Yes, we sell 10K trailer kits that come complete with everything you need to install axles on your trailer, with optional tire and wheel combos included. The information we need from you is the hub face to hub face measurement and the spring center to spring center measurement in order to know which axles you need.

Quick question before I order — when they say hub face to hub face, do they mean the outer face of each hub or from the mounting flanges? I've got a 102" wide equipment trailer and want to make sure I measure right the first time.

Hub face to hub face is measured from the flat mounting surface of one hub (where the wheel bolts on) to the same point on the opposite side. Lay a straight edge across and measure center to center. Spring center is the distance between the centers of your spring mounting bolts on each side of the frame. Both measurements need to be taken with the trailer on level ground and nothing hanging off the axle. Take your time — getting it wrong means the axle won't track straight and you'll eat through tires.

I bought a complete 10K kit last spring for my flatbed gooseneck. Came with the axle, hubs, drums, electric brakes, springs, hangers, U-bolts — everything. Added the 235/80R16 tire and wheel package. Took me about 6 hours per axle to swap out working alone in my shop. The hardest part was getting the old U-bolts off because they were rusted solid. If your old ones are corroded, budget extra time or get a cutoff wheel ready.

One thing to consider: you might save a few bucks buying the axle kit and sourcing tires separately, especially if you already have wheels in good shape. 10K axles typically run 8-lug on 16" wheels with a 6.5" bolt pattern. But if your wheels are beat up or you want the convenience, the combo package is hard to argue with. Just double-check the load range on the tires — you want at least Load Range E for a 10K axle to stay within capacity.

Make sure you specify whether you need electric brakes or hydraulic disc brakes when ordering. Most 10K kits come standard with 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" electric drum brakes, but if you're running a hydraulic setup you'll want to confirm that upfront. Also, oil bath hubs are standard on most 10K kits, so if you prefer grease-packed you may need to mention that.

Just a heads up — the axle weight rating and the tire weight rating are two different things. A 10K axle can handle 10,000 lbs, but your tires have their own max load stamped on the sidewall. If you're running single tires (not duals), each tire needs to be rated for at least 5,000 lbs to match the axle. I've seen guys put Load Range D tires on 10K axles and then wonder why they're blowing tires on the highway. Don't cheap out on rubber.

Bought two complete 10K kits for a tandem gooseneck rebuild last year. Everything fit and the quality was solid. One tip: when you get your spring center measurement, measure the actual bolt hole centers on both sides and take the average. My frame was slightly off from years of welding patches and the average saved me from ordering the wrong length.

Don't forget to factor in your spring center measurement carefully. On a lot of equipment trailers the spring hangers are welded to the frame, so your spring center is fixed. If you're also replacing hangers, you've got some flexibility. Standard spring centers for 10K tandem setups are usually somewhere around 31" to 33" but it varies by manufacturer. Measure twice.

title: How to Choose the Right Trailer Hub Grease Cap by Lug Count
body: How would I know which trailer hub grease cap I need? I'm not sure what size to order for my trailer hubs.
summary: Trailer hub grease cap size is determined by the number of lugs: 5-lug hubs use a 1.98" cap, 6-lug hubs use a 2.44" cap, and 8-lug hubs use a 2.72" cap.

comments.body: The easiest way to determine which grease cap you need is by counting the number of lugs on your trailer hub: 5-Lug Hubs (2K-3.5K axles) use a 1.98" outer diameter grease cap (Part# TPU21-41). 6-Lug Hubs (5.2K-7K axles) use a 2.44" outer diameter grease cap (Part# TPU21-42). 8-Lug Hubs (8K+ axles) use a 2.72" outer diameter grease cap (Part# TPU21-43). Just count your lugs and match the diameter.
Can confirm, the lug count method is the fastest way. I've been doing trailer service for 15 years and it's never steered me wrong. Count the lugs, grab the right cap. Takes all of 30 seconds.

One thing worth noting — if your hubs have EZ Lube fittings (the zerk fitting in the center of the dust cap), you need an EZ Lube grease cap, not a standard one. They look similar but the EZ Lube version has a rubber plug in the center so you can grease without removing the cap. Same diameter sizing applies: 1.98" for 5-lug, 2.44" for 6-lug, 2.72" for 8-lug. Just check if there's a zerk hole before you order.

Learned this one the hard way. Ordered a 2.44" cap for my boat trailer thinking it was a 6-lug and it was actually a 5-lug with aftermarket spacers someone had put on years ago. Ended up with a cap rattling around inside the hub at 60 mph. Always count the actual studs pressed into the hub flange, not whatever adapters or spacers might be on there.

If your old grease cap is dented or lost and you can't count lugs for some reason, you can also just measure the hub bore directly with a caliper. The cap OD matches the hub bore: 1.98", 2.44", or 2.72". Another option is rubber hub plugs instead of metal drive-in caps — they're easier to remove for inspections and they don't require a hammer to seat. We use them on all our rental fleet trailers.
What about 4-lug hubs? I've got a small 2,000 lb utility trailer with 4 lugs and none of those sizes fit. Is there a different cap for those?

Heads up — not every 6-lug hub takes the same cap. Most standard 6-lug trailer hubs on 5.2K to 7K axles use the 2.44" cap, but some imports and oddball manufacturers use a slightly different bore. If you order a 2.44" and it's loose or doesn't seat flush, measure the bore with calipers before hammering it in. A loose grease cap will vibrate out on the road and you'll lose your grease and eventually your bearings.

title: Lippert 122-094 Brake Drum Cross Reference for 6K Axles
body: I have a Lippert brake drum with 122-094 stamped in it. Do you have a replacement for this?
summary: The Lippert 122-094 is a 6-lug hub and drum for 6,000 lb trailer axles. Direct replacements are available in stock.

comments.body: The number 122-094 stamped in your brake drum identifies it as a 6-lug hub and drum for 6,000 lb trailer axles. We have this in stock and it's a standard replacement item.

For anyone ordering the replacement for the 122-094, make sure your bearing sizes match. Standard 6K hub and drums run a 25580 inner bearing and a 15123 outer bearing. If yours uses different bearing numbers, you might have an oddball setup and should double-check before buying. The races press into the drum, so if you're reusing races from the old drum, inspect them for pitting — any scoring means replace them.
Is the 122-094 a 6 on 5.5" bolt pattern? I've got a similar Lippert drum on my cargo trailer but the bolt pattern is 6 on 5.5" and I want to make sure I grab the right one.

Just swapped out the same drum on my enclosed trailer last month. Popped the old 122-094 off, bearings were toast. New one went on in about 45 minutes per side. One thing I'll add — set the bearing preload properly when you put it back together. Tighten the castle nut to about 50 ft-lbs while spinning the hub, back it off to finger tight, then tighten to the next cotter pin slot. Loose bearings on a 6K axle will chew up the spindle.

If you're replacing the whole hub and drum assembly, check whether it comes pre-greased with bearings installed or if it's bare. Some come with bearings and seals already pressed in, which saves a bunch of time. Others ship bare and you'll need to buy bearings, races, seals, and grease separately. The 6K bearing kit for this hub is pretty standard — inner 25580/25520, outer 15123/15245 — but verify against your spindle.

Worth mentioning — if you're buying a replacement hub and drum and the old races are already pressed into the new drum, check that they're seated fully and not cocked. I've seen aftermarket drums ship with races that aren't perfectly square. A race that's sitting even slightly crooked will destroy a bearing in a few hundred miles. Tap them in with a brass drift if needed and visually check they're flush all the way around.

Another option if you're upgrading: some guys go with a galvanized hub and drum for the 6K application, especially on boat trailers or anything that sees salt water. Costs a bit more than the standard painted one but the corrosion resistance is night and day. Same bearing sizes, same bolt pattern, just a different finish. Something to think about if your trailer lives near the coast.

I've run these Lippert 6K drums on two different trailers. Solid units, no complaints. The cross-reference part numbers make ordering easy when the OEM stamp is all you've got to go on. Good straightforward swap.

title: Do Dexter and Lippert 10K and Larger Axle Parts Interchange?
body: I see where the smaller axle components interchange between Dexter and Lippert axles. What about the larger 10K and above axles — do they interchange too?
summary: Dexter and Lippert components on 10K+ axles are interchangeable as long as measurements match, including bearing sizes and brake dimensions.

comments.body: You're not going to have any problems mixing Dexter and Lippert components on trailer axles over 10K lbs in the same manner as below 10K lbs, as long as the measurements on the replacement parts are the same — meaning bearing sizes are the same, brake dimensions match, etc. This happens quite often in our shop repairs where we'll use Dexter brakes on a Lippert axle. When doing this, make sure that you're using the correct capacity components with parts that match their applications.

Done this plenty of times. Put Dexter 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" electric brakes on a Lippert 10K axle last fall. Bolt pattern on the backing plate was identical, shoes fit the drum, magnets seated fine. Couldn't tell the difference from the factory setup. The key is matching the brake shoe width and drum diameter — if those line up, you're good.

On the bearing side, both Dexter and Lippert use the same Timken-style bearing numbers for 10K axles. Inner bearing is a 28682/28622 set and outer is a 25580/25520. The seals are the same diameter too. So hubs, drums, bearings, and seals all cross-reference. Where you might run into a snag is if one brand switched to a newer style hub — Dexter did this a while back on the 10K — so just confirm you're matching old-to-old or new-to-new.
What about the backing plates themselves? If I need to swap a backing plate on a 10K Lippert axle, will a Dexter backing plate bolt right up or do I need to worry about the flange bolt pattern?

Brake magnets interchange no problem between Dexter and Lippert on 10K and up. Same mounting arm, same electrical connections. The magnets on 12-1/4" brakes are all the same footprint regardless of brand. If you're doing a brake job and can't find Lippert magnets locally, grab Dexter ones — they'll bolt right in. Just make sure you match the brake size (12-1/4" x 3-3/8" vs 12-1/4" x 5" for 12K).

One thing to watch on the bigger axles — Dexter changed from an old style to a new style hub on 10K axles a few years back. The old style has a checker-plate pattern on the hub face. If you're mixing brands, make sure both hubs on the same axle are the same style, because the inner bearing journal diameter can be slightly different between old and new. Lippert drums will fit both as long as you match the bearing set. But don't put an old style hub on one side and a new style on the other thinking they're the same.

Honestly, if you're rebuilding a whole axle or doing a major overhaul, it might be worth just going all one brand to keep things simple for future parts ordering. Mixing works fine mechanically, but down the road when you need a bearing kit or a seal, you don't want to be scratching your head about which side is Dexter and which is Lippert. Label your parts or keep a note in your maintenance log.

We run a mixed fleet — some trailers came with Lippert axles, some with Dexter. On the 10K and 12K units we stock one set of brake parts and they fit everything. Springs, hangers, equalizers all interchange too. The only time we had an issue was with a 15K axle where the spindle nut size was different between an older Lippert and a newer Dexter. But 10K and 12K have been completely plug and play for us.

Can confirm everything above. Dexter and Lippert are so interchangeable on the heavy axles that most trailer shops don't even think about it. The industry standardized the bearing sizes and brake dimensions a long time ago for 10K and up. The real question is usually just old style vs new style, not Dexter vs Lippert.

One small detail — the grease seals on 10K Dexter and Lippert hubs are the same seal, but double-check the seal number if you're running oil bath vs grease. Oil bath seals and grease seals can have different lip configurations even though the outer diameter is identical. The seal sits in the same bore but the inner lip design matters. If you're mixing brands and also switching lubrication methods at the same time, just verify the seal type matches your setup.

title: Trailer Hub Leaking Oil: Bearing Failure Causes and Prevention Tips
body: My trailer hub is leaking oil and the seal blew out after about a year of use. The bearings appear damaged. Is this a warranty issue, and what could have caused this failure?
summary: Hub oil leaks and seal blowouts are typically caused by bearing failure from oil starvation or heat buildup, not product defects. Regular oil level checks, seal inspections, heat monitoring, and staying within load ratings are essential to prevent catastrophic hub failure.

comments.body: After reviewing the damage, this is consistent with a complete bearing failure caused by oil starvation or heat-related breakdown. In oil-lubricated hubs, maintaining the correct oil level and regularly checking the cap for leaks or cracks is absolutely critical. If the hub runs low on oil or if water contamination occurs, the bearings can overheat and fail — leading to internal damage and, in severe cases, total hub separation. This type of failure doesn't happen overnight and is not related to any product defect. It's most often the result of missed maintenance or running the trailer under load for extended periods without proper inspection. To avoid this: Check oil levels regularly especially before long hauls. Inspect oil caps and seals for damage. Monitor hub temperature periodically. Stay within load ratings. This is avoidable with the right maintenance schedule.

Had almost the exact same thing happen on my tandem boat trailer. Oil cap cracked on one side, didn't notice until I smelled something burning pulling into the ramp. By then the inner bearing was blue from heat. Outer bearing was scored too. Had to replace the spindle, both bearings, the seal, and the hub. All because of a $4 oil cap. Now I check every single trip.

There are some early warning signs you can watch for before it gets this bad. If you see oil streaks running down the inside of the wheel or dripping off the backing plate, that's your seal starting to go. If the hub feels noticeably hot to the touch after a drive (too hot to hold your hand on for more than a few seconds), something is wrong — either low oil, bad bearing, or overloaded. A laser temp gun pointed at the hub after a 20-mile drive should read under 150°F in normal conditions. Anything over 180°F and you need to pull over and investigate.

How full should the oil be in an oil bath hub? I topped mine off to the fill line but I'm not sure if that's the center of the hub cap window or the top of it. Don't want to overfill and blow the seal out the other direction.

Oil level should be at the center line of the hub — basically the halfway point of the oil cap window when the trailer is sitting level. Overfilling is almost as bad as underfilling. Too much oil creates pressure inside the hub when it heats up and expands, which can push the seal out from the inside. Underfilling means the bearings aren't getting lubricated on the upper rotation. When in doubt, fill to the midpoint of the sight glass and check it again after driving 50 miles.

I inspect oil bath hubs for a living and the number one cause of failure I see is water intrusion. People submerge their hubs at boat ramps, the hub cools down, creates a vacuum, and sucks water right past the seal. That water emulsifies the oil into a milky sludge that does not lubricate. If your oil looks milky or cloudy, drain it immediately, flush with fresh oil, and replace the seal. I see this kill bearings every single summer.

Caught mine early once — noticed a very faint wobble in the wheel at highway speed. Pulled over, jacked it up, and could feel play in the bearing when I grabbed the tire at 12 and 6. Adjusted the bearing preload, topped off the oil, and it was fine. But if I'd kept driving another hundred miles it would've been a roadside catastrophe. That slight wobble is your last warning before things go south fast.

I know you asked about warranty, but realistically bearing failures from oil starvation or water contamination are maintenance issues, not defects. No manufacturer is going to warranty a hub that ran dry. I'm not being harsh, just setting expectations. The upside is that prevention is cheap — an oil cap is a few dollars, and checking your oil level takes 30 seconds. The repair after a blowout is $300+ per side and a tow bill on top of that.

An infrared thermometer is the single best $25 tool you can buy for trailer maintenance. Point it at each hub after every long drive for the first few trips, then periodically after that. You'll build a baseline for what's normal on your trailer. A hub that's suddenly 30 degrees hotter than the other side is telling you something. Don't ignore it.

If the oil bath thing makes you nervous, consider converting to grease-packed hubs. I switched both my trailers from oil to grease and honestly it's less to worry about — no fluid levels, no leaking caps, no water emulsion. You do have to repack the bearings every 12,000 miles or annually, but I'd rather do that in my shop than deal with an oil leak on the interstate. Same seals work for both on most axle sizes.

Been hauling equipment for 20 years and I do a full bearing repack or oil change every fall regardless of mileage. Pull the hubs, inspect the bearings and races under a light, clean everything, repack or refill, new cotter pins. Takes about an hour per axle once you've done it a few times. Cheap insurance compared to a wheel coming off on the highway with a loaded trailer behind you.

If your bearings are already damaged, don't just replace the bearings — inspect the spindle too. A bearing that's been running hot can gall the spindle surface. If the spindle has rough spots or discoloration where the bearing rides, the new bearing will fail prematurely. You might be able to clean it up with fine emery cloth if the damage is minor, but a badly scored spindle means replacing the whole axle or at least the spindle.

Worth adding to the maintenance list: replace your cotter pins every time you pull a hub. They're literally a penny each and they're the last line of defense keeping the castle nut from backing off. I've seen guys reuse bent cotter pins and then wonder why their wheel passed them on the highway. New pin, every time, no exceptions.

title: Can You Switch From Oil to Grease on 10K and 12K Trailer Axles?
body: I have 10K and 12K trailer axles that currently use oil bath lubrication. If I want to switch to grease instead, do I need to buy a different seal or any additional parts?
summary: Switching from oil to grease on 10K and 12K trailer axles is simple — just drain the oil and pack with grease. The seal is the same for both oil and grease applications.

comments.body: Simply drain the oil and pack the bearings with grease. The seal is the same for both oil and grease applications on 10K and 12K axles. No additional parts are needed — it's an easy and straightforward swap. Just make sure you thoroughly clean out the old oil before packing with grease, and use a high-quality bearing grease rated for trailer use.

Did this on both axles of my dump trailer about two years ago. Drained the oil, pulled the hubs, cleaned everything with brake cleaner, packed fresh grease, and buttoned it back up. Been running fine ever since. The whole job took maybe 3 hours for both sides on two axles. No different seal needed, no special parts. Straightforward as it gets.

The cleaning step is where most people cut corners and pay for it later. You need to get ALL the old oil out — out of the hub cavity, off the bearings, off the spindle, everywhere. Residual oil will thin out the grease and reduce its effectiveness. I spray everything down with brake parts cleaner, let it dry completely, then pack the bearings by hand with a quality wheel bearing grease. Push grease through from the large end of the bearing until it comes out evenly all the way around the small end. Then coat the hub cavity with a thin layer before reassembly.
How often do you need to repack the bearings once you switch to grease? With oil bath I just checked the level. Grease seems like more hands-on maintenance in the long run.

Switched my entire fleet of six trailers from oil bath to grease over the last three years. Not a single bearing issue since. My main reason was eliminating the oil leak problem — every single one of those trailers had at least one hub weeping oil at some point. With grease, I repack once a year or every 12,000 miles, whichever comes first. On 10K axles hauling near capacity, I lean toward every 10,000 miles to be safe.

One critical thing — do NOT just drain the oil and pack grease on top of whatever residue is in there. Oil and grease do not mix well. The oil will break down the grease and you'll end up with a thin slurry that doesn't protect anything. Full disassembly, full cleaning, full repack. If you're going to do this, do it right.

Counterpoint: I actually prefer oil bath on my boat trailer specifically because I'm constantly submerging the hubs at the ramp. Oil provides better protection against water intrusion in that scenario because it fills the entire cavity. With grease, water can sit in the voids between the packed grease and cause rust. If your trailer never sees water, grease is simpler. If you launch boats regularly, oil bath might actually be the better choice.

For 10K and 12K axles, use a high-temp lithium complex or synthetic bearing grease rated for at least 400°F drop point. Standard chassis grease is NOT the same thing and won't hold up under the heat and load of heavy trailer bearings. The bearing grease will be labeled for wheel bearings specifically. Costs a few dollars more per tube but it's the only thing between your bearings and failure at 65 mph.

If you want the best of both worlds after switching to grease, install Bearing Buddy–style spring-loaded caps. They maintain a slight positive pressure on the grease and keep water out. Also makes it easy to add grease through the zerk fitting without pulling the hub. I run them on my 10K axles and they've been bulletproof. Just don't overfill them — one or two pumps from a grease gun is plenty. Overpacking forces grease past the inner seal and onto your brakes.

title: How to Identify Old Style vs New Style Dexter 10K Trailer Hubs
body: I need to replace the hub on my trailer but I'm not sure what capacity it is or whether it's an old style or new style Dexter hub. How can I tell the difference?
summary: Old style Dexter 10K hubs can be identified by their checker-plated pattern and skinnier drum profile. The 10K drum uses 3-3/8 inch wide brakes, while the deeper 12K drum uses 5-inch brakes.

comments.body: Here's how to identify whether you have an old style 10K Dexter hub or something else. First, check the part number stamped on the drum — for example, a 9-44 stamp is a Dexter 9K-10K drum part number. Even without a visible part number, you can identify the hub by its appearance. Old style 10K hubs have what's called a checker-plated pattern on them. This is only found on old style 10K hubs or newer 12K axle hubs. To distinguish between the two, look at the drum: the 10K drum is skinnier because it uses a 3-3/8 inch wide brake, while the 12K drum is much deeper because it uses a 5-inch wide brake. Checker-plated hub plus skinnier drum equals old style 10K. Checker-plated hub plus deeper drum equals 12K.

Another way to tell: measure the brake shoe width through the drum opening. If the shoes are 3-3/8 inches wide, it's a 10K. If they're 5 inches wide, it's a 12K. Both can have the checker-plate hub, but the brake width is the definitive answer. You can usually eyeball it — the 12K drum is noticeably deeper and heavier. If you can't see the shoes, measure the depth of the drum interior from the hub face to the friction surface.
Where exactly is the part number stamped? I've been looking all over my drum and I can't find anything. Is it on the outside face, inside the drum, or on the hub flange?

Went through this exact confusion on my dump trailer last year. Thought I had 10K axles because the hubs had that checker-plate look. Ordered 10K brakes and they were too narrow for the drum. Turned out I had 12K axles with 5" wide brakes. The drum depth was the giveaway — those 12K drums are noticeably deeper once you know what to look for. Cost me return shipping on the wrong brake kit. Measure before you order.

The bearing numbers are different between old style and new style 10K hubs, and that matters when ordering parts. Old style 10K uses a 25580 inner and 15123 outer. New style 10K uses a 28682 inner and 25580 outer — the old outer bearing becomes the new inner bearing, and the new outer is a different size altogether. Get the bearing numbers off your current setup before ordering anything.

Small clarification — not every checker-plate hub is a 10K or 12K. Some aftermarket 8K hubs also have a similar textured pattern, though it's less common. The surest way to identify your axle capacity is to look for a tag or stamp on the axle tube itself. Most Dexter axles have the capacity stamped into the tube near the spring seat. If the tag is gone and the stamp is unreadable, then you fall back on measuring the drum and brake width as described above.

If all else fails, pull one of the bearings and look up the number. That will tell you the spindle size, which tells you the axle capacity. Dexter publishes spindle-to-capacity charts. For example, a 2-1/4" spindle with a 28682 bearing is definitively a 10K new style. It's more work than eyeballing the drum, but it's the guaranteed answer if you're unsure.

The checker plate method has always been reliable for me on Dexter hubs. Seen hundreds of them come through the shop. Skinny drum with checker plate = old 10K. Deep drum with checker plate = 12K. Smooth hub face = new style or different capacity. Pretty easy once you've seen a few side by side.

New style Dexter 10K hubs dropped the checker-plate pattern and went to a smooth cast finish. They also have a slightly larger hub bore for the new bearing configuration. If your hub has a smooth outer face and the drum measures about 3-3/8" deep on the brake surface, you've got a new style 10K. The part number stamped on these newer drums is usually easier to read — look on the outside face near the lug studs or on the inner lip of the drum.

title: How to Cross Reference a Trailer Grease Seal by Part Number
body: I have a number on a grease seal — it reads TCM171255TB. Can you tell me if you have a replacement for it?
summary: The TCM171255TB grease seal is for 3,500 lb trailer axles. The cross-reference replacement part number is 10-19.

comments.body: That seal number, TCM171255TB, is a grease seal for 3,500 lb trailer axles. Our cross-reference part number is 10-19. When looking up trailer grease seals, the numbers stamped on the seal itself can often be cross-referenced to standard trailer part numbers.

The numbers on trailer grease seals follow a pattern that's useful to know. TCM is the manufacturer (a common seal brand in the trailer industry). The digits after that typically encode the shaft diameter, bore diameter, and width. So 171255 on your seal roughly corresponds to a 1.719" shaft OD, 2.565" bore, and a specific width. Knowing this lets you cross-reference to any brand — National, SKF, or the generic trailer part numbers. Saves a lot of guesswork when the original part number is worn off.

Had an old trailer with seals so worn the numbers were completely unreadable. Took one to the parts store and they mic'd it — measured the inner diameter (shaft size), outer diameter (bore), and width, then looked it up in a cross-reference book. Came back with the same 10-19 equivalent. If your seal numbers are gone, just bring the old seal in and they can match it by dimensions.
Does it matter which direction you install the seal? There's a smooth side and a lip side on mine and I want to make sure I don't put it in backwards.

For 3,500 lb axles, the standard grease seal dimensions are 1.719" inner diameter x 2.565" outer diameter. That's the 10-19 seal. It fits Dexter, Lippert, and most other 3,500 lb trailer axles with a standard 1-1/16" x 1-3/8" spindle. If you ever need to order by dimensions instead of part number, those are the numbers you want. Other common trailer seal sizes: 10-36 for 5.2K-7K axles (2.125" x 3.376") and 10-40 for 8K axles (2.250" x 3.376").

Yes, direction matters. The seal lip — the flexible rubber edge — faces inward toward the grease. It's designed to retain lubrication and keep contaminants out. If you install it backward with the lip facing out, it won't hold grease and water will get past it easily. Most seals have the open/lip side visible before you press them in, and the flat/smooth side faces outward after installation. Tap it in evenly with a seal driver or a socket that matches the outer diameter so you don't cock it in the bore.

The 10-19 is a solid seal, been using it on all my 3,500 lb axle trailers for years with zero issues. When you press it in, put a thin coat of grease on the outer edge of the seal too — helps it seat smoothly into the hub bore and provides an initial moisture barrier. Takes two seconds and it's cheap insurance.

title: What Does Tandem Mean in Trailer Axle Terminology?
body: I keep seeing the word "tandem" when shopping for trailer axle kits and hanger kits. What exactly does tandem mean in trailer terminology?
summary: In trailer terminology, tandem simply means two. A tandem axle trailer kit includes two axles, and a tandem axle hanger kit includes all the suspension hardware needed for a two-axle setup.

comments.body: Tandem means two. So when you see a "tandem axle trailer kit," it means you are getting two axles. Similarly, if you're ordering a tandem axle hanger kit, that means it includes everything you need for a two-axle trailer setup. You'll also hear "triple axle" for three-axle setups. But tandem is by far the most common configuration for utility, car hauler, and equipment trailers.

Another way to think about it — tandem just refers to two things placed one behind the other. Same word gets used for tandem bicycles. On trailers, it means two axles inline. The big advantage over a single axle is stability, especially at highway speeds. Less sway, better weight distribution. If you're hauling over about 3500 lbs consistently, tandem is the way to go.

Ran a single 3500 lb axle on my utility trailer for years. Blew a tire on the highway once and almost lost the whole rig. Switched to a tandem setup after that. With two axles, if one tire goes flat you can usually still limp to the shoulder safely. That alone was worth the upgrade for me.

Quick question related to this — when people say "tandem axle hanger kit" does that come with the equalizer too? Or is the equalizer separate? I'm trying to price out rebuilding my suspension and want to make sure I order everything.

Yes, a tandem axle hanger kit typically includes the hangers, equalizers, and bolts for a two-axle setup. The equalizer is the rocker arm that sits between the two axles and lets the suspension flex independently. Without the equalizer, the tandem setup wouldn't work correctly because one axle would take all the impact over bumps instead of distributing the load.

One thing to keep in mind — tandem doesn't always mean better. For light loads like a small landscape trailer or a jet ski, a single axle is easier to maneuver, lighter on fuel economy, and cheaper to maintain. Half the bearings, half the brakes, half the tires. Tandem really starts making sense above about 5000 lb GVWR in my experience.

Small clarification: you'll sometimes see "tandem" used loosely by sellers to describe any multi-axle trailer, but technically tandem is specifically two axles. If it's three axles, that's a triple or tri-axle. I've seen a few eBay listings calling triple axle trailers "tandem" which just confuses people shopping for parts.

title: Will Carter 8K Brakes Fit 7200 lb Dexter Trailer Axles?
body: I have a 7200 lb Dexter trailer axle and need replacement brake assemblies. The Dexter part number I have is K23-429-00. Will Carter 8K brakes work as a replacement?
summary: Carter 8K brake assemblies (12-1/4 x 2-1/2 inch) are designed to fit both the new style 8K Dexter axles and 7200 lb Dexter axles, which share the same brake size.

comments.body: That Dexter part number is a 7200 lb brake assembly. Our Carter 8K brake assemblies — part number KC23-623 (right hand) and KC23-622 (left hand) — are 12-1/4 inch x 2-1/2 inch, made specifically for the new style 8K Dexter axles with the skinny brake as well as 7200 lb Dexter axles, which also use the same 12-1/4 x 2-1/2 inch brake size. So yes, the Carter brand will interchange perfectly and fit your 7200 lb Dexter axle. All Carter brake assemblies are self-adjusting, so you don't have to manually adjust them after installation.

Can confirm the Carter 8K brakes fit perfect on the 7200 lb Dexter. Swapped mine out last spring. Bolt pattern and drum diameter are identical. The self-adjusting feature is a nice upgrade — I used to have to crawl under and turn the star wheel adjuster every few months on the old ones.

One thing to double check before ordering — make sure you know which side is which. The right hand (KC23-623) goes on the passenger side and the left hand (KC23-622) goes on the driver side. People mix these up all the time because they think "right" and "left" refer to their perspective standing behind the trailer, but it's based on the vehicle's forward-facing orientation.

Replaced my Dexter 7200 lb brakes with the Carter 8K assemblies about 8 months ago on my enclosed landscape trailer. Over 12,000 miles on them now with zero issues. Stopping power feels the same or maybe slightly better than the factory Dexter assemblies. Installation was straightforward if you've done brake work before — maybe 45 minutes per side.

When you install new brake assemblies, make sure you also inspect the drum for scoring or a worn lip. New shoes on a scored drum will wear unevenly and you'll be right back where you started. Also worth checking your brake controller amperage output while you're at it. A lot of guys run them way too low on 7K axles and wonder why their trailer doesn't stop well.
Do I need new drums too when switching from Dexter to Carter brakes, or do the existing drums work with the Carter assemblies?

No, the existing drums are fine as long as they're not scored or worn past spec. The Carter assemblies use the same 12-1/4 x 2-1/2 inch drum as the Dexter 7200 lb. Same bolt pattern too. Just swap the backing plate assembly and you're good.

One gotcha to be aware of — the Carter 8K brakes are for the "new style" 8K Dexter axle, which uses the thinner 12-1/4 x 2-1/2 inch brake. The OLD style 8K Dexter used a 12-1/4 x 3-3/8 inch brake, which is a completely different assembly. Make sure you verify your drum size before ordering. The 7200 lb axles are all 12-1/4 x 2-1/2 so no issue there, but if you see this thread and have an older 8K Dexter, double check.

Had the same situation on my dump trailer — 7200 lb Dexter axles, needed new brakes. Went with Carter and saved a decent chunk compared to OEM Dexter pricing. Honestly couldn't tell you the difference in braking feel. They just work.

If you're already pulling the brakes apart, might be worth considering whether electric-over-hydraulic disc brakes make sense for your setup long-term. I know that's a bigger investment, but if you ever tow heavy down mountain grades, disc brakes with hydraulic actuation are a different world. Just something to think about for the future.

title: Why Are Trailer Tires Listed by Specs Instead of Brand Name?
body: I noticed your website doesn't list specific tire brand names on the trailer tires you sell. Why is that?
summary: Trailer tire manufacturers sometimes stamp different brand names on the same tire across production runs. Tires are listed by specifications instead of brand to avoid confusion.

comments.body: Because the manufacturer doesn't always send us the same brand name tire. They are the exact same tire but stamped with different names at times when we receive them from the factory. Rather than listing a brand and having customers think they received the wrong product, we list tires by their specifications — size, load range, ply rating, and construction type. The tires come from the same factory, are rated for the same weight, are the same size, and have the same specs. The only difference is the name branded on the sidewall.

Makes total sense. I've ordered the same tire size three different times from different suppliers and gotten Loadstar, Kenda, and one with a brand I'd never heard of. All had the same load range, same ply, same size. Couldn't tell the difference once they were on the trailer.

This is actually common across the whole trailer tire industry, not just one supplier. Trailer tires are ST rated (Special Trailer), and the factories that produce them often make the same tire under multiple brand labels. What actually matters is the size like ST225/75R15, the load range (C, D, E), and the ply rating. Those determine how much weight the tire can handle — the brand name on the sidewall doesn't change the construction.

Learned this the hard way years ago. Ordered a specific brand from a different supplier, complained when I got a different name on the sidewall. Supplier showed me they were literally the same tire from the same factory. Same DOT number prefix and everything. Now I just buy by size and load range and don't stress about the name stamped on them.
So if the brand doesn't really matter, what should I actually focus on when comparing trailer tires? Just load range and size? What about radial vs bias ply — does that make a real difference?

Radial vs bias is probably the biggest real decision you'll make on trailer tires. Radial (the "R" in the size code, like ST225/75R15) runs cooler at highway speeds, lasts longer, and gives a smoother ride. Bias ply has stiffer sidewalls, which some guys prefer for load stability, and they're usually cheaper upfront. For highway towing I'd go radial every time. For short-distance stuff around a property or farm, bias ply works fine and saves money.

One thing people get wrong — trailer tires are NOT interchangeable with passenger car or light truck tires even if the size looks similar. ST tires have reinforced sidewalls designed for the vertical load and lateral stresses specific to trailers. Putting a P-rated or LT-rated tire on a trailer is asking for a blowout because the construction isn't designed for how trailers load and flex. Always stick with ST rated.

Also worth checking — the date code on the sidewall matters more than the brand. Look for the DOT stamp, the last four digits tell you the week and year of manufacture. For example, "2423" means week 24 of 2023. Even if a tire has never been used, I wouldn't put one on that's more than 5-6 years old. Rubber degrades from UV and ozone exposure even sitting in a warehouse.

title: Will 8K Trailer Axles Fit My Frame? Backing Plate Clearance Guide
body: I want to purchase an 8K tandem axle kit but need to make sure the axles are wide enough to fit my trailer. My frame is 83 inches wide. What are the backing plate to backing plate measurements on the 95-inch and 97-inch hub face 8K axles?
summary: For an 83-inch wide trailer frame, the 97-inch hub face 8K axle with 80-inch spring center is the recommended choice. The 95-inch hub face 8K axle measures 83-3/8 inches backing plate to backing plate.

comments.body: Typically, if you have an 83-inch frame, you would use an 80-inch spring center. In that case, you would need to purchase the 8K axle with the 97-inch hub face. If you purchased the 95-inch hub face axle instead, the brake flange to brake flange measurement is 85-1/4 inches, and the actual backing plate to backing plate (the measurement that matters for frame clearance) is 83-3/8 inches. So with an 83-inch frame, the 95-inch hub face 8K axle would be extremely tight. The 97-inch hub face with 80-inch spring center would be the safer choice.

The answer above is spot on. I have an 83-inch frame on my flatbed and went with the 97-inch hub face 8K axles with 80-inch spring centers. Fit perfectly with about an inch of clearance between the backing plates and the frame rails on each side. If I'd gone 95-inch hub face it would've been touching.

Here's a quick reference I keep for 8K axle fitment:

- 95" hub face with 74" spring center = backing plate to backing plate roughly 83-3/8"
- 97" hub face with 80" spring center = backing plate to backing plate roughly 85-3/8"

You want at least 1-2 inches of clearance between the backing plates and the inside of the frame rails. With an 83" frame, the 97" hub face gives you that margin comfortably.

A buddy of mine tried to squeeze 95-inch hub face axles under an 83-inch frame. The backing plates were touching the frame on one side right out of the gate. When the suspension flexed even slightly going over bumps, the plates would grind against the steel. He ended up having to cut and reweld the frame wider by 2 inches per side, which was way more work and money than just ordering the right axle to begin with.

Don't forget to account for tire clearance too, not just backing plates. With 8K axles you're probably running 16-inch wheels with ST235/80R16 tires or similar. Make sure you have enough room between the tire sidewall and the frame rail at full suspension compression. I like to see at least 1.5 inches of clearance at full bump. Load the trailer to max weight and measure before you call it done.
What about the 89-inch hub face option for 8K axles? I've seen some listings with that measurement. Does that just have a shorter spring center, or is it a completely different axle tube?

The 89-inch hub face is a real option. It would typically use a shorter spring center around 72 inches. That's designed for narrower frames, like some boat trailers and smaller enclosed trailers in the 72-78 inch frame width range. Same axle capacity, just a narrower track width. Make sure your wheel and tire combo still clears the frame at that width.

One thing I see people confuse constantly — "hub face" and "spring center" are two completely different measurements. Hub face is the distance from the outside face of one hub to the outside face of the other hub. Spring center is the distance between the spring mounting pads welded on the axle beam. You need both numbers to figure out if an axle fits your trailer. Don't mix them up when ordering or you'll get the wrong axle.

If you're right on the edge measurement-wise, I've seen people use spacer plates between the springs and the axle to nudge positioning slightly. But honestly, it's better to just order the correct hub face measurement from the start. Spacers add variables, can change your ride height, and if they shift under load you've got a tracking problem.

For anyone reading this and trying to measure their own frame — measure the INSIDE width between the frame rails, not the outside. That inside dimension is what matters for backing plate clearance. I've seen guys measure outside-to-outside and end up 4-5 inches off because they forgot to subtract the rail thickness on both sides.

title: Complete Trailer Axle Maintenance Schedule: Bearings, Brakes, and More
body: I just purchased new Carter trailer axles. Do you have a recommended maintenance schedule for them, like when to add oil, repack bearings, and general upkeep?
