summary: Trailer axle maintenance requires checking bearings and lubrication every 6-12 months or 3,000-12,000 miles, with more frequent service for heavy use or marine environments.

comments.body: Trailer axle maintenance requires checking bearings and grease every 6-12 months or 3,000-12,000 miles, with more frequent service for heavy use or marine environments. Monthly or before each trip: check tire pressure, tire wear, and lug nut torque. Every 3 months or 3,000 miles for heavy use: inspect brakes, grease hubs, and check for worn suspension parts. Every 6 months or 6,000 miles: inspect axle beam for damage, check for loose bolts, and check brake magnets and shoes. Annually or 12,000 miles: fully repack wheel bearings, inspect bearing condition, replace grease seals, and adjust brakes. Use high-quality grease and avoid mixing different types. Boat trailers require more frequent lubrication. For newly purchased trailers, check lug nuts and suspension bolts after the first 50 miles of use.

Solid maintenance guide. I'd add one thing — if your axles use oil bath hubs instead of grease-packed, check the oil level through the sight glass on the cap every time you hook up. Takes five seconds and can save you from a burned bearing. The oil should be visible at about the halfway mark on the sight glass when the trailer is level.

I pull my boat trailer through saltwater ramps about 20 times a season. I repack bearings every spring and do a visual inspection mid-summer. Saltwater is absolutely brutal on bearings and seals. My first year with the boat I skipped the mid-season check and had a bearing seize on I-95 coming back from the coast. Smoke pouring off the hub, had to get towed. Never skipped it again.

One maintenance item that gets overlooked — the leaf springs themselves. Check them for cracks, separation between leaves, and sagging. A cracked spring won't fail all at once. It'll gradually sag to one side and cause uneven tire wear on that axle. I check mine visually every time I change oil on the truck, roughly every 5,000 miles.

What type of grease do you guys recommend for repacking wheel bearings? I've been using regular automotive wheel bearing grease from the parts store but someone told me I should be using marine-grade grease since my trailer sits outside uncovered.

For any trailer that sees water or sits outside year-round, use a marine-grade wheel bearing grease. It has much better water washout resistance than standard automotive grease. Most guys I know use Lucas Marine Grease or Royal Purple Marine — just make sure whatever you pick is NLGI #2 rated for wheel bearing use. And the critical thing: never mix different grease types or brands in the same hub. If you're switching, clean out all the old grease completely first.

I haul horses about 15,000 miles a year with a gooseneck. I do a full bearing repack every 10,000 miles and inspect brakes at the same time. Caught a cracked brake magnet last year during a routine check that could've left me with no brakes on the rear axle at highway speed with 4,000 lbs of horses behind me. Boring work but it absolutely pays off.

Something easy to forget — check your brake wiring connections for corrosion, especially at the axle-to-frame junction where the plug connectors are. Those are exposed to road spray, mud, and salt and they corrode over time. A corroded connection means weak or zero braking force on that axle. I clean mine and apply dielectric grease every spring.

Want to clarify something from the original answer — the "check after first 50 miles" advice applies to ALL fasteners on a new trailer, not just lug nuts. That includes U-bolts, hanger bolts, spring bolts, equalizer bolts, and tie plate bolts. Everything settles and loosens slightly during initial break-in. I've seen equalizer bolts back out on brand new trailers because nobody retorqued after the first few trips. It's a 15-minute job that prevents real problems.

If you're tired of repacking bearings every year, consider upgrading to oil bath hubs. The conversion kit isn't cheap upfront but maintenance drops way down — just check the oil level regularly and do a full oil change once a year. I switched both axles on my travel trailer to oil bath and it's been so much less hassle, especially for long highway trips from the Midwest to Florida and back.

For guys running dump trailers or anything with hydraulics — add checking your hydraulic fluid level and cylinder pins to your regular maintenance routine. Those pins wear over time, and if one fails mid-dump you've got a dangerous situation. A five-minute check every 3 months takes almost no effort.

Tire pressure is honestly the most neglected maintenance item I see. People check it once when they buy the trailer and never again. Under-inflated ST tires on a trailer generate excess heat and cause blowouts, and trailer tire blowouts at 65 mph can rip your fender off or worse. I keep a dedicated tire pressure gauge in the truck and check cold pressure before every trip. The correct PSI is molded into the tire sidewall — don't rely on a placard that might be wrong or missing.

Learned the hard way about lug nut torque. Threw a wheel on the highway because I hand-tightened the lugs after a roadside flat change and forgot to go back with the torque wrench. Luckily it bounced into a ditch and didn't hit anyone. Now I carry a torque wrench in every truck. Most 1/2-inch trailer lug nuts torque to 90-120 ft-lbs depending on the stud size — check your axle manufacturer's spec.

title: Carter Aluminum Oil Cap Replacement for Dexter 10K Plastic Caps
body: I have a 2021 model trailer with Dexter 10K axles and the factory plastic oil cap (part number 21-88). Does the Carter forged aluminum oil cap fit as a direct replacement?
summary: The Carter 10K forged aluminum oil cap (KC21-302) is a direct replacement for the Dexter 21-88 plastic oil cap, Dexter Fortress caps, and Valcrum caps.

comments.body: Yes, the Carter 10K forged aluminum oil cap fits and replaces the Dexter part number 21-88 plastic oil cap perfectly. The correct Carter part number is KC21-302. This aluminum oil cap also replaces the Dexter Fortress caps and Valcrum caps. The forged aluminum construction is significantly more durable than the factory plastic caps and provides a better, longer-lasting seal. It's a direct bolt-on replacement — no modifications needed.

Installed two of these on my 10K Dexter axles last month. The KC21-302 drops right in where the plastic 21-88 cap was. Fit is tight and clean. The aluminum feels way more substantial in your hand — the factory plastic caps always felt like they'd crack if you overtightened them even slightly.

The plastic Dexter caps on my enclosed trailer cracked twice in two years. The second time I lost oil on the highway and didn't notice until I smelled burning from the hub. Caught it before the bearing fully went but it was close. Switched to the Carter aluminum caps after that and haven't had a single issue in over a year of regular use.

When you swap to the aluminum cap, take a minute to clean the hub face where the cap seats. Any old sealant, road grime, or corrosion on that surface can prevent a proper seal. I wipe mine down with brake cleaner and then apply a thin bead of RTV silicone around the cap edge before pressing it in. Belt and suspenders approach, but zero leaks so far.
Do these aluminum oil caps work with the EZ Lube spindle setup? My Dexter 10K axles have the grease fitting on the end of the spindle and I'm not sure if the oil bath cap is compatible with that.

Oil bath caps and EZ Lube caps are two completely different systems. If your hubs are set up for EZ Lube grease, you need a grease cap, not an oil bath cap. The KC21-302 is specifically for oil bath hubs. Easy way to tell — if your current cap has a sight glass or fill plug, it's oil bath. If it just has a rubber plug or dust cap with a zerk fitting on the spindle, that's EZ Lube. Don't mix them up.

If the plastic caps keep cracking and you don't want to spend the money on aluminum, the Dexter Fortress caps are a harder plastic with a reinforced metal ring that holds up better than the standard 21-88. But honestly for the $10-15 difference per cap, the Carter forged aluminum is the better long-term investment. You'll never replace them.

Make sure when you order the KC21-302 that you confirm it's the 10K version. Carter makes aluminum oil caps for 8K, 7K, and other axle sizes too, and they look very similar but have different diameters. The 10K cap won't fit an 8K hub and vice versa. Ask me how I know — had to eat return shipping on a pair because I grabbed the wrong ones.

title: What Is the Offset on Standard Trailer Wheels?
body: What is the offset of common trailer wheels? I want to make sure I'm getting the right fitment for my trailer.
summary: Most standard single trailer wheels have a zero (0) offset, meaning the wheel is centered with equal distance on both sides of the hub mounting surface.

comments.body: Zero offset is the most common on all single trailer wheels. That means the wheel is centered in the middle, so you have the same distance both forward and backward on the hub — or in other words, in and out of the hub. This is standard across most trailer wheel sizes.

Yep, zero offset is standard. Been working with trailer parts for a long time and I've yet to see a factory single trailer wheel that's anything other than zero offset. Keeps the hub loads balanced and makes fitment straightforward across different axle brands.

Zero offset means the mounting surface of the wheel sits exactly at the centerline between the inner and outer bead seats. On passenger vehicles you see positive and negative offsets to accommodate suspension geometry, but trailers don't need that — the axle spindle dictates everything. Zero offset keeps even loading on the bearings and centers the tire in the fender opening.

What about dual wheel setups? I've got a tandem axle trailer and I'm thinking about converting to dually configuration for more load capacity. Do the inner and outer wheels both need to be zero offset, or does one need to be different?

For dual wheel setups, the inner wheel is typically a standard zero-offset wheel mounted normally. The outer wheel gets mounted using a wheel adapter or spacer that provides the correct spacing between the two rims. Some dual wheel conversion kits specify their own offset for the outer wheel, so you'd need to match whatever the adapter manufacturer recommends for your bolt pattern and hub.

I want to clarify that zero offset on trailer wheels is a simpler concept than offset on car wheels, even though the term is the same. On a car, offset affects scrub radius and handling dynamics. On a trailer, it just means the mounting flange is centered in the wheel. But be careful with cheap import wheels sold online as "trailer wheels" — some actually have a slight positive offset. If you're buying from an unknown source, measure before you mount.

Bought budget trailer wheels online once that were listed as zero offset. Turns out they were about half an inch positive. Didn't realize until I noticed the inside edges of my tires wearing faster than the outside. The bearings probably weren't thrilled about the uneven loading either. Ended up replacing them after one season. Lesson learned — buy from a reputable trailer parts supplier.

For anyone trying to measure offset on a wheel they already have — lay it face down on a flat surface, put a straight edge across the back lip, and measure from the straight edge down to the hub mounting face. Then flip the wheel and measure the same way from the front. If both measurements are equal, it's zero offset. If the back measurement is larger, it's positive offset. Simple check that takes two minutes.

If you ever need to push the wheel out slightly for fender clearance, hub-centric wheel spacers are an option. But use ones specifically rated for trailer use, not the universal ones from the auto parts store. And make sure your wheel studs are still long enough for full thread engagement on the lug nuts after adding the spacer. I've seen guys run spacers and only get 3-4 turns on the nut — that's asking for a wheel to come off.

title: Al-Ko K08-490-90 Hub Drum Replacement Cross Reference for 10K Axles
body: Do you have the K08-490-90 hub drum kit? I have a 10K heavy duty axle and need a compatible replacement.
summary: The K08-490-90 is an Al-Ko/Hayes 10K heavy duty hub drum kit. Rockwell part number 120865-1P475A is a direct replacement with 8x6.5" bolt pattern and 5/8" studs.

comments.body: Yes, the part number you referenced is a hub drum kit — the K08-490-90 is for the Al-Ko and Hayes 10K heavy duty #120 spindle axle with electric or hydraulic brakes, 4.7" pilot and 5/8" studs x 18. The Al-Ko part number for the 4.75" hub and drum is 568273, and the 4.88" version is 568270. The Hayes part number for the 4.75" hub drum is 09080587. We stock the Rockwell 10K Heavy Duty Hub & Drum, part number 120865-1P475A (8x6.5" bolt pattern, 5/8" studs, hub drum only) or the 120865-1P475A-C which is the complete kit. This Rockwell hub and drum will directly replace the Al-Ko K08-490-90.

I swapped out the Al-Ko K08-490-90 on my 10K tandem last fall with the Rockwell 120865-1P475A and it bolted right up. Same 8x6.5 bolt pattern, same 5/8" studs. Only thing I'll mention is double-check your pilot diameter — the 4.75" and 4.88" versions look almost identical but you don't want to force-fit the wrong one onto your spindle.

One thing the answer doesn't mention — when you get the Rockwell hub drum, make sure you also pick up the correct grease seal. The Al-Ko seal and the Rockwell seal aren't always the same part number even though the hub is a direct swap. On the 10K HD spindle you'll want a 10-36 seal. Ask me how I know… had to make a second trip to get the right one.

Quick question for anyone who's done this swap — does the Rockwell hub drum come with new races pressed in, or do you need to press your own? My old Al-Ko hub had the races pretty well seized in there and I had to use a drift punch to knock them out.

Confirmed, the Rockwell complete kit (120865-1P475A-C) comes with races already pressed in plus bearings, seal, and cap. If you're just getting the hub drum only (120865-1P475A) you'll need to press your own races. For the 10K HD spindle the bearing combo is typically 25580 inner and 14125A outer but verify against your spindle. The complete kit is worth the extra cost if you're doing a full rebuild anyway.

I run 10K Al-Ko axles on my car hauler and went through this exact cross-reference headache last year. The Hayes 09080587 is the same hub too if you can find one, but the Rockwell seems to be more widely stocked. Made sure to torque my lug nuts to 120 ft-lbs after the swap and re-torqued after 50 miles. No issues at all through about 8,000 miles now.

If you can't find the Rockwell in stock, another option is to have your existing Al-Ko hub drum re-machined if the drum surface is still within spec. A local brake shop can turn the drum for about $30-40 per side. Only makes sense if the drum isn't cracked or worn past the max diameter stamped on it. But if you need new bearings and seals anyway, a fresh hub drum kit is the better move.

Just a heads up for anyone doing this on a trailer with hydraulic surge brakes — when you pull the old hub drum off, inspect the brake shoes and the backing plate while you're in there. The 10K HD drums are thick and heavy, and if your brake shoes are down to 1/16" or less it's not worth putting a new drum on old shoes. I usually do shoes and hardware at the same time if I'm already tearing into it.

title: Lippert 295924 Seal Replacement for 12K to 16K Trailer Axles
body: Do you have the Lippert 295924 seal? I need a replacement for my heavy duty trailer axle.
summary: The Lippert 295924 is a seal for 12K-16K trailer axles. The 10-56 seal is a direct cross-reference replacement.

comments.body: Yes, the Lippert 295924 is a seal for 12K through 16K trailer axles. You can use the 10-56 seal in place of the Lippert 295924 — it's a direct replacement.

The 10-56 seal is definitely the correct cross for the Lippert 295924. I've installed probably 50 of these on 12K and 15K Lippert axles. One thing to be aware of — make sure you install it with the lip facing inward toward the bearings. The seal lip should ride on the spindle journal surface. If you flip it the wrong way it won't retain grease and you'll cook your bearings in short order.

Replaced both seals on my 16K Lippert axles last month using the 10-56. They press right in with a seal driver or a piece of PVC pipe that matches the outer diameter. Don't use a hammer directly on the seal face — you'll distort it. I use a 3" PVC coupling as a makeshift driver and it works perfectly every time.

While you're in there replacing the seal, it's worth inspecting the spindle surface where the seal lip rides. If there's a groove worn into the spindle from the old seal, the new one will just leak in the same spot. You can get a speedi-sleeve to go over a grooved spindle — it gives the new seal a fresh surface to ride on. Saved me from having to replace an entire spindle on a 15K axle.

Does anyone know if the 10-56 seal works on the Lippert 10K axles too, or is it strictly for the 12K-16K range? My Lippert 10K uses a different part number on the seal and I want to make sure I'm not mixing things up.

No, the 10-56 is specifically for the 12K through 16K Lippert axle spindle diameter. The 10K Lippert axles use a smaller spindle and a different seal — usually a 10-40 or 10-36 depending on the specific 10K model. The spindle OD is different so even though they look similar they're not interchangeable. Always match the seal to your spindle diameter.

If you're doing seals you might as well do the full bearing and seal kit. Saves you from tearing it apart again in 6 months if a bearing starts going. The kits for 12K-16K Lippert axles usually include inner and outer bearings, races, seal, cotter pin, and spindle nut. Costs maybe $25-30 more than just the seal alone and gives you peace of mind.

title: Is the CoPartner ST225/75R15 12-Ply Tire Good for Aluminum Trailers?
body: Would the CoPartner ST225/75R15 12-ply trailer tire be suitable for an aluminum trailer? Or is the CoPartner tire more of a semi truck tire? I currently have Westlake 225/75R15 tires on my trailer.
summary: The CoPartner ST225/75R15 12-ply tire works great on aluminum trailers. It's a heavy duty Load Range F all-steel tire that handles loads and road conditions better than standard options.

comments.body: The CoPartner tire would work great on aluminum trailers. It's a heavy duty tire, Load Range F, and it's all steel construction so it's going to handle your loads and road conditions much better and last quite a bit longer than a standard trailer tire. It's an excellent upgrade from the Westlake tires.

I've been running the CoPartner ST225/75R15 Load Range F on my 24-foot aluminum enclosed for about 12,000 miles now. They ride noticeably smoother than the Westlakes I had before, and the all-steel construction gives me a lot more confidence towing on the interstate at 65 mph. The sidewalls are much stiffer so you don't get that sway feeling when a semi passes you. Definitely not a semi truck tire — the ST designation means it's purpose-built for trailer use.

Just to clarify for anyone confused — "ST" stands for Special Trailer. These are specifically designed for trailer axle loads and tracking characteristics. They're NOT the same as LT (Light Truck) tires. The CoPartner ST225/75R15 is engineered for trailer duty with stiffer sidewalls and different tread compounds than what you'd put on a truck. Load Range F means 12-ply rating which handles 2,830 lbs per tire at 80 PSI.

What PSI are you guys running these at? I know Load Range F is rated to 80 PSI but I've heard some people running them lower for a softer ride on aluminum trailers. Worried about running too low and generating excess heat.

Run them at the max PSI on the sidewall — 80 PSI for Load Range F. Trailer tires aren't like truck tires where you can air down for comfort. Underinflating a trailer tire is the fastest way to a blowout because they generate way more heat when underinflated. The stiff sidewall is a feature, not a bug. I check mine with a quality gauge before every trip.

I switched from Westlake to CoPartner on my aluminum boat trailer and the difference is night and day. The Westlakes started showing sidewall cracking after about 2 years regardless of tread wear. I'm 18 months into the CoPartners and no cracking, no cupping, even tread wear across all four. The all-steel belts really do make a difference in longevity.

Something to keep in mind with the 12-ply on an aluminum trailer — the stiffer tire might transmit more vibration to the trailer frame compared to an 8-ply or 10-ply. On a steel frame trailer you'd never notice, but aluminum can ring a bit more. That said I still think it's worth it for the load capacity and durability. Just make sure your cargo is secured well because the ride is a touch firmer.

If you're on the fence between the CoPartner and other brands in that size, the Taskmaster is another solid all-steel option in the ST225/75R15 Load Range F. Slightly different tread pattern but similar specs. The CoPartner tends to be a few bucks cheaper per tire from what I've seen. Both are miles ahead of the basic Westlakes.

Ran Westlakes on two different trailers and had sidewall failures on both within 3 years. Switched everything over to all-steel 12-ply tires and haven't had a single issue in 4+ years. The CoPartner is a legit tire for the money. One tip — if you're storing your aluminum trailer outside, get some tire covers. UV is what kills trailer tires more than anything, even the good ones.

I'll add that if you're upgrading to the 12-ply Load Range F from a lower ply rating, double check that your wheels are rated for 80 PSI. Some older aluminum trailer wheels were only rated for 65 PSI max which matches Load Range D or E tires. Putting 80 PSI into a 65 PSI rated wheel is asking for trouble. The wheel should have a max PSI stamped or stickered on it somewhere.

Strongly recommend picking up a TPMS (tire pressure monitoring system) if you're running Load Range F tires. At 80 PSI you really want to know immediately if you start losing pressure. A slow leak at highway speed on a trailer tire can go from "low pressure" to "shredded tire" in minutes. I use a basic 4-sensor TPMS that reads out in the cab and it's saved me twice now.

title: Can You Custom Build a Trailer Axle to My Specifications?
body: My trailer axle has a 41.5" spring center. Do you custom build axles to non-standard measurements?
summary: Custom trailer axles are available and typically take 3-7 weeks to manufacture. You'll need to call in with your exact specifications to place a custom order.

comments.body: Yes, we do custom build trailer axles. Custom axles typically take 3-7 weeks to manufacture. We would need you to call us with your exact specifications so we can get the order placed correctly. If your spring center or hub face measurements don't match our standard sizes, a custom order is the way to go.

Before you go the custom route, have you verified that 41.5" isn't close enough to a standard size? Common spring centers are 33", 34", 35", 40", 42", 46", and 50". If you're measuring center-to-center of the spring seats and getting 41.5", it might be worth double-checking — sometimes the measurement is off by a bit if the tape isn't perfectly centered on the spring pads. A half inch can be the difference between custom and off-the-shelf.

I ordered a custom axle about two years ago for a specialty lowboy trailer with a 37" spring center. The process was pretty straightforward — called in, gave them my spring center, hub face, axle capacity, brake type, bolt pattern, and spindle size. Took about 5 weeks to get it. Fit perfectly. The wait is the hardest part but if your measurements are truly non-standard there's really no other option.

Another option if you're handy with a welder — you could move your spring hanger brackets to match a standard axle size. If your hangers are bolt-on that's even easier. Depends on whether you'd rather wait 3-7 weeks for a custom axle or spend a weekend repositioning hangers. On some trailers moving the hangers is actually simpler, especially if the frame is straight and you can just re-drill.

What capacity axle do you need? That'll affect lead time and cost quite a bit. A custom 3,500 lb axle is a lot simpler and cheaper than a custom 7K or 10K. Also, are you running electric brakes or no brakes? And what bolt pattern — 5 lug, 6 lug, 8 lug? The more info you have ready when you call in, the faster the order goes.

Just a word of caution from experience — when you give them your spring center measurement, measure it three times from different reference points. I ordered a custom axle once, was off by 3/4 of an inch on my measurement, and had to wait another month for the correct one. Custom axles are typically non-returnable since they're built to your spec. Measure center-to-center of the spring seat pads, not the edges.

Had a custom 7K built with a 38" spring center for a dump trailer conversion. Total cost was about 15-20% more than the equivalent standard axle. The 3-7 week window is accurate — mine came in right at 4 weeks. They welded the spring seats exactly where I specified. One thing I'd recommend: also specify your hub face measurement so the overall axle width matches your fenders and tire clearance.

If you end up going custom, make sure to specify whether you need straight axle or cambered. Most trailer axles have a slight upward camber so they flatten out under load. A straight axle will bow downward when loaded. Also specify drop or no-drop on the spindles if that matters for your ride height. These are details that can get overlooked on a custom order and they'll build exactly what you tell them.

I'll second what others said about triple-checking measurements. But also — take a photo of your current axle setup showing the spring seats, spindle type, and brake backing plates before you call. It helps the sales team verify you're ordering the right config. I've seen guys order electric brake axles when they needed hydraulic, or get the wrong spindle for their existing hubs. A photo saves everyone headaches.

title: What Size Axles Does a Kaufman 20K Car Hauler Use?
body: I have a Kaufman car hauler with 20K capacity. It has two 10,000 lb axles but I don't know the measurements. What would the typical specs be?
summary: Most Kaufman car haulers with 10K axles use a 70" hub face with 42" spring center, but you should always measure your axle to confirm before ordering.

comments.body: I see a lot of Kaufman trailers using the 10K axle with a 70" hub face and 42" spring center. But as always, I would recommend measuring your axle yourself to ensure we get you the correct replacement axles. The spring center measurement is especially important to get right.

I have a 2019 Kaufman 20K car hauler and can confirm — mine came with 10K axles, 70" hub face, 42" spring center. Electric brakes on both axles, 8 on 6.5" bolt pattern with 1/2" studs. That said, Kaufman has used slightly different specs over the years depending on the model and production run, so definitely measure yours to be safe.

Have you tried contacting Kaufman directly with your VIN? They can usually pull up the exact axle specs for your specific trailer. Their customer service is pretty responsive. That way you don't have to guess — you'll know the exact spring center, hub face, spindle size, bearing numbers, everything. Saves you from measuring and potentially getting it wrong.

Here's how to measure if you want to verify yourself: Spring center is measured from the center of one spring mounting pad to the center of the other. Hub face is measured from the face of one hub (where the wheel mounts) to the face of the other hub on the opposite side. You'll need a long tape measure or a straight edge and tape for the hub face. Do it on level ground with the trailer unhitched and sitting on jack stands.

I haul cars on a Kaufman and one thing I'll mention — some of the older Kaufman 20K models used a slightly shorter spring center, like 40" instead of 42". If your trailer is pre-2015 or so, don't assume it's 42". Even a 2" difference on the spring center means the axle won't bolt in. The 70" hub face has been pretty consistent across Kaufman though.

Does your Kaufman have electric brakes or hydraulic disc brakes? Some of the newer 20K Kaufman haulers come with hydraulic disc setups. That changes what you need to order for replacement axles since the spindles and mounting hardware are different between electric drum and hydraulic disc. Check if you see a brake line running to each wheel or just an electrical wire.

Bought replacement 10K axles for my Kaufman about a year ago. The 70" hub face / 42" spring center combo was spot on for my 2020 model. I went with electric brake axles with the 8x6.5 bolt pattern. Everything lined up with the existing spring hangers and brake wiring. Took me about 4 hours per axle to swap with a floor jack, jack stands, and basic hand tools. Not a bad weekend project if you're mechanically inclined.

One more measurement to grab while you're under there — the spindle length and diameter. On most Kaufman 10K axles you'll find the standard 2" round spindle with a 10" overall spindle length. This matters because it determines which bearings and hubs fit. If you can pull a hub and read the bearing numbers off the old ones, that's the most foolproof way to confirm you're ordering the right setup.

I made the mistake of ordering axles based on what I "thought" my Kaufman specs were without measuring. Ended up with a spring center that was 2 inches off. Lesson learned — always crawl under there with a tape measure. It takes 10 minutes and saves you the hassle of returning an axle and waiting for the correct one. The spring center measurement is king.

title: Which Trailer Axle Measurement Matters Most: Spring Center or Hub Face?
body: I have three Load Rite trailers that need new axles. The hub face measurements are all different but the spring centers are all 70". Does it matter that the hub faces are different, or does only the spring center measurement really matter?
summary: The spring center measurement is the most critical and must be exact since it determines how the axle bolts into your existing spring hangers. Hub face can vary slightly and still work fine.

comments.body: The most important measurement is the spring center measurement — that has to be accurate. The hub face measurement can vary a little bit and still work out just fine, but the spring center needs to be exact so it will bolt back into your existing spring hangers that are welded on the trailer. Always get the spring center right first, then confirm the hub face is close.

The accepted answer is right — spring center is the measurement that has to be dead-on because those spring hangers are welded to the frame and you can't easily move them. Hub face affects your overall track width, meaning how far your tires stick out or tuck in relative to the fenders. A half inch difference on hub face usually just means the tire sits a quarter inch further in or out on each side, which is rarely an issue. But if your spring center is off even an inch, the bolt holes won't line up.

Learned this one the hard way on a utility trailer rebuild. Ordered an axle with the right hub face but wrong spring center. The axle physically wouldn't drop into the spring hangers — the mounting eyes were about 1.5" off from where they needed to be. Had to send it back and wait two weeks for the correct one. Now I always measure spring center first, hub face second.

On your Load Rite trailers — how different are the hub face measurements? If they're all within an inch or two of each other, you might be able to order one standard axle that works across all three. The spring center being the same (70") is good news. A slightly different hub face might just mean your wheel track is a touch wider or narrower on one trailer vs another, which is usually fine as long as the tires clear the fenders.

To put some numbers on it — most axle manufacturers consider hub face to be within spec if it's plus or minus about 1" from what you order. So if you order a 74" hub face axle, you might get one that measures 73.5" or 74.5" and that's considered normal. Spring center though? That needs to be exact to the half inch at most. If your hangers are at 70" spring center, order 70" spring center.

One scenario where hub face does matter a lot: if you're running tandem axles and the hub faces are significantly different between the two, your tires won't track straight. The front axle tires will be at a different width than the rear axle tires. On a single axle trailer it matters less, but on a tandem you really want both axles to have matching hub face measurements or you'll get uneven tire wear and weird handling.

Here's how I measure spring center to make sure I get it right every time: put a mark at the exact center of each spring mounting pad on the axle tube. Then measure from mark to mark. That's your spring center. Don't measure from the edge of the pad — measure from center to center. On a lot of axles the pads are about 2" wide, so measuring edge-to-edge vs center-to-center could throw you off by an inch or more.

Also worth noting — on some Load Rite boat trailers I've seen, the original axles were Torflex (torsion) style which don't have a traditional spring center measurement at all. If any of your three trailers use torsion axles, you need the start-to-start measurement of the torsion arm brackets instead. Different measurement entirely. Just making sure we're comparing apples to apples here.

The thing that can bite you with hub face being too far off is fender clearance. If the hub face is significantly wider than the original, your tires might rub or stick out past the fenders which could be a DOT issue depending on your state. If it's significantly narrower, you might have clearance issues with the frame or suspension components. So while it doesn't need to be exact, you don't want it wildly different either — try to stay within 2" of the original.

Had a similar situation with three landscape trailers all needing axles. All had 62" spring center but hub faces ranged from 71" to 74". Ordered all three with 72" hub face and they all worked fine. Tires cleared the fenders on every one. The one that was originally 74" just had the tires tucked in about an inch more per side — no big deal. Spring center was the non-negotiable.

If you're nervous about getting the hub face wrong, one thing you can do is get adjustable spring seats. Some axle suppliers offer spring seats that can slide along the axle tube before you tighten them down. That way you can dial in the spring center exactly and adjust the hub face slightly if needed. Not all axles offer this but it's worth asking about, especially if your measurements are borderline between two standard sizes.

title: Lippert 8K Torsion Axle Hub Drum 696104 for Kaufman Mini 5 Car Haulers
body: I have a Lippert 8K torsion axle and need a hub for it. The bearings are the same size inner and outer, and the hub reads 696104. Can you help me find the right part?
summary: The 696104 casting is a special 8K brake hub drum for Lippert LCI torsion axles commonly found on Kaufman Mini 5 Car Haulers. It uses 25580 bearings for both inner and outer.

comments.body: This is a special 8K Brake Hub Drum for the Lippert LCI Kaufman Mini 5 straight spindle trailer axle. Part number 696107 (casting number 696104). Here are the specs: 8,000 lb capacity, 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" brake drum size, fits Lippert LCI axle type A80-B-MINI5-TOR. It uses 25580 bearings for both the inner and outer — that's what makes this hub special. The pilot is 4-7/8" ID, and the races come already pressed in. This brake hub is commonly found on Kaufman Mini 5 Car Haulers with torsion axles. This is a special straight spindle hub, so please confirm this matches your setup before ordering.

That 25580 inner and outer bearing setup is the dead giveaway that this is the Lippert straight spindle hub, not a standard 8K hub. A normal 8K hub uses a larger inner bearing (like a 25580 inner and a 15123 outer, or similar stepped combo). The fact that both bearings are the same size means this is a unique spindle — do NOT try to put a standard 8K hub on this axle, it won't fit.

I have a Kaufman Mini 5 with these same Lippert torsion axles. Getting the right hub was a pain until I found the 696107 part number. The casting number 696104 is what you see stamped into the hub itself, but the actual part you order is 696107. Came with races pre-pressed for the 25580 bearings. Dropped right on. Just make sure you pack those bearings well — I use a bearing packer tool and Valvoline full synthetic marine grease.

For anyone with this hub — what size brake shoes does it take? I'm seeing 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" in the specs above. Is this the same as a standard 8K electric brake shoe or is it a different size because of the straight spindle setup? Want to make sure I order the right shoes when I do my brakes.

The 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" brake shoes are the same as standard 8K electric brake shoes — the drum size is the same, it's just the hub and spindle that are different on this Lippert setup. So you can use regular 8K brake shoes and hardware. The backing plate and magnet are standard 8K electric as well. It's really only the hub and bearings that are unique to this axle.

When you're packing the 25580 bearings on this hub, pay attention to the spindle nut torque. The typical procedure is to tighten the spindle nut to about 50 ft-lbs while rotating the hub to seat the bearings, then back it off and re-tighten to 15-20 ft-lbs finger tight, then back off to the nearest cotter pin hole. You want just a tiny bit of end play — maybe .001" to .005". Too tight and you'll overheat the bearings. Too loose and the hub wobbles.

If you're struggling to find just the hub drum, another route is to pick up the complete hub assembly that includes the hub, drum, bearings, races, seal, and dust cap all pre-assembled. Costs more but you literally just slide it on the spindle and torque the nut. For a torsion axle setup where everything is integrated and hard to get at, the complete assembly saves a lot of frustration.

I'll add that if you're replacing just one side, try to do both sides at the same time if budget allows. The other hub has the same mileage on it and those 25580 bearings don't last forever, especially on a torsion axle that doesn't have as much suspension travel to absorb road shock. Torsion axles put more stress on the hub and bearing assembly than leaf spring setups. I replace both sides every time now after having a bearing failure on the side I didn't replace.

title: What Is the Backspacing on 17.5 Inch Trailer Wheels?
body: What is the backspacing on the 17.5" trailer wheel with the -0.19 offset? I need to know the exact measurement.
summary: The backspacing on the 17.5" trailer wheel with -0.19 offset is 4-3/8", measured from the ground to the back of the wheel when placed flat with the hub face up.

comments.body: The backspacing is 4-3/8". To measure this yourself, sit the wheel flat on the ground with the hub mounting surface facing up, stick a tape measure in the center hole, and measure from the ground to the back of the wheel where the hub mounts. That measurement should come out to 4-3/8" on the 17.5" wheel with the -0.19 offset.

4-3/8" backspacing sounds right for the -0.19 offset 17.5" wheels. Just to make sure we're all speaking the same language — backspacing and offset are related but not the same thing. Offset is the distance from the wheel centerline to the hub mounting surface, measured in inches or mm. Backspacing is the distance from the hub mounting surface to the inner edge of the wheel. A negative offset like -0.19" means the hub mounting surface is slightly inboard of the wheel centerline, pushing the tire outward a tiny bit.

What bolt pattern are you working with on the 17.5" wheel? Most 17.5" trailer wheels I've seen come in 8 on 6.5" bolt pattern for 7K-10K axles. If you're matching this to a specific axle, make sure the bolt pattern and the pilot bore diameter match too. The backspacing is important but it's only one piece of the fitment puzzle.

I run 17.5" wheels on my flatbed with the 4-3/8" backspacing and they clear everything fine — fenders, leaf springs, brake drums. If you're swapping from a different size wheel (like 16") to the 17.5", make sure the new tire/wheel combo clears your fender height. The 17.5" wheel with a 215/75R17.5 tire has a slightly larger overall diameter than a typical 16" setup which can affect fender clearance on some trailers.

The measurement method described in the answer is spot on. I'll add one detail — make sure the surface you set the wheel on is truly flat. If you measure on uneven ground or a gravel surface, your measurement will be off. I use a piece of flat plywood on my garage floor. Also, measure at two or three points around the circumference and average them, because some wheels can have slight variations in the mounting surface.

If the -0.19" offset doesn't give you enough clearance for your setup, some manufacturers offer 17.5" trailer wheels in a zero offset or even positive offset configuration. Zero offset gives you about 4.5" backspacing on a 6.75" wide wheel, which tucks the tire in a bit more. Depends on whether you need the tires further out for stability or further in for fender clearance. Just something to consider if the -0.19 offset doesn't work out.

When mounting 17.5" wheels, torque the lug nuts to spec and re-torque after the first 50-100 miles. Most 17.5" trailer wheels with 8 on 6.5" bolt pattern take 1/2"-20 lug nuts torqued to about 120 ft-lbs for steel wheels. If you have aluminum 17.5" wheels the torque spec might be different — usually around 100-110 ft-lbs. Check the wheel manufacturer's specs because over-torquing can warp the mounting surface and cause wheel runout.

title: What Measurements Do I Need to Upgrade From 7K to 8K Axles?
body: What information do I need to provide in order to upgrade from 7K to 8K trailer axles? I want to make sure I order the right size.
summary: To upgrade from 7K to 8K axles, the spring center to spring center measurement is the most important spec to provide. Hub face to hub face is helpful but the spring center alone is often enough to determine the right axle.

comments.body: We really just need to know the spring center to spring center measurement and the hub face to hub face measurement. But really, if you can provide us with the spring center measurement, we can typically figure out what you have based off that measurement alone. The spring center is the critical number for getting the upgrade right.

Quick question on this — when you go from 7K to 8K, does the brake size change too? I know 7K axles typically run 12x2 electric brakes but I'm not sure if 8K bumps up to 12-1/4 x 3-3/8. That would affect the backing plates and drums you need to order along with the axle.

Yes, 8K axles use 12-1/4 x 3-3/8 inch electric brakes — bigger shoes and bigger drums than the 7K setup. So you'll need new drums, backing plates, and brake assemblies. The hub bolt pattern also changes on most 8K axles to 8 on 6.5 inches, so your existing wheels probably won't carry over either. Plan for that in your budget.

Did this exact upgrade on my 24-foot equipment trailer last year. Went from 7K Dexter axles to 8K. The spring center measurement was the same at 33 inches so the hangers didn't need to change at all — just pulled the old axles out, slid the new ones in, and bolted up. Whole job took about 4 hours with a buddy and a floor jack. Well worth it if you're regularly loading near capacity.

One thing people forget — measure the drop on your current axle too. Spring-under vs spring-over, and the actual drop dimension at the spindle matters for ride height. If your 7K is a straight axle and your 8K replacement is a drop axle (or vice versa), the trailer will sit at a totally different height. Write down the drop measurement before you order.

Also worth confirming whether your current 7K axle is a 5 on 4.5 bolt pattern or 8-lug. Some 7K axles already run 8 on 6.5 if they were specced with heavy duty hubs. If you're already on 8-lug, the wheel swap is a non-issue. Just check before you start buying new wheels.

If you're not sure how to measure the spring center, it's from the center of the front spring hanger bolt to the center of the rear spring hanger bolt. Use a tape measure along the frame rail. Most common spring centers on utility and equipment trailers are 33", 35", or 36". If you can snap a photo of the axle tag or data plate, that usually has the spec printed right on it too.

Don't forget tires. Going from 7K to 8K you'll want at least a Load Range E tire rated for the higher capacity per wheel. A lot of guys upgrade the axle but leave the old ST225/75R15 tires on there — those might not be rated high enough for the 8K capacity split across 4 tires. Check the tire sidewall for the max load rating.

Learned this the hard way — I measured my spring center wrong the first time because I measured to the outside of the hanger instead of the bolt center. Was off by almost 2 inches and the axle I ordered didn't sit right. Had to send it back and wait another week. Measure to the center of the bolt, not the edge of the hanger bracket.

The accepted answer is spot on, spring center is the number one measurement. I'd add: take a photo of a tape measure laid across it and send that to whoever you're ordering from. Eliminates any confusion. I've done maybe a dozen axle swaps and the spring center has matched every time as long as you measure correctly.

While you're at it, are you running electric or hydraulic brakes on your 7K setup? If you're switching to electric on the 8K, make sure your brake controller can handle the higher amp draw from the larger 12-1/4 inch magnets. Most 7-way controllers are fine but some of the cheaper ones max out around 2 axles of 7K brakes.

title: Dexter 9-123 Brake Drum Cross Reference for 9K and 10K Axles
body: Do you have the Dexter drum 9-123 in stock? I need a replacement brake drum for my trailer axle.
summary: The Dexter 9-123 is a brake drum for 9K-10K axles manufactured after April 2023. The direct cross-reference replacement part number is TPU-8-430-5.

comments.body: The Dexter 9-123 is a trailer brake drum for 9K-10K axles made after April 2023. The Trailer Parts Unlimited part number that interchanges with the Dexter drum is TPU-8-430-5. This is a direct replacement — same specs, same fit.

Ordered the TPU-8-430-5 for my 10K tandem dump trailer. Fit was perfect, bolt pattern lined right up. Same 8 on 6.5 pattern as the original Dexter drum. No issues after about 3,000 miles of hauling gravel.

Does anyone know what the equivalent part is for 9K/10K axles made BEFORE April 2023? I have an older gooseneck and the drum numbers don't match the 9-123. Wondering if there was a different Dexter part number for the pre-2023 drums.

Just a heads up — the 9K and 10K brake drums are 12-1/4 x 3-3/8 on the standard setups, and the bolt pattern is 8 on 6.5 inches. Make sure you verify that matches what you're replacing before ordering. I've seen a few oddball trailers with 12-1/4 x 5 inch brakes on 10K axles and those use a completely different drum.

Had to replace both drums on my gooseneck flatbed last fall. The Dexter originals had worn past the max diameter — you could feel the lip with your finger. The cross-reference drum from TPU was the same casting dimensions. I compared them side by side before installing. Bearings and seals seated identically.

When you swap the drum, it's a good time to inspect the bearings and replace the grease seal while you're in there. The 9K/10K hubs typically use a 25580 inner bearing and a 02475 outer bearing. Seals are cheap insurance — I always replace them when the drum comes off.

One more thing — when you put the new drum on, check for any casting flash around the hub pilot and the bearing seats. I've had aftermarket drums need a light cleanup with emery cloth on the pilot diameter before the hub would slide on smoothly. Nothing major, just a minute of work, but don't force it.

title: Dexter Hub A-219 Cross Reference for 7K Trailer Axles
body: Do you have a Dexter hub with the part number A-219? I need a replacement hub and drum for my 7K trailer axle.
summary: The Dexter A-219 is a 7K trailer hub and drum assembly with 1/2-inch studs. The direct cross-reference replacement part number is 90865A-17.

comments.body: The Dexter A-219 is a 7K trailer hub and drum with 1/2-inch studs. Our cross-reference part number is 90865A-17, which is a direct replacement that will fit your axle.
Ran the 90865A-17 on my 7K equipment trailer for about a season now. Fits exactly like the Dexter A-219 it replaced. Same pilot, same bearing bores, same stud circle. No complaints.

Is there a version of the A-219 with 5/8-inch studs instead of 1/2-inch? I've got a 7K axle but with the 8-lug pattern and 5/8 studs. Just want to make sure I don't accidentally order the wrong stud size.

For anyone ordering this hub, the bearing sizes you'll need are 25580 for the inner and 15123 for the outer on the standard 7K Dexter setup. Races are 25520 inner and 15245 outer. If you're doing a full repack or new install, grab a seal kit too — the grease seal is what keeps everything protected.

Upgraded my boat trailer from stock hubs to the A-219 equivalent a couple years back because the originals were pitted from saltwater. These aftermarket hubs have been solid. I pack them with marine-grade bearing grease and they've held up through two seasons of boat ramp launches.

Make sure you verify the bolt pattern before ordering. The A-219 is specifically an 8 on 6.5 inch bolt pattern with 1/2-inch studs. If your 7K axle runs a different lug pattern — some older 7K setups used 6 on 5.5 — this hub won't work. Check your wheel bolt circle first.

Don't forget the grease seal when you install the new hub. The seal presses into the back of the hub over the inner bearing and keeps dirt and water out. On 7K hubs it's typically a 2.125 x 3.376 seal. Press it in flush and square — a block of wood and a hammer works, or use a seal driver if you have one.

title: Timken Bearing 28682 Cross Reference Numbers for 12K Trailer Hubs
body: What is the cross-reference number for the Timken bearing 28682? I need to find a compatible replacement for my 12K trailer hub outer bearing.
summary: The Timken 28682 is the standard outer bearing for 12K trailer hubs with a 2.250-inch inner diameter. It cross-references with National Bearings 28682, SKF BR28682, and numerous other manufacturer part numbers.

comments.body: The Timken 28682 cross-references with the common bearing number 28682, which is the standard outer bearing for Dexter 12K hub assemblies measuring 2.250 inches inner diameter. Key cross-reference part numbers include: National Bearings 28682, SKF BR28682, Redneck Trailer Supplies 550401, Cummins 5086774AA, and Four Seasons 56643. Other industry cross-reference numbers include Lisle 53430, MSC Industrial 234011, and many OEM-specific numbers. This is a very widely available bearing and all cross-references are fully interchangeable.

Important thing to remember: the 28682 is just the bearing cone. You also need the matching race, which is the 28622. The race presses into the hub and the cone rides on the race. Don't reuse an old race with a new bearing — they wear as a matched set. Always replace both together.
What's the inner bearing number for 12K hubs? I know the 28682 is the outer, but I need to replace the full set and I'm not sure which inner goes with it.

Inner bearing on Dexter 12K hubs is the HM218248 with the HM218210 race. That's a pretty beefy bearing — 3.543" OD on the race. Between the 28682 outer and the HM218248 inner, you've got a solid bearing setup for heavy loads.

I went with the SKF BR28682 on my 12K flatbed gooseneck last summer. Exact same dimensions as the Timken, pressed right onto the spindle with no issues. About 8,000 miles on them hauling equipment and they're running smooth. I pack them with Valvoline multi-purpose bearing grease and check them every 5,000 miles.

One thing — I've heard guys say you can mix bearing brands but you should never mix a cone from one brand with a race from another. The tolerances between manufacturers can vary just enough to cause premature wear. If you buy a Timken cone, get a Timken race. Same goes for SKF or National.

Instead of ordering the bearing and race separately, you might want to look at a complete bearing kit for 12K hubs. Usually includes both inner and outer bearings with races, the grease seal, and a cotter pin. Ends up being about the same price and you know everything matches. Saves you from accidentally getting the wrong race.

All those cross-reference numbers listed above are interchangeable, can confirm. I've used Timken, National, and SKF in 12K hubs and never had a problem with any of them. Quality is comparable across the board for standard trailer use. Just make sure you're buying from a reputable source — there are counterfeits floating around on some of the discount sites.

When you install the new bearing, pack it with grease thoroughly before putting it on the spindle. Get grease into every roller gap — I use a bearing packer tool but you can do it by hand if you push grease into the large end and work it through until it comes out between each roller on the small end. Don't just smear grease on the outside and call it good. Under-greased bearings on a 12K axle hauling heavy loads will fail fast.

title: How Wide Are the Leaf Springs on 15K and Heavy Duty Trailer Axles?
body: How wide are the springs on 15K trailer axles? Are they the same width as springs on other heavy-duty axle capacities?
summary: Leaf springs on 15K trailer axles are 3 inches wide, the same width used on 12K, 16K, and some heavy-duty 10K axles. All Hutch suspension springs are also 3 inches wide regardless of capacity.

comments.body: The springs on 15K axles are 3 inches wide. They are the same width as 12K, 16K, and sometimes you will even see 10K heavy-duty axles with 3-inch wide leaf springs. However, if you're using Hutch suspension, then all the Hutch suspension springs will be 3 inches wide regardless of the capacity axles you have.

To add some context, the lighter duty axles — your 3.5K, 5.2K, and 6K — typically use 1-3/4 inch wide springs. Once you get to 7K and 8K, most go to 2-inch wide springs. Then at 10K heavy-duty and above, you jump to the 3-inch wide springs. So there's basically three tiers of spring width depending on capacity.

How many leaves are typically in a 15K spring pack? I'm looking at replacing the springs on my triaxle dump and want to make sure I get the right count. The old ones are pretty beat up and I can't tell if any leaves are missing.

Replaced all the springs on my 16K tandem equipment trailer last year. All 3 inches wide, just like the answer says. The main difference between the 15K and 16K springs isn't the width — it's the number of leaves and the arch. More leaves and a different arch give you the higher rating. Width stays at 3 inches across those heavy-duty capacities.

Worth noting that the 10K capacity is sort of a crossover point. I've seen standard 10K axles with 2-inch springs and heavy-duty 10K axles with 3-inch springs. If you're replacing 10K springs, measure the width before ordering — don't just assume it's 2 or 3 inches. The 15K and above are always 3 though, no ambiguity there.

If you're running a heavy-duty application and you're tired of leaf spring maintenance, air ride suspension is worth considering for 15K+ axles. Higher upfront cost but you get adjustable ride height, smoother ride, and less wear on the trailer frame. Trade-off is more complexity and air bags can fail if they get road debris damage. Not for everyone but it's an option.

Can confirm the Hutch detail in the answer — every Hutch suspension spring I've dealt with has been 3 inches wide regardless of axle capacity. That's just how they build their system. Also worth mentioning that the spring seat pads on the axle need to match the spring width. A 3-inch spring needs a 3-inch spring seat welded to the axle tube. If you're mixing components, make sure they line up.

Another dimension that changes as you go up in capacity is the spring eye diameter. Lighter springs use a 9/16-inch or 5/8-inch eye bolt, but once you get into 3-inch wide heavy-duty springs for 12K-16K axles, the eye bolts are typically 3/4-inch diameter. Make sure your hangers accept the right bolt size if you're upgrading spring capacity.

title: Inside Brake Drum to Drum Measurement on 8K Axles With 82 Inch Hub Face
body: What is the measurement from the inside brake drum to the other inside brake drum on the 8K trailer axles with an 82-inch hub face and 12-1/4 x 3-3/8 inch brakes?
summary: The inside brake flange to brake flange measurement on 82-inch hub face 8K trailer axles with 12-1/4 x 3-3/8 inch brakes is 69-1/2 inches.

comments.body: The measurement from inside brake flange to inside brake flange on the 82-inch hub face 8K axles is 69-1/2 inches. This is an important measurement to verify when checking whether the axle will clear your trailer frame.

This measurement matters because it tells you how much clearance you have between the brake assemblies and the inside of the trailer frame. If your frame is narrower than 69-1/2 inches between the rails, the brakes are going to hit. Always check this before ordering if you're fitting new axles to an existing trailer.

Does anyone know the inside drum-to-drum measurement on the 74-inch hub face 8K axles with the same 12-1/4 x 3-3/8 brakes? I'm working with a narrower trailer and need to figure out if the 74 hub face will clear.

Had to verify this exact spec when I was building an 8K tandem car hauler. The 69-1/2 inch inside measurement gave me plenty of room with my 72-inch inside frame width. I measured with the drums fully seated and the backing plates bolted up. No interference at all.

For anyone wondering how to get this measurement on an axle that's already on the trailer — put a long straight edge or tape measure from the inside face of one brake drum across to the inside face of the other drum. Make sure you're measuring the drum face, not the backing plate edge. The backing plate actually extends a bit further inward on some setups.

Just to be clear, this 69-1/2 inch number is specific to the 12-1/4 x 3-3/8 brake setup on the 82-inch hub face axle. If someone is running 12-1/4 x 5 inch brakes (which some heavy-duty 8K axles use), the inside measurement will be different because the drum and backing plate are wider. Always confirm which brake size is on the axle.

69-1/2 inches sounds right to me. I pulled the same measurement when I swapped my drums last season. One tip: if you're tight on clearance, make sure the brake magnet wires and the adjuster mechanism on the backing plate aren't sticking out past the drum face. Sometimes they can add a fraction of an inch that causes interference with the frame.

Keep in mind that 8K axles also come in a 95-inch hub face configuration for wider trailers. On those, the inside drum-to-drum measurement is going to be larger since the spindles are farther apart. So if you're working with a wider frame and need more clearance, the 95-inch hub face variant might be the better fit. Check with your supplier for that specific inside measurement.

title: What Trailer Axle Do I Need to Build a 102 Inch Wide Trailer?
body: I'm looking for a trailer axle kit to build a 102-inch wide trailer. What size axle do I need for this width?
summary: For building a 102-inch wide trailer, you need a 95-inch hub face axle with an 80-inch spring center.

comments.body: For a 102-inch wide trailer, you would need the 95-inch hub face with 80-inch spring center trailer axles. This is the standard configuration for trailers at that width and keeps you within road-legal dimensions.

The 95-inch hub face is the standard for 102-inch wide trailers, but the overall width depends on your tire and wheel combination too. With a standard 235/80R16 tire on a 16x6 wheel, the tire sticks out about 3-1/2 inches past the hub face on each side. That puts you right at about 102 inches total. If you run a wider tire, you could go over 102 and have DOT issues.

What capacity axle are you looking at? The 95-inch hub face / 80-inch spring center combo is available in everything from 3.5K to 8K. If this is a flatbed or equipment trailer, I'd go at least 5.2K per axle for a single or 7K per axle for a tandem setup. What are you planning to haul?

Built a 102-inch wide car hauler a few years back using 7K axles with the 95-inch hub face and 80-inch spring center. Everything lined up exactly like the answer says. The key was making sure the spring hanger spacing matched the 80-inch spring center — once that was right, the rest was straightforward. Used 235/80R16 tires and came out to about 101-3/4 inches overall.

Just to be really clear on the regulations — DOT maximum trailer width is 102 inches (8 feet 6 inches) for highway use in all 50 states. That's measured at the widest point, which is usually the outside of the tires or fenders. So when you spec your axle and tire combo, make absolutely sure the total width including tires doesn't exceed 102 inches or you'll need an overwidth permit.

One thing to watch out for — if you're running fenders mounted inside the frame rails, the fender width and standoff can push your overall width past 102 inches even if the tires are within spec. I've seen guys build to 102 on the axle and then add fenders that stick out another inch on each side. Measure everything before you weld the fender mounts.

If you're building from scratch and don't absolutely need 102 inches, consider going with an 86-inch hub face and 72-inch spring center for a 96-inch wide trailer instead. Narrower trailers are easier to tow, you get better rearview mirror visibility, and you don't have to worry about tight parking lots or narrow driveways. Just a thought depending on what you're hauling.

When you order the axle, make sure to spec the brakes at the same time. Electric brakes are the most common for utility and equipment trailers. On a 5.2K or 6K axle, you'll get 10-inch brakes. On a 7K, you're looking at 12x2 inch brakes. This affects the drum and backing plate dimensions and is part of the overall axle build.

Are you going single axle or tandem? For a 102-inch wide trailer, most builds I've seen are tandem axle for stability. Single axle works if you're keeping it short (like a 10-12 foot deck), but anything longer really benefits from two axles. The spring center stays at 80 inches either way.

Built mine with the 80-inch spring center on a tandem 7K setup. Used standard double-eye slipper springs with a 33-inch spring center between hangers. The hangers welded right to my 2x6 rectangular tube frame with even spacing. If your frame is a different size, the hanger brackets are available for different tube widths — just make sure you specify that when ordering.

The 95-inch hub face with 80-inch spring center is definitely the go-to for 102-inch wide builds, can confirm. I'll add that the spring seat pads on the axle should be positioned for the 80-inch center and welded square. If you're ordering a complete axle, this is all done for you. If you're having a bare tube built, make sure the spring seats are positioned and welded by someone who knows the spec.

Something a lot of first-time builders overlook: wheel offset. A zero-offset wheel keeps the tire centered on the hub, but some trailer wheels have a slight positive offset that tucks the tire in a bit. On a 102-inch build where every fraction of an inch counts, the wheel offset can mean the difference between legal and overwidth. Check the backspacing on whatever wheels you plan to run.

title: Are Trailer Hub and Drums EZ Lube or Standard Grease?
body: Are the 7K hub and drums EZ lube hub and drums? I want to make sure I'm ordering the right type for my trailer axle setup.
summary: Hub and drums work for both EZ lube and standard grease axles. The spindle itself determines whether an axle is EZ lube, not the hub and drum.

comments.body: The hub and drums are made for both EZ lube and standard grease axles. The hub and drum itself does not determine if the trailer axle is easy lube or not. What determines it is the trailer spindle itself. The trailer spindle will come with a grease zerk already built onto the spindle for you to easily grease up your bearings. So whether you have EZ lube spindles or standard spindles, the same hub and drum will work for either application.

Good clear answer. I'll second this — the hub and drum is just a shell with bearing bores and studs. It doesn't know or care whether the spindle behind it has a grease zerk or not. Same part, either way.
How can you tell if your existing spindle is EZ lube without pulling the hub off? I bought a used trailer and I'm not sure what I've got.

Look at the end of the spindle where the dust cap or grease cap sits. On an EZ lube spindle, there's a rubber grease fitting (zerk) built right into the end of the spindle, accessible through a hole in the dust cap. On a standard spindle, there's no zerk — just a smooth spindle end with a plain dust cap pressed on. You can usually spot the difference without removing anything.

Switched from standard grease to EZ lube spindles a few years ago on my landscape trailer and I love the convenience. Instead of pulling the hubs every year to repack, I just hit the zerk with a grease gun every few months. Takes about 30 seconds per hub. That said, you can't just add a zerk to a standard spindle — the EZ lube spindle has an internal passage that routes grease from the zerk through to the bearing area. It's a different forging.

One thing people get wrong: EZ lube does NOT mean you never have to repack your bearings. The zerk lets you add grease between full services, but you should still pull the hubs, inspect the bearings, and do a proper repack every 12,000 miles or once a year — whichever comes first. I've seen guys just pump grease in for years without ever checking the bearings, and by the time they look, the inner seal has blown out and the inner bearing is toast.

The dust cap is another visual clue. EZ lube caps usually have a small rubber plug in the center that you pop out to access the zerk fitting. Standard caps are just a plain stamped steel cap with no hole. If you see a rubber plug in the cap, you've got EZ lube spindles.

If you really want low-maintenance hubs and you're hauling heavy, oil bath hubs are another option worth looking at. Instead of grease, the hub runs in a bath of gear oil and has a translucent cap so you can see the oil level. Very common on boat trailers and heavy commercial trailers. The downside is they can leak if the seals aren't perfect, and if you lose the oil, the bearings go fast. But for high-mileage applications they're hard to beat.

Whether you run EZ lube or standard, make sure you're using the right grease. For trailer bearings, a lithium-based NLGI #2 bearing grease is the standard. If you're running a boat trailer that sees saltwater, go with a marine-grade grease that has corrosion inhibitors. Don't mix grease types — if you're switching from one grease to another, do a full repack and clean the old grease out first.

title: What Is a Lippert 8K Hybrid Axle and Why to Avoid It
body: I'm looking for a Lippert 8K hub drum with part number 380827. Do you have this in stock?
summary: The Lippert 380827 is a "hybrid" 8K hub drum that uses smaller 12"x2" brakes, essentially a glorified 7K axle. A true 8K axle uses 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" brakes and a 3-1/2" heavy duty axle tube.

comments.body: This is a hub and drum assembly for a "hybrid" 8K axle that has the 12" x 2" brake assemblies. The only real difference between this hub and a 7K hub and drum is that it uses the 02475 outer bearing, so they call this an 8K hybrid axle. Unfortunately, we do not support nor stock these axles as we feel this is nothing more than a glorified 7K axle that companies are charging you double the price for and calling them 8K axles. This is solely my opinion and my views on the 8K hybrid axles. If you would like a real 8K axle with 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" brakes and a 3-1/2" heavy duty axle tube, then check out Carter 8K trailer axles.

Wait so I'm confused — if it has the same 12"x2" brakes as a 7K, what exactly makes it "8K"? Is it literally just the outer bearing being a 02475 instead of the standard one? Because that seems like a pretty thin upgrade to justify doubling the price.

Yep, that's basically it. The 02475 outer bearing has a slightly larger inner diameter (1.250") vs the standard L68149 (1.378" OD cone) on the 7K. So the spindle neck is marginally bigger on the hybrid, which technically allows a higher static load rating. But the brake drums, brake shoes, magnet size — all identical to the 7K setup. That's why people call it a glorified 7K. The stopping power hasn't changed at all.

Bought a trailer off Facebook Marketplace last year — seller swore it was a "true 8K axle" setup. Got it home, looked at the brakes, 12"x2". Same as every 7K I've ever owned. Paid 8K pricing for 7K braking. Ended up swapping both axles out for Carter 8K with the 12-1/4"x3-3/8" brakes. Night and day difference when I'm hauling a loaded car down a grade. Lesson learned — always check brake size before buying a used trailer.

Here's the quick way to spot a hybrid vs a real 8K without crawling under the trailer: look at the axle tube diameter. Real 8K (Carter, Dexter) has a 3-1/2" tube. Lippert hybrid 8K has a 3" tube — same as their 7K. You can measure it in 10 seconds with a tape measure wrapped around the tube. 3" tube = hybrid/glorified 7K. 3.5" tube = real 8K.

Had the hybrid 8K on a flatbed I was using for construction materials. Fine around town, but I took a load of concrete blocks across the Ozarks and those brakes faded bad coming down a long 6% grade. You could smell the shoes burning. Swapped to Carter 8K the following week and never looked back. The bigger 3-3/8" brake shoes make a massive difference in heat dissipation.

If you're already stuck with the hybrid axle and can't justify swapping the whole thing out right now, at least keep the brake magnets fresh and make sure your brake controller gain is set properly. Replace the magnets every 12,000 miles or so — they wear faster on the smaller 12"x2" assemblies because they're working harder to stop the same weight. It won't fix the fundamental problem but it buys you time.

The cost difference is what kills me. I priced out two hybrid 8K axles from a dealer — came to about $1,800 for the pair with brakes. Two Carter real 8K axles with 12-1/4"x3-3/8" electric brakes and hub drums ran me about $2,200 total. For $400 more you get the correct tube size, proper brakes, and actual 8K stopping power. It's a no-brainer.

Actually, I want to add some nuance here. The hybrid designation isn't completely fabricated — the spindle and bearing upgrade does raise the static load capacity to 8,000 lbs from a structural standpoint. The axle beam won't fail at 8K. The problem is dynamic braking. You have 8K of weight being stopped by brakes designed for 7K. It's like putting sedan brakes on a pickup truck. The truck might handle the weight fine rolling down the highway, but try stopping on a steep hill with a full payload.

Just to confirm what the original reply said — Carter 8K is the way to go here. The 3-1/2" heavy duty tube, 12-1/4"x3-3/8" self-adjusting brakes, and the larger spindle all add up to an axle that's actually engineered for 8,000 lbs. One thing I'll add: make sure when you order the Carter 8K that you specify 5/8" studs if you're running 17.5" wheels, or 9/16" if you're running 16" wheels. Both options are available.

title: Do You Stock Torsion Axles or Are They Special Order?
body: Do you stock torsion axles? I need one for my trailer and want to know what the availability and lead time looks like.
summary: Torsion axles are not stocked due to the huge number of variations. They are special order only and typically take 4+ weeks to manufacture and deliver.

comments.body: Unfortunately, we do not stock torsion axles. There are too many variances when it comes to torsion axles, and we would have to stock hundreds of different ones to even get close to guessing what you would need. We do sell them, however they are all special order and take 4+ weeks to get in. If you can get the serial number that's engraved on the axle tube itself, typically in the middle, that would ensure we get you the exact axle you need. It should be around a 9-digit number.

Where exactly is this serial number on the torsion axle? I crawled under my trailer and can't find anything. Is it stamped into the metal or on a sticker? My axle tube is pretty rusty so it might be hard to read.

The serial number is typically stamped directly into the axle tube metal, usually dead center between the two torsion arms. On Dexter torsion axles it's around 9-10 digits. If it's rusted over, try hitting it with a wire wheel on an angle grinder — the stamps are deep enough that surface rust usually won't obliterate them. On Lippert/LCI torsion axles, sometimes there's a small metal tag riveted to the tube instead of a stamp.

Plan ahead if you go this route. I ordered a torsion axle replacement last August and it took 6 weeks to arrive. My trailer sat in the yard the whole time. If you're anywhere near a busy season (spring/summer for boat trailers especially) I'd expect closer to 8 weeks. Wish I had ordered mine in the winter when the lead times are shorter.

Depending on your situation, it might be worth considering converting from torsion to leaf spring suspension entirely. Leaf spring axles are stocked everywhere, parts are cheap and available same day, and installation is straightforward if you can weld. You'll need spring hangers welded to the frame and a set of leaf springs plus a standard round axle. The ride quality is slightly different — leaf springs are a bit stiffer — but for utility or equipment trailers most people won't notice. Just a thought if the 4-8 week wait is a dealbreaker.

If you can't find the serial number, you can still order one — you just need to know these specs: axle capacity (lb rating), arm length measured from center of tube to center of hub bolt pattern, arm angle (up or down from horizontal, usually specified in degrees), inner arm spread (distance between mounting brackets), and the hub bolt pattern. Get those five measurements right and the manufacturer can build you a match. It takes more work but it's doable.

Four-plus weeks is the best case scenario honestly. I ordered a Dexter torsion axle for my center console boat trailer in June and it was 9 weeks before it shipped. Granted that's peak season. But just set your expectations accordingly — this isn't a next-day-ship kind of item. If your trailer is down and you need it running, leaf spring conversion might be your fastest path.

One more tip — check salvage yards and trailer recyclers in your area. I've found used OEM torsion axles with matching serial numbers for common boat trailer brands like Load Rite, Venture, and EZ Loader. If the rubber torsion cords aren't cracked or dried out, a used torsion axle can have plenty of life left. Saves you the wait time and usually costs about half of new. Just make sure the capacity and arm measurements match your setup exactly.

title: Does an 8K Axle Have a Bigger Tube Than a 7K Trailer Axle?
body: Does an 8K axle have a bigger axle tube than the 7,000 lb trailer axles? I'm trying to understand the structural differences between the two.
summary: A true 8K axle like Carter or Dexter has a larger 3-1/2" tube, while Lippert 8K axles only have a 3" tube — the same size as 7K axles.

comments.body: A real 8K axle like the Carter brand has a bigger tube, yes. Dexter also has a bigger 3-1/2" axle tube like the Carter axles do. The Lippert axles, however, only have a 3" axle tube, which is the same as 7K axles. This is an important distinction when you're comparing 8K axles between brands — not all 8K axles are built the same.
Is there an easy way to measure the tube diameter without removing the axle? I'm trying to figure out if mine is a real 8K or one of those Lippert hybrids everyone talks about.

Yeah, just wrap a flexible tape measure around the tube and divide by 3.14. A 3" tube will measure about 9.42" circumference, and a 3-1/2" tube will be about 11". Or if you have a caliper big enough, just clamp it on. Easiest spot to measure is right in the middle of the tube where there's nothing in the way. Takes 30 seconds.

Bought what was advertised as an "8K Lippert axle" on a used equipment trailer. Got it home and wrapped the tape around the tube — 9.4 inches, so right at 3" diameter. Same as the 7K axles I pulled off my utility trailer. The brakes were 12"x2" too. It was a hybrid and the seller either didn't know or didn't care. If the tube isn't 3-1/2", it's not a true 8K regardless of what the sticker says.

To be fair, a 3" tube can technically hold 8K from a beam-strength perspective — the tube itself isn't going to bend or fail at that weight. The real problem is everything else that comes with the hybrid: undersized brakes (12"x2" vs 12-1/4"x3-3/8"), smaller brake shoes, less heat dissipation surface area. The tube diameter is just the most visible indicator that tells you what class of components you're dealing with. Bigger tube = bigger everything else too.

Here's a rough guide for tube sizes by capacity:
- 2K-3.5K: 2-3/8" round tube
- 5.2K-7K: 3" round tube
- Carter/Dexter 8K: 3-1/2" round tube
- 10K: 3-1/2" round tube (sometimes 4" on heavy duty models)
- 12K+: typically 4" or 5" tube
If you measure 3" and someone's calling it 8K, it's a hybrid or mislabeled.

If you already own a trailer with the Lippert 8K hybrid axle (3" tube), don't panic and rip it out immediately. Just be realistic about what you're working with. Treat it like a strong 7K — keep your loads under 7,000 lbs per axle and you'll be fine. The brakes will handle that weight no problem. It's only when people load them up to the full 8K rating repeatedly that the braking limitations become dangerous, especially on grades.

Switched from Lippert 7K to Carter 8K on my car hauler last spring. The 3-1/2" tube is noticeably stiffer — less flex on uneven roads and the trailer tracks way better at highway speed. The bigger brakes are confidence-inspiring too. I haul a 5,500 lb car regularly on mountain roads in West Virginia and the Carter 8K stops like it should. Couldn't say the same about the old setup.

Good info in this thread. One more thing to note — the spindle diameter is also different between a real 8K and a 7K/hybrid. A true 8K has a larger spindle to accept bigger bearings (typically 25580 inner and 02475 outer). The 7K and hybrid use the L68149/25580 combo.
