So the hubs, drums, and bearings are NOT the same between a real 8K and a 7K — make sure you're ordering the right parts for what you actually have.

title: Can I Use 16 Inch Wheels on 8K Carter Axles With 5/8 Studs?
body: Can I use 16" wheels on the 8K Carter axles that have 5/8" studs? I want to make sure the wheel size is compatible before I order.
summary: Yes, 8K Carter axles with 5/8" studs accept both 16" and 17.5" tire and wheel combos.

comments.body: Yes, you can run the 16" or 17.5" tire and wheel combos with the Carter 8K trailer axle. The 16" wheels and the 17.5" wheels both allow for either 9/16" or 5/8" studs, so you have flexibility in your tire and wheel setup.

Running 16" steel wheels on my Carter 8K tandem setup for about two years now with the 5/8" studs. No issues at all. I'm using ST235/80R16 Load Range E tires — rated at 3,640 lbs per tire which gives me plenty of margin on the 8K axle.

Make sure you're ordering wheels with the correct bolt pattern. The Carter 8K uses 8 on 6.5" (8x6.5") bolt pattern. And the lug holes on the wheel need to accommodate 5/8" studs — some cheaper 16" trailer wheels are drilled for 9/16" studs only and the 5/8" studs won't pass through. Double-check the listing before you order.
Do you need different lug nuts for 5/8" studs vs 9/16"? I've been running 9/16" on everything and I'm not sure if my lug nuts will work if I switch to Carter 8K.

Yes, 5/8" studs require 5/8"-18 lug nuts. They are physically larger than 9/16" lugs and are NOT interchangeable. If you try threading a 9/16" lug nut onto a 5/8" stud, it won't thread on at all. Most trailer parts suppliers sell them individually or in packs of 16 for the 8-lug setup. Torque spec on 5/8" lug nuts is typically 120-140 ft-lbs.

If you're on the fence between 16" and 17.5", consider this: 17.5" tires generally have higher load ratings per tire and run cooler at sustained highway speeds because of the larger diameter. But 16" tires are cheaper, more widely available at tire shops if you get a blowout on the road, and the lower profile can matter if you're tight on fender clearance. For most people hauling under 12K total, 16" is perfectly fine.

One thing that trips people up: just because a wheel physically bolts on doesn't mean it's rated for the load. A 16" wheel meant for a 3,500 lb axle might only be rated for 2,150 lbs. On an 8K axle you need wheels rated for at least 4,000 lbs each. Check the load rating stamped on the wheel — it's usually on the back or inside the barrel. Cheap imported wheels from big box stores are often underrated for heavy axles.

title: Can I Replace a Square Trailer Axle with a Round Axle?
body: I need to replace my boat trailer axle but it's a square axle. You don't seem to have square axles. What do I do?
summary: Yes — you can use a round axle in place of a square axle with no issues. Simply purchase a U-bolt kit for the round axle diameter (e.g., 2-3/8" for 3.5K). Make sure the spring center measurement matches your existing axle.

comments.body: You can use a round axle in place of a square axle no problem. You would just need to buy a U-bolt kit for the round trailer axle and then you will be good to go. Be sure to double check your spring center measurements on your current axle to make sure they are the same.
What size round axle replaces a 2" square tube? My old boat trailer has a 2" square and I'm trying to figure out what the equivalent round tube diameter is for ordering U-bolts and everything.

A 2" square axle is typically found on 2,000-3,500 lb rated boat and utility trailers. The equivalent round tube for that capacity is 2-3/8" diameter. Order your U-bolt kit for a 2-3/8" round axle and you'll be set. If your square axle is 1.5" then you'd be looking at a 2" round tube, but that's pretty rare — mostly on very small jet ski trailers.

Did this exact swap on my 2004 EZ Loader boat trailer last fall. Had the original 2" square axle and it was corroded beyond repair — the corners were paper thin from salt water exposure. Bought a 3,500 lb round axle with 73" hub face and 58" spring center, which matched my old setup. Bolted right in with the new U-bolts. Honestly the round axle felt like an upgrade — the galvanized round tubes hold up way better against corrosion than the painted square ones.

Step by step for the swap: 1) Measure spring center on your existing square axle before removing anything. 2) Note whether your springs sit over or under the axle. 3) Remove the old square axle by unbolting the U-bolts. 4) Check your leaf springs — if they're still in decent shape you can reuse them. 5) Set the new round axle in place on the springs and install the new round-profile U-bolts. 6) Torque the U-bolts to spec (usually 35-55 ft-lbs for 3.5K, check your specific size). 7) Reinstall wheels and check alignment by measuring hub face on each side.

One thing the original answer didn't mention — make sure your new U-bolt spring seats have the curved/cupped profile for a round tube. Square axle spring seats are flat on top. If you try to reuse the old flat spring seats with a round tube, the axle will rock side to side in the saddle and can actually shift under hard braking or on rough roads. The cupped seats cradle the round tube and keep everything locked in place. Most U-bolt kits come with the correct seat plates but worth double checking.

Did a square-to-round swap on a buddy's old Highlander boat trailer and we made a rookie mistake — kept the old flat spring plates because "they seemed fine." First time we hit a big bump on the highway the axle shifted about a quarter inch in the spring seat. Trailer pulled hard to the left until we stopped and reset it. Don't skip the proper round spring seats. Learned that one the hard way.

If you can, get the round axle in hot-dip galvanized instead of painted, especially for a boat trailer. The galvanized coating holds up way better to repeated submersion and salt exposure. It costs a little more but you'll get years more life out of it. Painted axles on boat trailers start rusting within the first season if you're launching in salt water.

Good call on the round tube swap. Your existing leaf springs will work fine as long as they aren't cracked or sagging. The spring eye dimensions and spring width are the same regardless of whether the axle is square or round. Only the U-bolt kit and spring seat change. If your springs are older than 10 years or have visible cracks at the spring eyes, though, I'd replace them at the same time while you have everything apart. It's cheap insurance.

title: How Do I Measure My Trailer Axle? Spring Center & Hub Face Guide
body: I need to replace my trailer axle but I'm not sure how to get the right measurements. What measurements do I need to provide to order the correct replacement axle?
summary: The most important measurement is spring center to spring center on the same axle. Next, measure hub face to hub face — from the outside of one hub where the studs protrude to the other side. Always double-check your bolt pattern (5, 6, or 8 lug) to ensure the replacement axle fits.

comments.body: The most important measurement to get is spring center to spring center on the same axle. Next you can get hub face to hub face measurement. This is the measurement from outside of hub where the studs protrude out from the hub to the other side of the axle where the studs come out from the hub. Always verify your bolt pattern as well.
What if I already removed the old axle and only have the frame with the spring hangers welded on? Can I still figure out the measurements I need?

Yes — if your spring hangers are still welded to the frame, measure from the center of one front hanger bolt hole to the center of the same-side front hanger bolt hole on the other side. That gives you the spring center. For hub face, you'll need to know your trailer's overall outside width and work backward, or look up common combinations for your trailer make/model. A lot of standard utility trailers use these combos:
- 48"-60" wide frame: 73" hub face / 58" spring center
- 72" wide frame: 89" hub face / 74" spring center
- 82"-83" wide frame: 95" hub face / 80" spring center

I messed this up on my first axle replacement and it was an expensive lesson. Measured what I thought was hub face but I was actually measuring from the outside of the brake drum on each side. Ended up with an axle about 3 inches too long. Hub face is measured from the flat mounting surface of each hub — where the wheel studs stick out — to the same point on the other side. Remove the wheels and tires first so you can see exactly what you're measuring.

Here's my method for accurate spring center measurement: have someone hold one end of the tape measure at the exact center of one spring pad (the welded pad on the axle tube where the spring sits). Pull the tape to the center of the spring pad on the other side. That's your spring center. If you're measuring from the hangers instead, make sure you're going center-to-center on the same hanger position (front-to-front or rear-to-rear) on each side.

People get confused between hub face and backing plate to backing plate — they are NOT the same measurement. On a 7K axle with a 95" hub face, the backing plate to backing plate measurement is about 86". That 9" difference has tripped up a lot of people. Hub face is the wider measurement. If you accidentally give someone the backing plate measurement when they need hub face, you'll end up with an axle that's too short.

Don't forget to count your lugs while you're under there. 4-lug is typically 2K axles, 5-lug is 3.5K, 6-lug is 5.2K-7K, and 8-lug is 7K-12K. Getting hub face and spring center right doesn't help if you order an axle with the wrong bolt pattern for your existing wheels. I'd also check whether your studs are 1/2", 9/16", or 5/8" — especially important if you're going from an older axle to a newer one.

Pro tip: take photos of everything before you start disassembly. Photograph the spring hangers, the spring pads, the hub face from the front, and put a tape measure in each photo for reference. If you forget a measurement later you can go back to the photos. I also write the measurements on the frame rail with a paint marker so they're right there when I'm ordering.

One thing that's bitten me: if your trailer has been in a wreck or was loaded unevenly for years, the spring hangers might not be perfectly symmetrical anymore. Measure from both sides independently and compare. If the left spring center doesn't match the right spring center, you've got a bent frame or shifted hangers. Fix that before ordering a new axle or your new axle won't sit straight.

Also worth noting — if you have a tandem axle trailer, measure BOTH axles. I've seen trailers where one axle was replaced previously with a slightly different spring center than the original. If you just measure one and order two replacements based on that, one might not line up with the hangers. Always verify each axle independently.

To add to the original answer — when ordering a replacement axle you should also know: brake type (electric or no brakes), brake size (10", 12", or 12-1/4" — check the diameter of your existing drum), and whether you want over-slung or under-slung spring mounting. Most trailers are over-slung but if you have a low-deck trailer it might be under-slung. The spring center and hub face get you 80% of the way there, but these details matter for getting the complete correct axle.

title: Can You Use 17.5 Inch Tires and Wheels on 7K Trailer Axles?
body: I have 7000 lb trailer axles and want to know if I can run 17.5" tires and wheels on them. Is this possible?
summary: Yes, you can use 17.5" wheels and tires with 7K–12K trailer axles. Carter 7K axles use 9/16" studs, allowing both 16" and 17.5" tire/wheel combos. Do not use 17.5" wheels if your axle has 1/2" studs — risk of broken studs under load.

comments.body: Short answer is yes. You can definitely use 17.5" wheels and tires with the 7k-12k trailer axles. The Carter 7k axles use a 9/16" stud allowing you to have the option to run both either 16" or 17.5" tire wheel combo. It is not recommended if you have 1/2" studs to use 17.5" wheels however, so always double check that.

Important clarification on stud sizes: older 7K axles (pre-2015 or so) commonly came with 1/2" studs. Newer Carter and Dexter 7K axles use 9/16" studs. Before you spend $800+ on a set of 17.5" wheels and tires, pull a lug nut off and check your stud diameter. If you have 1/2" studs, the 17.5" wheels aren't safe at full load — period.

Upgraded to 17.5" wheels on my tandem 7K equipment trailer about 8 months ago. Best upgrade I've done. The tires run noticeably cooler on long highway hauls — I check hub and tire temps with an infrared thermometer at every fuel stop and I'm seeing 15-20 degrees lower temps compared to the old 16" setup. The larger diameter means the tire rotates fewer times per mile so there's less friction buildup.

What's the weight difference between a 16" and 17.5" wheel and tire combo? I'm hauling an excavator that's right at the limit on my tandem 7K and I don't want to eat into my payload capacity with heavier wheels.

Roughly 10-15 lbs more per wheel for the 17.5" assembly vs a comparable 16". On a tandem that's about 40-60 lbs total across four wheels. With a 14,000 lb combined capacity on tandem 7K axles, that's negligible. You won't notice it. The ride quality improvement and better load ratings more than make up for the slight weight increase. A typical 17.5" tire in Load Range H is rated around 4,805 lbs per tire vs about 3,520 lbs for a 16" Load Range E.

People keep saying you can't run 17.5" on 1/2" studs, and they're right, but here's the thing — you can upgrade the studs. A machine shop or axle shop can press out the 1/2" studs and press in 9/16" studs for about $5-8 per stud. On a 6-lug hub that's $30-48 per hub. It's cheaper than buying a whole new axle if your current 7K is otherwise in good shape. Just make sure you get the correct length studs for the 17.5" wheel — they're slightly longer than 16" studs to accommodate the thicker wheel barrel.

The stud size issue is the tip of the iceberg honestly. Axles with 1/2" studs usually also have smaller spindles and lighter-duty hub castings designed for the original load rating. Pressing in bigger studs doesn't change the underlying hub strength or the spindle fatigue limit. If your axle is an older 7K with 1/2" studs, it was probably built to a 6K or even 5.2K standard that's been uprated on paper. I'd be cautious about loading it to full 7K even with new studs.

Confirming that Carter 7K with 9/16" studs is a solid platform for 17.5" wheels. I'm using the H-range 215/75R17.5 tires on my tandem setup and they've been outstanding. Over 25,000 miles with no uneven wear and the tread is barely showing use. If you're buying new axles anyway, go Carter 7K with 9/16" studs and 17.5" wheels — it's the best value setup for a working tandem trailer in the 7K class.

title: Will Carter Trailer Axle Parts Replace Dexter? Interchangeability Guide
body: I have a Dexter 7K trailer axle. Will the parts interchange with a Rockwell axle or Carter axle?
summary: Yes — for 7K axles and below, all parts (hubs, drums, brakes, bearings, seals) interchange between Dexter, Carter, Rockwell, and Lippert. For 10K and above, parts also interchange as long as bearing sizes and measurements match.

comments.body: Yes, all parts will interchange. Rule of thumb is any trailer axle 7k and below, all parts are the same and will interchange between various brands. For 10k and above, you won't have any problems mixing Dexter and Lippert components as long as the measurements on the replacement parts are the same — bearing sizes, etc.

Does this include brake assemblies too? I know hubs and drums interchange but I wasn't sure about the actual brake backing plates and shoes. I need to replace just the brakes on my Dexter 7K and Carter brakes are about $30 cheaper per assembly.

Yes, brake assemblies interchange fully between Carter, Dexter, Lippert, and Rockwell for the same capacity class. Same bolt pattern on the backing plate, same shoe size, same magnet. For 7K (and 5.2K/6K) it's all 12"x2" brakes. The mounting holes line up perfectly. I've mixed and matched brands for years across my fleet of 6 trailers and never had a fitment problem.

I maintain about a dozen trailers for our landscaping company and I buy whatever brand is in stock and cheapest at the time. Running Carter hubs on Dexter axles, Lippert brakes on Carter axles — you name it. For 3.5K through 7K, it's all completely interchangeable. Hubs, drums, brakes, bearings, seals, grease caps. Same inner bearing (25580), same outer bearing (L68149 on 5.2K-7K), same seal, same everything.

Here's a quick cheat sheet for common brake sizes by capacity to make sure you're matching correctly:
- 2K idler: no brakes (hub only)
- 3.5K: 10" x 2-1/4" electric brakes
- 5.2K/6K/7K: 12" x 2" electric brakes
- 8K (real): 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" electric brakes
- 10K: 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" electric brakes
- 12K: 12-1/4" x 5" electric brakes
As long as you match the brake size within the same capacity, any brand will bolt up to any other brand's axle.

One exception worth noting: Dexter's Nev-R-Adjust brake assemblies have a proprietary internal adjuster mechanism that's different from standard self-adjusting brakes. They still bolt up to the same backing plate mounting pattern and use the same drum size, so they're physically interchangeable. But if you're replacing just the adjuster or internal components, the Nev-R-Adjust parts are Dexter-specific. For a complete assembly swap though, it doesn't matter — any brand's complete assembly will work.

If you're mixing brands, it's a great opportunity to upgrade your bearings and seals. I always use Timken-brand bearings regardless of what axle I'm putting them on. The generic imported bearings that come with some cheaper hub kits are fine for light duty but I've had a couple fail early under heavy loads. Timken costs maybe $8-10 more per set and they're made to tighter tolerances. Worth it for peace of mind.

Had a Dexter 7K with a spun inner bearing 400 miles from home on a trip hauling my side-by-side. Found a local trailer shop that had Carter hubs and brakes on the shelf. Bolted the Carter hub drum right onto my Dexter spindle, installed the Carter brake assembly, packed the bearings, and was back on the road in about an hour and a half. Complete drop-in replacement. That day made me a believer in interchangeability.

For 10K and above, things are still interchangeable but you need to pay closer attention to bearing numbers. The 10K+ axles use larger bearings and the exact numbers vary between old-style and new-style hubs. For example, a new-style Dexter 10K uses 28682 outer and 3984 inner, while the old-style used different numbers. Just pull the bearing out of your existing hub, read the number off the cone, and order matching bearings. The hub and drum will bolt right up as long as the bearing races match your spindle.

Confirming what everyone's saying — full interchangeability is the norm across Carter, Dexter, Lippert, and Rockwell/Quality. This also applies to Rockwell American axles which are essentially the same as Quality brand. If you see any of those names on your axle tag, rest assured the parts from any of the other brands will fit. Just match capacity, bearing numbers, and brake size and you're golden.

title: Do I Need to Change Wheels When Upgrading from 7K to 8K Trailer Axles?
body: I want to upgrade my trailer from 7K axles to 8K axles. Do I need to change my wheels and tires too?
summary: No — 7K and 8K axles both use the 8-lug on 6.5" bolt pattern, so you can reuse your 16" or 17.5" wheels. However, check that your tire load rating supports the extra capacity. 10-ply tires (~3,520 lbs each) are too low for 8K — you need at least 14-ply or 17.5" tires.

comments.body: No, the 7k and 8k axles have the same bolt pattern. So you can use both 16" tires and wheels or 17.5" tires and wheels on either trailer axle. However, pay attention to your tire load rating. If your tires can't handle the weight, upgrading the axle becomes pointless. Your setup is only as strong as your lowest-rated component.

Can confirm — both 7K and 8K axles use the 8-on-6.5" bolt pattern. Your existing wheels bolt right on. The real thing to check is the tire load range. Most 7K setups come with Load Range D tires which are rated around 2,500 lb each. If you're actually loading to 8K capacity you'll want Load Range E or better, otherwise the tires become your weak link.

Did this exact swap on my 14K tandem dump trailer last spring. Pulled the old 7K Dexter axles and dropped in 8K replacements. Kept my 16" wheels and ST235/80R16 Load Range E tires — everything lined up perfectly. Only hiccup was I had to get longer U-bolts because the 8K axle tube is a slightly larger diameter (3" round vs 2-3/8" on the 7K). Don't forget that part.

Quick note that most people overlook: if you're upgrading from 7K to 8K, double check your leaf springs and hangers too. The springs need to match the axle capacity or you'll sag under load. 8K axles typically pair with heavier double-eye springs rated for 4,000 lb each on a tandem setup. Your old 7K springs probably aren't rated high enough.

Just to add to what's been said — the hub bore on 7K and 8K wheels is the same, so the wheel centers correctly on the hub either way. No adapter plates, no new lug nuts, nothing. Biggest mistake I see people make is upgrading the axle but keeping the old Load Range D tires. At highway speed with a full load that's asking for a blowout.

Something nobody mentioned yet: when you go to 8K axles make sure your brake controller can handle the extra braking force if you're running electric brakes. The 8K brake magnets are larger and pull more amperage. Shouldn't be an issue with a decent proportional controller, but if you're running an old time-delay unit you might need to bump the gain up.

I had a buddy who upgraded his axles but forgot that his tires were only rated for 2,540 lb each. Loaded the trailer up, made it about 80 miles on the highway before a tire let go. The sidewall just gave out. Lesson learned — your setup is only as strong as the weakest part, and tires are usually it.

One more thing to consider: if your trailer was originally rated for 14K GVWR with two 7K axles, simply bolting on 8K axles doesn't automatically make it a 16K trailer. The frame, coupler, and safety chains also have ratings. Check with the manufacturer before loading above the original GVWR.

Worth considering 17.5" wheels if you're upgrading anyway. The larger diameter tire runs cooler at highway speed and typically has a higher load rating. I run 215/75R17.5 Load Range H on my 8K tandem equipment trailer and they handle the weight beautifully, even in Texas summer heat.

title: What Size Trailer Axle Do I Need for a Car Hauler?
body: I want to build a car hauler trailer. What width of trailer frame would I need and what axles?
summary: An 82" wide frame is typical for a car hauler. Most builders use 3.5K to 8K axles. For 3.5K–7K axles, a 95" hub face with 80" spring center is standard. For 8K axles, use a 97" hub face with 80" spring center — these are the widest road-legal options.

comments.body: 82" wide frame is typical for a car hauler trailer. People put anything from 3.5k axles to 8k axles on car haulers. The 95" hub face 80" spring center is typically what people use for 3.5k - 7k axles and on a 8k axle they will use a 97" hub face with 80" spring center. These are the widest road legal axles you can use for your car hauler trailers.

Depends on what you're hauling. If it's just regular sedans and small SUVs, a pair of 5.2K axles on a tandem gives you 10,400 lb GVWR which is plenty. If you're looking to haul full-size trucks or bigger SUVs, go 7K tandem (14K GVWR). I built my car hauler with 5.2K Dexter axles and I've hauled everything from Civics to F-150s without any issues.

Built mine two years ago. 82" wide C-channel frame, 20 feet deck length with a 2-foot dovetail and slide-in ramps. Running tandem 7K axles with electric brakes on both axles. Here's my advice: go wider than you think on the ramp width. I did 16" wide ramps and wish I'd gone 18". Also go with at least 7K if you ever plan to haul anything besides compact cars. The weight adds up quick — the trailer itself will be 2,500-3,000 lb empty.

On the frame width — 82" between the fenders is pretty standard for a car hauler. That gives you roughly 84" between the tires which is enough to fit any passenger car. For the crossmembers, 3" channel on 16" centers works well. Some guys go 12" centers on the ramp area since that's where you get the most stress from loading.

Make sure you put electric brakes on both axles, not just one. I've seen people try to save $150 by only braking the rear axle on a car hauler and it's not enough stopping power when you've got a 4,000 lb vehicle sitting on the deck. Both axles with brakes, and a good proportional brake controller in the tow vehicle.

What kind of ramps are you planning? Fixed dovetail, slide-in ramps, tilt deck, or hydraulic? That decision affects your axle placement and tongue weight calculation. Tilt decks need the axles positioned further back than a standard dovetail. Just something to think about early in the build.

For axle spacing on a tandem car hauler, 42" center-to-center is typical. Make sure you set them so you get roughly 10-12% tongue weight. On a 20-foot deck trailer the axles usually end up centered around 13-14 feet back from the coupler. If your tongue weight is too low the trailer will sway; too high and you overload the hitch.

I went with 3.5K axles on my first car hauler because I thought I'd only be hauling small stuff. Within a year I was trying to load a crew cab Silverado and was way over capacity. Sold that trailer at a loss and built a 7K tandem. Moral of the story: go bigger than you think you need. The price difference between 3.5K and 5.2K axles is minimal and you'll appreciate the headroom.

Consider drop axles if deck height matters to you. A standard straight 5.2K axle with 15" tires puts your deck around 22-24" high. Drop axles bring it down to about 18-20", which makes loading easier and gives the vehicle a lower center of gravity during transport. Tradeoff is they cost a bit more and you lose some ground clearance.

Don't forget about the fenders! With 95" hub face axles on an 82" wide frame, your tires will sit outside the frame. You'll need fenders or you'll be spraying rocks and mud everywhere. I like the diamond plate bolt-on fenders — they look good and protect the car you're hauling from road debris.

One more thing — match your coupler to your GVWR. If you're running tandem 7K axles (14K GVWR), you need a 2-5/16" ball coupler rated for at least 14K. A 2" ball coupler is only good for about 3,500 lb. I know it sounds obvious but I've seen it done wrong more times than I'd like to admit.

title: How to Know If Trailer Brake Axle Is Installed Correctly
body: How do I know if I installed my trailer brake axle the right way so the brakes are not backwards?
summary: Make sure the wires coming out of the brake axle face toward the rear of the trailer. Some backing plates have L/R stickers — left is driver side, right is passenger side (like sitting in your truck). If no stickers, wires facing rearward confirms correct orientation.

comments.body: The easiest way to know you installed your trailer brake axle correctly is to make sure that the wires coming out of the brake axle are facing towards the back of the trailer. Additionally at times, there will be little stickers on the backing plates that say left and right. The left side is the driver side and the right side is the passenger side.

Another quick check besides the wire direction: look at the brake adjuster star wheel through the slot on the backing plate. On most Dexter and Lippert brake assemblies, the adjuster should be at the bottom of the backing plate and the star wheel should face toward the front of the trailer. If the star wheel is at the top or facing rearward, the axle is flipped.

I installed my first brake axle backwards and didn't realize it until the brakes barely worked. The trailer would pull to one side under braking and the drums got super hot. Pulled it out, flipped it 180 degrees so the wires pointed to the rear, and everything worked perfectly after that. Felt dumb but it's an easy mistake.

If you've already got it bolted down and you're not sure, here's the simplest test: jack up one side so the wheel is off the ground, connect the brake controller, and have someone apply the brakes. Try to spin the wheel by hand. It should lock up or drag heavily. Then check the other side the same way. If one side locks and the other barely drags, something's wrong — either the axle is backward or the magnets need adjusting.
What actually happens if it's installed backwards? Do the brakes not work at all, or do they just work poorly? Asking because I'm about to install mine and I want to know what to look for.

To answer Sue's question — they'll still work, just not well. The brake shoes are designed to be self-energizing in the forward direction. When the axle is backward, the shoes fight against the drum rotation instead of grabbing with it. You get maybe 40-50% braking effectiveness, uneven wear on the shoes, and excessive heat. Not a safety situation you want on the highway.

I always mark mine with a paint pen before installation. Quick arrow on the axle tube pointing toward the rear of the trailer. Takes two seconds and saves a lot of headaches down the road, especially if you ever have to pull the axle for service and reinstall it.

One thing that tripped me up: on some newer Dexter axles the wire exits are on the top of the backing plate instead of the bottom. The wires still need to face rearward, but the exit position looked different from the YouTube videos I was watching. Don't go by wire position on the plate — go by wire direction relative to the trailer. Rear = correct.

title: What Does 'Spring Pads Loose' Mean When Ordering a Trailer Axle?
body: When looking at your axle options I see some have 'pads loose' for the spring center. What does this mean?
summary: Spring pads loose means the rectangular mounting pads are not welded to the axle beam — they ship separately so you can weld them at the exact position your trailer requires. This is ideal for uncommon trailer widths where pre-welded pad positions don't match your hangers.

comments.body: The spring pads come loose so you can weld them where you want, or we can also weld them where you want for an extra charge. When the spring pads are pre-welded in place then they are for exactly that width of trailer. However if you have an uncommon trailer width, pads loose might be the best option for you. It provides more flexibility so you can weld the spring pads where you need them.

Basically the spring pads are the little flat brackets that get welded onto the axle tube — they're what the leaf springs sit on. "Loose" means they ship unattached so you position them yourself. You measure your trailer's spring hanger spacing, mark the axle tube, and weld the pads in place. It's a pretty straightforward job if you can stick weld or MIG weld.

Ordered pads loose on a 6K axle for a custom flatbed I was building. My spring hanger spacing was 31" which isn't a standard width anybody stocks. Having the pads loose let me set them exactly where I needed them. Just measure from center of pad to center of pad, double check it matches your spring hanger centers, and weld them on. Used a framing square to keep them aligned straight.
How thick of a weld do you need on the spring pads? I've got a 110V flux core welder. Is that enough or do I need something bigger?

Tim — a 110V flux core will work for 3.5K and 5.2K axles. For 7K and 8K axles I'd recommend at least a 220V MIG or stick welder. The pads on heavy axles are thicker steel and you want full penetration on the weld. A good 3/16" fillet weld all the way around the pad is what you're aiming for. If you're not confident in your welds, pay the extra to have them pre-welded — it's worth the peace of mind.

Important detail: measure from the CENTER of the axle tube outward to each pad, not from end to end. The spring center dimension is always measured center-to-center. If your trailer has a 33" spring center, each pad gets welded 16.5" out from center in both directions. Sounds obvious but I've seen guys measure from one pad to the other and end up off by the width of a pad.

If your trailer width is anything close to standard — 60", 65", 72", 80" spring center — honestly just order them pre-welded and save yourself the hassle. Pads loose is really for custom builds or oddball widths. The few bucks extra for pre-welded is worth not having to worry about alignment and weld quality.

Also make sure you orient the pads correctly on the tube. The pads have a curved side that matches the round axle tube and a flat side where the spring sits. Might seem obvious but if you flip one upside down the spring won't seat flat and you'll get a weird ride. Dry fit everything before you strike an arc.

title: What Is a Cambered Trailer Axle? Why Is My Axle Bent in the Center?
body: The axle arrived and I installed it but it comes bent in the center. I don't know if that's normal but there is a rim that doesn't look very straight.
summary: That bend is called camber — it's intentional. A cambered axle is designed to flatten under load, distributing weight evenly across the tires. This extends tire life compared to a straight axle, which would bow downward under weight and cause uneven wear.

comments.body: That is called a camber. It makes it where the tires will last longer vs a straight axle. Under load the axle straightens out, distributing the weight evenly.

Totally normal. Most trailer axles come with a slight upward bow built in from the factory — that's the camber. On a typical 3.5K to 7K axle it's usually about 1 to 1.5 inches of rise at the center. It looks wrong when it's sitting on the ground with no weight, but once you load the trailer the axle flattens out and the tires sit perfectly perpendicular to the road.

Ha, I panicked when my first axle showed up and called the supplier thinking they sent me a damaged one. They walked me through it — it's supposed to be like that. Once I bolted everything up and set the trailer on the ground, the tires looked perfectly straight. Put a couple thousand pounds of mulch on it and the axle was dead flat.

You mentioned a rim that doesn't look straight — can you clarify? If the tires have a slight negative camber (tops lean inward) with no load, that's the axle camber doing its job. But if one wheel leans significantly more than the other, or if it wobbles when you spin it, that could be a different issue like a bent spindle or improperly seated bearing.

One way to check if you have normal camber vs an actually bent axle: measure from the bottom of the axle tube at center to the ground, then measure at each end near the spring pads. They should be roughly equal on both sides. If one side is noticeably higher than the other, you may have a bend that isn't factory camber. Factory camber is always symmetrical.

Important thing to know: if you consistently overload a cambered axle beyond its rating, the camber can reverse over time and the axle develops a permanent downward sag. At that point the tires will toe out and wear on the inside edges really fast. I've seen this on landscaping trailers that guys load way beyond the rated capacity. If the center of the axle droops below the ends, it's time for a new axle.

Not all axles are cambered though. Torsion axles are typically straight since the suspension is built into the arm. And some lighter duty straight tube axles come without camber. If you're comparing a cambered spring axle to a friend's torsion axle and wondering why yours looks bent, that's probably why.

The camber also helps with tire life as mentioned. Without it, when you load the trailer the axle bows downward and the tires develop a positive camber — tops lean outward. That puts all the wear on the outside edge of the tread. With factory camber built in, loaded weight straightens the axle and the tires wear evenly. I've gotten 30,000+ miles on a set of ST225/75R15s on my cambered 6K axle hauling equipment.

To the OP — if you just installed it and haven't loaded it yet, put the trailer on the ground and load it to about 50-75% capacity. Then get down and eyeball the tires from behind. They should look straight up and down or very close to it. If they still lean in or out significantly under load, then you might have a problem. But I'd bet you're fine — this question comes up all the time.

title: Trailer Vibrating at 55 MPH: Diagnosis and Fix Guide
body: My trailer is shaking and vibrating at around 55 MPH. What could be causing this?
summary: In 80%+ of cases, trailer vibration at highway speed is caused by tire/wheel balance issues or worn bearings. Check tire pressure and condition first, then feel the hubs after a drive — hot hubs mean bearing problems. Also inspect for bent axles, loose U-bolts, and worn spring bushings.

comments.body: If your trailer is shaking or vibrating at around 55 MPH, the most common reasons are: 1) Tire/wheel balance issues or flat spots from sitting too long. 2) Bad or worn tires with separated belts. 3) Hub or bearing problems causing looseness. 4) Bent axle or loose U-bolts. 5) Worn leaf spring bushings or shackles. 6) Improper load distribution. In 80%+ of cases, it's bad tires, bad balance, or loose hub.

Start with the cheapest and most common fix first: tires. If the trailer has been sitting for more than a few months, the tires can develop flat spots that cause vibration at highway speed. Spin each tire by hand and look at the tread — if it's flat on one section or the tread has a wavy pattern, the tire is toast. Also check the date code on the sidewall. Trailer tires older than 5-6 years should be replaced regardless of tread depth.

Had the exact same problem on my enclosed cargo trailer. Drove me crazy for weeks — vibration kicked in right around 55 and got worse up to about 65. Turned out one of the tires had a separated belt. Looked perfectly fine on the outside, tread was good, no visible damage. But when I took it to a tire shop they could feel the bulge by running their hand along the tread. Replaced both tires on that axle and it was smooth as glass.

Before you start replacing parts, jack up each wheel and check for play. Grab the tire at 12 and 6 o'clock and try to rock it — any clunking or movement means your bearings are loose or worn. Then grab at 3 and 9 o'clock and do the same — that checks for spindle wear. Also spin the wheel and listen. Grinding or rumbling means the bearings need to be repacked or replaced. On Dexter axles the inner bearing is a L68149 and outer is a L44649 on most 3.5K setups.

How long has the trailer been sitting? And is it loaded or empty when you feel the vibration? A lot of times vibration at 55 mph on an empty trailer is just harmonic resonance from the tires and it goes away under load. If it vibrates loaded too, that's a different story.

People forget that trailer tires need to be balanced just like car tires. Most tire shops won't balance trailer tires unless you ask, and most trailer manufacturers ship them unbalanced from the factory. I've fixed 55 mph vibration on three different trailers just by getting the tires balanced. It's a $15/tire fix — try it before you tear into bearings and axles.

Had a vibration that drove me nuts. Turned out to be loose U-bolts. The axle had shifted slightly in the spring perch and was sitting crooked. Torqued the U-bolts back down to spec — 45 ft-lbs for 7/16" and 65 ft-lbs for 1/2" U-bolts on leaf spring axles — and the vibration went away. U-bolts can loosen up after the first few hundred miles, especially on a new trailer. They should be re-torqued after the first trip.

Also check your lug nuts. Loose lugs will cause a wobble that feels exactly like a balance issue. Torque spec for most trailer wheels is 90-120 ft-lbs depending on the lug size. 1/2"-20 lugs get 90 ft-lbs, 9/16"-18 lugs get 120 ft-lbs. Re-torque after the first 50 miles on new wheels and then periodically after that.

If you've got a tandem axle trailer, try swapping the tires from one axle to the other to isolate which one is causing the vibration. If the vibration changes character or goes away, you know it's a tire/wheel issue on that specific axle. Process of elimination saves a lot of guessing.

One thing that's often misdiagnosed: the vibration at a specific speed (like 55 mph) that goes away above and below that speed is almost always a balance or tire issue. A bearing problem usually gets progressively worse with speed and doesn't go away at higher speed. A bent axle causes vibration that increases steadily with speed. Knowing this narrows your troubleshooting.

Embarrassing confession: spent two days chasing a vibration on my utility trailer. Replaced bearings, had tires balanced, checked everything. It was the spare tire mounted under the tongue. The bracket had loosened and the spare was bouncing around at highway speed. Check the obvious stuff first.

Don't overlook load distribution either. If all the weight is at the back of the trailer and the tongue is light, the trailer will sway and vibrate at speed. Rule of thumb is 10-15% of the total loaded weight should be on the tongue. I've seen people load a trailer tail-heavy and blame the axles when it was really just bad weight distribution.

I had the same symptom — vibration starting at 55 mph. Wound up being worn leaf spring bushings. The rubber in the eye bushings was completely gone and the spring bolts were just metal-on-metal in the hangers. New bushing kit was about $25 and fixed it. Worth checking if the trailer has some miles on it.

title: Oil Bath vs Grease Trailer Hubs: Which Is Better?
body: I'm ordering new axles and can't decide between oil bath and EZ-lube grease hubs. What are the pros and cons?
summary: Oil bath hubs are better for highway and heavy-duty use — oil dissipates heat more effectively and requires less frequent service. Grease (EZ-lube) hubs are simpler and work well for lighter or infrequent use. To switch from oil to grease on 10K–12K axles, simply drain the oil and pack with grease — the seal is the same.

comments.body: Oil bath hubs are great especially for highway speeds. If your trailers see a lot of highway mileage, oil bath is ideal. For switching from oil to grease on 10K and 12K axles, simply drain the oil and pack with grease. The seal is the same. Easy and simple.

Here's my breakdown after running both types:

Oil bath pros: continuous lubrication, runs cooler, easy to inspect (sight glass shows oil level and condition), better for high-speed long-distance highway use. Cons: can leak if seals are worn, messier if you have to pull the hub, need to check oil level periodically.

Grease (EZ-lube) pros: simpler setup, less messy day-to-day, easier for most DIY guys to service with a grease gun, widely available bearing grease at any auto parts store. Cons: grease breaks down with heat over time, harder to tell when bearings need service, requires periodic repacking.

For highway trailers I go oil bath every time. For around-town utility trailers, grease is fine.

I've been running oil bath hubs on my enclosed car hauler for about 60,000 miles. Check the sight glass every trip, top off the oil once a year, and the bearings still look brand new when I pull them for inspection. The oil keeps them cool on long hauls through the desert — I regularly tow Phoenix to LA and back. Wouldn't switch to grease for highway work.

How often do you actually need to service each type? I use my trailer almost every day but it's all local runs, never more than 30-40 miles. Trying to figure out which one is less maintenance hassle for my situation.

Luke — for local use like yours, EZ-lube grease hubs are honestly the easier choice. Hit the zerk fitting with a grease gun every 6 months or 6,000 miles and you're good. Oil bath needs the oil level checked more frequently and if a seal starts weeping (which they eventually do) it'll make a mess on your wheels and brakes. Oil bath really shines when you're doing sustained 65+ mph for hours.

One big thing with oil bath: do NOT submerge them in water. If you're running a boat trailer and backing into the lake, the hubs cool down quickly and create a vacuum that sucks water past the seals. Water in the oil destroys bearings fast. For boat trailers, grease hubs with Bearing Buddy caps are the way to go. The positive pressure from the spring-loaded cap keeps water out.

The sight glass on oil bath hubs is a huge advantage people don't talk about enough. You can literally see the oil condition at a glance — if it's milky, you've got water contamination. If it's dark and gritty, the bearings are wearing. With grease hubs you have no idea what's happening inside until you pull the hub apart. I've caught two bad seals early just by checking the sight glass at fuel stops.

Had grease hubs fail on me once during a 900-mile trip. The inner seal let go somewhere around mile 400 and I didn't know until I smelled burning grease at a rest stop. Hub was scorching hot, bearings were trashed. Had to get towed to the nearest shop. Since then I switched everything to oil bath — at least I can see the oil level and catch problems before they strand me.

One thing to be aware of: if you're switching from oil bath to grease on a used axle, make sure you get ALL the old oil out before packing with grease. Oil and grease don't mix well — the oil will thin out the grease and it'll run right out of the bearings. Flush with brake cleaner, let it dry completely, then pack with fresh grease. Same goes the other direction — don't just dump oil into a hub that still has old grease in it.

For what it's worth, the original post mentions 10K and 12K axles for switching from oil to grease. On lighter axles (3.5K, 5.2K, 6K) the seal types might be different between oil and grease configurations, so it's not always a straight swap. Check with the axle manufacturer before switching on the smaller stuff. On the heavier axles the seals are typically the same and it's a simple swap.

I run a mix on my fleet — oil bath on the highway trailers and EZ-lube grease on the dump trailers that stay local. Both work fine for their intended use. The guys who have problems are usually the ones who never service either type. Whether it's oil or grease, it still needs periodic attention. Bearings don't care what lubricant you use as long as it's fresh and adequate.

title: How to Wire Trailer Brake Axle: No Polarity Needed
body: I bought a new trailer brake axle. How do I hook up the wires for the electric brakes?
summary: There is no polarity on trailer electric brake wires — connect either wire to hot or ground. Just make sure the wires coming out of the axle face toward the rear of the trailer to confirm correct axle installation.

comments.body: There is no polarity in the wires, so you can connect either wire to hot or ground. Ensure the wires coming out of the axle are positioned facing towards the rear to confirm that the axle is installed correctly.

Yep, no polarity is correct — the electric brake magnets work on AC from the brake controller, so it doesn't matter which wire goes where. Just connect the two wires from the axle to the brake feed wire and ground wire from your trailer harness. The white wire from the axle backing plate leads are typically connected to the blue (brake) wire on a standard 7-pin trailer plug.

First time I wired trailer brakes I spent way too long trying to figure out which wire was positive and which was negative. Glad someone told me it doesn't matter. Here's what I did: ran a 12-gauge wire from the 7-pin connector's brake pin (blue wire) down the frame to each axle, then spliced into each brake wire with weatherproof butt connectors. Ground wire goes to the trailer frame or the ground pin on the connector. Took about an hour total for a tandem.
After you get it all wired up, how do you test that the brakes are actually working before you hit the road? Is there a way to check without a brake controller?

Sue — easiest test is to jack up one wheel at a time, hook up 12V to the brake wire and ground (even a car battery with jumper wires works), and try to spin the wheel by hand. It should lock up or drag heavily. If it spins freely, you've got a wiring issue or the magnets aren't making contact with the drum. Once you hook up the brake controller, you can adjust the gain while watching the brake controller's built-in ammeter. Most 10" brakes on a 3.5K axle pull about 3 amps each.

Couple things that'll save you headaches: use at least 12-gauge wire for the brake circuit, 10-gauge if you're running a tandem with brakes on all four wheels. The voltage drop over a long wire run can weaken your braking significantly. And make sure every splice is sealed — exposed copper on the underside of a trailer corrodes fast. I use adhesive-lined heat shrink butt connectors on everything. Regular crimp connectors will green up and fail within a year or two.

Quick correction: while the brake magnets themselves aren't polarity-sensitive, your brake controller's ground connection absolutely matters. Make sure you have a solid ground from the brake controller in the tow vehicle to the truck frame, and a solid ground from the trailer plug to the trailer frame. A bad ground is the number one cause of weak or intermittent trailer brakes. I sanded the frame paint off and bolted a ring terminal directly to bare metal on both the truck and trailer side.

Something nobody mentioned yet — put a dab of dielectric grease on every connector and splice before you seal it up. It keeps moisture out and prevents corrosion. Especially important if you're anywhere with salt on the roads or near the coast. Costs about $4 for a tube at any auto parts store and it'll make your wiring last way longer.

title: Can I Move Spring Pad Seats That Are Welded on the Axle?
body: Can I move the spring pad seats that are welded on the axle to where I need them?
summary: Yes — you can cut and re-weld spring pads to a different position on the axle beam. TPU offers this service for $100 per axle. Alternatively, order axles with spring pads loose and weld them at the exact spring center your trailer requires.

comments.body: Yes you can. We do this all the time for customers. If you prefer us to move the spring seats where you need on the axles, we charge $100 per axle to do so. Or you can buy the axle with spring pads loose and weld them where you need.

Done this on two axles myself. The trick is cutting the old pads off clean with a grinder, not a torch. Torch warps the tube if you linger too long. Then I wire-wheel the area, tack the new position, measure diagonally corner to corner on the frame to make sure you're square, and then finish the weld. Used 6013 rods at about 90 amps on a 2-3/8" round tube and it came out solid.

Just a heads up — if you're moving them more than a couple inches from the original location, double check that your new spring center still falls within the manufacturer's recommended range relative to the hub face. There's a minimum distance from the hub (usually around 11") before you start de-rating the axle capacity. I've seen guys move pads too close to the hubs and not realize they've turned a 3500lb axle into something closer to a 2500lb rated setup.

I moved spring pads on a 6000lb Dexter axle last year when I was widening my trailer frame by 4 inches. Bought the pads loose from TPU and welded them at 62" spring center instead of the factory 58". Worked fine, just make sure you measure from the center of each pad to the hub face on both sides so it's symmetrical. If one side is off even half an inch your trailer will pull to one side going down the road.

What kind of welder do you have? If you're running a flux core or MIG that changes the approach a bit. Stick is honestly the easiest for this job since you're outside and wind won't mess with your shielding gas. Either way just make sure you get full penetration around the pad — it's a load-bearing weld.

One thing nobody ever mentions: once you cut the old pads off, roll the bare axle on a flat surface before welding the new ones on. I've had axles that looked straight but had a slight bend from years of overloading. Better to find that out before you spend time repositioning pads on a bent tube. If it wobbles more than about 1/8" you might be better off starting with a fresh axle.

Had mine done at a local welding shop for $75 per axle since I don't have a welder. Took the guy about 30 minutes each. Brought my own spring pads and just had him tack, measure, tack, measure again, then full weld. If you're not confident in your welding this is the kind of joint where I wouldn't wing it — these pads hold your trailer's entire suspension load.

Also worth noting if you're buying the loose spring pads, they come in different widths. Standard slipper spring pads are typically 1-3/4" or 2" wide to match your leaf spring width. Make sure you order the right size or the spring will sit cockeyed in the pad and wear unevenly.

title: What Is the Difference Between Over-Slung and Under-Slung Trailer Axles?
body: What is a over slung trailer axle? What's the difference between over-slung and under-slung?
summary: Over-slung means the leaf springs sit on top of the axle beam — this is the most common configuration. Under-slung means the springs are mounted underneath the axle, which lowers the trailer's ride height. Choose under-slung when you need a lower deck height.

comments.body: An over-slung trailer axle means the springs are over the axle. Under-slung trailer axles would be where the springs are under the axle. Over-slung is the most common configuration.

The biggest practical difference is ride height and ground clearance. Under-slung drops your trailer deck about 3-4 inches lower than over-slung on the same axle. That's why you see it a lot on car haulers and equipment trailers where you want the deck as low as possible for loading. The tradeoff is you lose ground clearance under the axle, which can be a problem on rough terrain or steep driveways.

Most boat trailers run under-slung because you want the hull sitting low on the bunks for better stability during towing. My 21-foot bowrider is on under-slung 3500lb Dexter axles and the keel sits maybe 18 inches off the ground which makes for a real steady ride even at highway speed. Wouldn't want it any higher.

One thing to watch out for with under-slung: your U-bolts and spring mounting hardware are different. Under-slung spring seats are shaped so the spring hangs below the axle tube, and the U-bolts wrap from underneath. If you're converting from over to under-slung you need the correct spring seats, longer U-bolts, and new tie plates. Don't try to reuse the over-slung hardware.

Quick visual way to remember it: over-slung = springs ride on top of the axle like a saddle. Under-slung = springs hang below the axle like a hammock. Over-slung is probably 80-90% of utility and cargo trailers you'll see on the road.

I switched my flatbed from over-slung to under-slung to get the deck lower for loading my mini excavator. Dropped it about 3.5 inches which made a huge difference on the ramp angle. But I had to add new fenders because the tires sat higher relative to the frame. Just something to think about if you're considering a conversion.

Also worth mentioning that torsion axles are a third option that avoids the over/under question entirely. They use internal rubber cords inside the axle tube instead of leaf springs. You lose the adjustability of spring suspension but gain independent wheel movement and no spring maintenance. Common on smaller enclosed trailers and boat trailers under 5000 lbs.

Don't forget that going under-slung also changes your tongue weight distribution slightly since you're lowering the load relative to the axle centerline. On a tandem it's usually not a big deal but on a single axle trailer with heavy loads it can make the trailer more sensitive to weight balance. Just keep that in the back of your mind.

Something I learned the hard way — if you're ordering a replacement axle and you currently have under-slung, make sure you specify that when ordering. The spring seats are welded in a different orientation. I ordered a "standard" axle once not thinking about it and the spring pads were set up for over-slung. Had to cut them off and re-weld. Easy enough fix but annoying when you're trying to get a trailer back on the road.

title: How Far Should Spring Pads Be from the Hub on a Trailer Axle?
body: I purchased a 95" hub face axle and want to weld the spring pads to 74" spring center. Would that hurt anything?
summary: Yes — placing spring pads too far from the hubs de-rates the axle significantly. The manufacturer guideline is no less than 11 inches and no more than 18 inches from the hub. For a 74" spring center, use an 89" hub face axle instead to stay within safe limits.

comments.body: Yes this would de-rate your axle a lot. If you need your spring centers to be close to 74 inches then I would recommend going with an 89 inch hub face axle so your axle wouldn't be de-rated. Based on the manufacturer's guidelines, the springs should be placed no less than 11 inches and no more than 18 inches from the hub.

To put some numbers on why this matters: a 3500lb axle with a 95" hub face is engineered so the bending moment at the spring seat is within the tube's yield strength. If you move the spring pads inward to 74" spring center, you're increasing the unsupported cantilever length from the pad to the hub by roughly 10 inches on each side. That extra leverage multiplies the stress on the axle tube significantly. You might not see a problem right away but under a full load, especially hitting a pothole, you could fatigue-crack the tube near the spring seat.

This is actually the number one thing I warn people about when they're building custom trailers. Everyone wants to adjust spring centers to fit their frame width, but you have to start with the right hub face dimension for your frame. The 11" to 18" rule from the hub that the previous answer mentioned is there because the engineers tested where the tube can handle the bending loads. Go outside that window and you're basically voiding the axle's rating.

Had a buddy who did exactly this on a 7000lb axle — moved the pads inboard about 8 inches past what they should've been. Looked fine for about six months then he noticed his tires wearing unevenly. Turned out the axle tube had a slight permanent bend right at the spring pad from the extra stress. Ended up replacing the whole axle anyway, which cost way more than just ordering the right hub face length to begin with.

So just to make sure I understand the math here — on a 95" hub face axle, the hub-to-hub distance is 95 inches. If you put spring pads at 74" spring center, each pad is about 10.5 inches from the hub. That's right at the lower limit of that 11" minimum. So technically you're borderline, which probably means under real-world loading conditions you'd be over the limit. Better to go with the 89" hub face where 74" spring center puts you at 7.5 inches of cantilever... wait, that's less than 11". Am I thinking about this wrong?

Gus — spring center is the distance between the two spring pads, not the distance from pad to hub. On a 95" hub face with 74" spring center, each pad is (95 - 74) / 2 = 10.5" from the hub face. That's just barely under the 11" minimum. On an 89" hub face at 74" spring center it would be (89 - 74) / 2 = 7.5" from the hub face to the pad, which is actually worse, not better. The correct move would be an 89" hub face at roughly 60-65" spring center to stay within the 11-18" range. Or just buy the right axle for whatever spring center your frame needs.

The real question is why do you need 74" spring centers? Is that what your trailer frame is set up for? If so, you want roughly a 96-110" hub face axle depending on your tire/wheel combo and fender clearance. That keeps you in the safe zone. What's your frame width and what tires are you running?

Just to add one more point — de-rating isn't just about structural failure. Your insurance and liability exposure changes too. If that axle fails and it turns out the spring pads were placed outside the manufacturer's spec, you could have trouble with any claim. Probably an unlikely scenario but when you're talking about a $150-200 axle, just getting the right one seems like cheap insurance.

I always tell people to call the axle supplier with their frame width, desired tire size, and load rating before ordering. They can calculate the correct hub face measurement for you. It takes five minutes and saves you from exactly this kind of headache.

title: Dexter 8-285 Hub Drum Replacement: Cross Reference & Carter Equivalent
body: I'm looking for a replacement for a Dexter 8-285 hub drum. Do you have an interchangeable part?
summary: The Dexter 8-285 is an 8K hub and drum with 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" brakes, 5/8" studs, and 8x6.5" bolt pattern. The Carter equivalent (BD-8K058) is a direct replacement with the advantage of a screw-in oil cap that supports both oil and grease lubrication.

comments.body: Yes that is a Dexter 8K hub and drum that uses 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" brakes. It has 5/8" studs and grease. We have this in the Carter brand that fully interchanges with this hub and drum. The only difference is that it uses a screw-in oil cap instead of a press-in grease cap. This allows you to have both options to either use oil lubrication or grease.

Running the Carter replacement on my 8K cattle trailer for about two years now. Fit was perfect — same bolt pattern, same bearing sizes (inner 25580 / outer 14125A), same brake drum diameter. The oil bath cap is actually a nice upgrade over the old Dexter grease cap in my opinion. I can see the oil level through the cap and it runs cooler on long hauls.

For anyone searching, the Dexter 8-285 cross references to a few different part numbers depending on the year. The Carter equivalent works for all of them as long as you verify it's the 8K version with 12-1/4" x 3-3/8" brakes. There's also an 8-285 in a 7K configuration with smaller brakes — make sure you're not mixing those up. Easiest way to confirm is measure your brake drum diameter.

One thing I'll mention about the oil vs grease question — if you switch to the oil bath cap on the Carter hub you'll want to use a lightweight gear oil, usually 75W-90 or whatever the cap manufacturer recommends. Fill to the line on the cap, not to the brim. And check it every few thousand miles because they can seep a little around the seal until everything seats in. After the first 500 miles I topped mine off and they've been rock solid since.

Just curious — are the studs the exact same length on the Carter as the Dexter? I had an issue once with aftermarket hub drums where the studs were about 1/4" shorter and my lug nuts weren't getting full thread engagement. Probably fine but I want to know before I order.

I've replaced three Dexter 8-285 hubs with Carter units across two different trailers. Stud length was identical on all of them — 5/8"-18 x 2" studs. Full thread engagement with standard 5/8" cone-seat lug nuts. No issues. The castings look just as good as the Dexter originals, honestly I think they might come from the same foundry.

When you swap the hub drum, do yourself a favor and replace the inner grease seal and bearings at the same time even if they look okay. A new set of Timken or National bearings plus seals is like $25-30 per hub and you already have everything apart. No sense putting a brand new hub on old bearings.

Don't forget to torque your lug nuts properly after the swap. For 5/8" studs on an 8K hub drum the spec is typically 120-140 ft-lbs. And re-torque after the first 25-50 miles. I use a torque wrench every time, not an impact gun for the final tightening. Seen too many warped drums from overtightened lugs.

title: What Size Trailer Axle for a 5x8 Utility Trailer?
body: What size axle do I need for a 5' x 8' trailer?
summary: A 5x8 utility trailer typically uses a 3,500 lb axle with a 73" hub face and 58" spring center, with a 5-lug bolt pattern. Always measure your existing spring center and bolt pattern to confirm before ordering a replacement.

comments.body: Without knowing your exact measurements I can only take a knowledgeable guess and say you would have a 3500 lb trailer axle with a 73" hub face / 58" spring center axle. Remember this is just a guess, always double check your spring center to spring center measurement and bolt pattern if it's a 5 lug to ensure the replacement trailer axle will fit.

The 3500lb / 73" hub face guess is probably right for most 5x8 trailers but please actually measure before ordering. I've seen 5x8s with anywhere from a 2000lb idler axle up to a 3500lb braked axle depending on what the builder spec'd. Measure spring center to spring center (center of one spring pad to center of the other) and hub face to hub face (inside of one hub flange to inside of the other). Those two numbers are what you need to order the correct axle.

A lot of the smaller 5x8 utility trailers come with a 2000lb idler axle, not a 3500. If you're mostly hauling lawn clippings, mulch, or light loads a 2000lb is plenty and they're cheaper. But if you're loading it up with gravel, concrete blocks, or anything heavy, the 3500 is the way to go. What are you planning to haul?

Also make sure you know your bolt pattern before ordering. Most 5x8 trailers with 3500lb axles run a 5 on 4.5" bolt pattern, but some of the lighter 2000lb setups use a 4 on 4" pattern. Count the number of lug studs on your hub and measure between them. If it's 5 lugs on 4.5" centers, that confirms the 3500lb class axle.

Something to consider — do you want a straight axle or a drop axle? A lot of 5x8 utility trailers use a drop axle to get the deck height lower for easier loading. The drop is typically 4 inches. If your current axle has a bend in it near the spring pads (looks like a shallow Z shape), that's a drop axle and you'll want to match that when you order the replacement.

I'd add that on a 5x8, your spring length matters too. Most 3500lb single-axle setups use 25-1/4" double-eye springs or slipper springs. If you're replacing just the axle and reusing your existing springs, make sure the new axle's spring pads match your spring width — usually 1-3/4" wide for that size trailer.

When I replaced the axle on my 5x8, I went ahead and upgraded from a 2000lb idler to a 3500lb with electric brakes. Best decision I ever made. The trailer stops so much better now, especially loaded. Cost me about $180 for the axle and another $200 for brake assemblies and a controller. If your trailer doesn't have brakes and you ever tow on hills or in traffic, seriously consider the upgrade while you have it apart.

title: Can I Use a VIN Number to Find What Size Trailer Axle I Need?
body: Can I give you my VIN number from my trailer so you know what size axle I need?
summary: No — there is no trailer VIN lookup tool that provides axle specifications. You will need to physically measure your axle: spring center to spring center and hub face to hub face. The axle tag (if present) on the center of the tube will also have key specifications.

comments.body: No sir, there is no trailer VIN lookup software that provides that information. We will need you to measure your axle. Get the spring center to spring center measurement and hub face to hub face measurement.

Yeah unfortunately trailers aren't like cars where you can punch a VIN into a database and get every spec. Trailer manufacturers don't have a standardized VIN decoding system that includes axle specs. The VIN will tell you the manufacturer, year, and maybe the GVWR, but nothing about hub face, spring center, bolt pattern, or axle diameter. You really do have to get under there with a tape measure.

Here's exactly what to measure and how:

1. Spring center to spring center — measure from the center of one spring pad to the center of the other, along the axle tube.
2. Hub face to hub face — measure from the inside face of one hub mounting flange to the other.
3. Axle tube diameter — use calipers or wrap a string around the tube and divide by 3.14. Common sizes are 2" round, 2-3/8" round, or 3" round.
4. Bolt pattern — count the lugs and measure the bolt circle diameter.

With those four numbers any axle supplier can get you the right replacement.

The one thing a VIN can sometimes help with is figuring out your trailer's GVWR if the sticker has worn off. You can contact the manufacturer with the VIN and they might be able to tell you the original gross vehicle weight rating. That at least narrows down whether you have a 3500lb, 5200lb, or 7000lb axle. But you'll still need physical measurements to order the right replacement.

I wish the industry would standardize this. Car guys have it so easy — plug in a VIN and you know every bolt on the vehicle. Trailer world is the wild west. Every manufacturer seems to use whatever axle length and spring center they feel like, even on the same model from year to year. Measuring is the only sure way.

Pro tip: while you're under there measuring, snap a few photos of the axle tag if there is one. Some axles (Dexter, Lippert, etc.) have a stamped metal tag on the tube with the capacity, hub face, and spring center printed right on it. If yours still has a readable tag you might not even need to measure — just read off the numbers. They're usually spot-welded near one of the spring pads.

Another thing — if your trailer has a data plate (usually riveted to the tongue or frame near the coupler), it sometimes lists the axle capacity and brand. Not the detailed measurements, but at least the weight class. Between the data plate and your own measurements you should have everything you need to order.

I've been down this road. Called three trailer dealers with my VIN and none of them could tell me my axle specs. One of them said "that's not how trailers work" which was frustrating but accurate. Spent 10 minutes under the trailer with a tape measure and had all the numbers I needed. It's really not that hard once you know what to measure.

title: What Is the Bolt Pattern on 14 Inch Trailer Tires and Wheels?
body: I don't know what bolt pattern I have but I do have a 14" trailer tire and wheel. How do I figure it out?
summary: 14" trailer tires and wheels almost always use a 5 on 4.5" bolt pattern. The only common size with multiple bolt pattern options is 15" — those can be 5x4.5", 5x4.75", 5x5", or 6x5.5". For 13" and smaller, it's typically 4x4" or 5x4.5".

comments.body: If you have a 14" trailer tire and rim then it's going to be a 5 on 4.5" bolt pattern. Really, the only size tire wheel that has 4 different bolt patterns are 15" trailer tire and wheels. However I do come across a few random bolt patterns that are not 15" that do have something other than a 5x4.5" bolt pattern, so it's always best to check.

Easiest way to check your bolt pattern at home: count the lug studs, then measure from the center of one stud straight across to the center of the opposite stud (or on a 5-lug, from the center of one stud to the far edge of the stud two positions away). For a 5 on 4.5" pattern the center-to-center measurement across is about 4.5 inches. If you have a bolt pattern gauge tool it takes five seconds but the tape measure method works fine.

The previous answer is right that 14" trailer wheels are almost always 5 on 4.5", but I'll throw this out there — I have a vintage 1980s boat trailer with 14" wheels that has a 5 on 4.75" bolt pattern (same as old GM cars). It's rare but it does exist on some older trailers. The difference between 4.5" and 4.75" is small enough that the wheels look like they should fit but the bolt holes won't quite line up. If your trailer is older, double check.

I got burned by this once. Ordered a set of 14" trailer wheels online assuming 5 on 4.5" because "that's what all 14 inch trailer wheels are." Turns out my little Harbor Freight trailer had a 5 on 4.5" hub but the center bore on the new wheels was too small. The bolt pattern matched but the hub cap stuck out too far and the wheel wouldn't seat flat. Make sure you check center bore too, not just bolt pattern.

While you're at it, check whether your lug studs are 1/2"-20 or 1/2"-13 thread. Most 14" trailer hubs use 1/2"-20 fine thread lug nuts. If you try to put coarse thread nuts on fine thread studs you'll cross-thread them instantly. Easy mistake if you're buying new lug nuts.

Here's the quick cheat sheet for common trailer bolt patterns by wheel size:
- 8" wheel: 4 on 4" or 5 on 4.5"
- 12" wheel: 4 on 4" or 5 on 4.5"
- 13" wheel: 5 on 4.5"
- 14" wheel: 5 on 4.5" (almost always)
- 15" wheel: 5 on 4.5", 5 on 5", 5 on 5.5", or 6 on 5.5"
- 16" wheel: 8 on 6.5" (mostly 8K and up)

So yeah, 15" is the one where you really need to measure because there are four common patterns.

If you don't have a ruler handy, another old-school trick is to pull one wheel off and lay it face-down on a piece of cardboard. Trace the bolt holes with a pencil. Then you can measure the pattern at your workbench without crawling under the trailer. Also makes it easy to bring the cardboard template to the parts store.

Once you've confirmed the bolt pattern and have the right wheels, don't forget proper torque on the lug nuts. For 1/2" studs on a 14" trailer wheel, torque spec is typically 90-100 ft-lbs. And re-torque after the first 25 miles, then again at 50 miles. I know it sounds excessive but trailer wheels loosen more than car wheels because of the road vibration and the way the bearings load differently.

title: Will an ST225/75R15 Tire Work in Place of a 235/75R15?
body: Will an ST225/75R15 work in place of a 235/75R15 trailer tire?
summary: Yes — an ST225/75R15 can replace a 235/75R15. The 235 is 10mm wider and marginally taller, but both fit the same 15" rim. Check that the narrower tire fits your wheel well without rubbing, and verify the load rating meets your weight requirements. ST-rated trailer tires typically have higher load capacity than similarly sized LT tires.

comments.body: YES, an ST225/75R15 tire can often work in place of a 235/75R15 tire. The 235/75R15 tire is 10 millimeters wider than the ST225/75R15 tire. Since both tires have the same aspect ratio and rim diameter, their overall diameters will be slightly different. Make sure the tire can fit without rubbing and check the load capacity ratings.

I've run both sizes on different trailers. The ST225/75R15 has a slightly smaller overall diameter — about 28.3" vs roughly 28.9" for the 235/75R15. In practice that difference is barely noticeable, maybe a quarter inch of ride height on each side. Where you really want to pay attention is the load rating. Make sure the ST225/75R15 you're buying has at least the same load capacity as the 235 you're replacing. Load range D and E are common in both sizes but double check the sidewall markings.

This is the part people overlook. An ST225/75R15 Load Range D is rated for 2540 lbs at 65 psi, while a 235/75R15 (if it's a P-rated passenger tire) might only be rated for 1984 lbs at 35 psi. So actually the ST tire could be an upgrade in terms of capacity even though it's narrower. BUT if the 235 is also an ST-rated tire, check the specific load ratings because they can vary by brand.

Made this exact swap on my enclosed cargo trailer about a year ago. 235/75R15 tires were getting hard to find locally in ST ratings, but the ST225/75R15 was in stock everywhere. Bolt on, no rubbing, no clearance issues. Been towing about 8,000 miles since then with zero problems. They ride the same as far as I can tell.

One thing to watch for — make sure you're comparing ST (Special Trailer) to ST. I've seen people run a P-metric 235/75R15 on a trailer because it was cheaper, but P-rated tires aren't designed for trailer duty. They have different sidewall construction and tend to overheat at highway speeds under trailer loads. Always run ST-rated tires on a trailer if possible.

Both of those tires fit a standard 15x6 wheel with no issue. The 225 actually sits a tiny bit narrower on the rim which can give you slightly more fender clearance if that's tight on your trailer. I've seen fender rub with 235s on some boat trailers where the bunks flex — the 225 fixed it without needing to modify the fender.

Don't forget to adjust your tire pressure when switching sizes. The correct pressure is whatever is stamped on the tire's sidewall for max load, not what was on the old tire. ST225/75R15 Load Range D is usually 65 psi max. If you were running the 235 at a lower pressure you'll want to bump it up to match the new tire's spec. Low pressure on trailer tires is the number one cause of blowouts.

Since the overall diameters are slightly different, if your trailer has a GPS-based speed sensor or an odometer (some larger enclosed trailers do), the reading will be off by about 2%. Probably doesn't matter for most people but I figured I'd mention it. For standard utility and cargo trailers with no electronics on the axle it's a non-issue.

I run ST225/75R15 Load Range E on my tandem dump trailer. They're rated for 2830 lbs each at 80 psi. Rock solid and I actually prefer the slightly narrower profile — seems to track a little better in crosswinds compared to the wider 235s I had before. Could be my imagination but that's my experience over about 15,000 miles.

title: Best brake kit for a 3500lb tandem trailer?
body:
I have a 16ft tandem utility trailer rated at 3500lb. Currently has no brakes but I want to add electric brakes to both axles.

What kit should I get? I've been looking at the Dexter and Lippert options but not sure which is better value.

My axles are 2" round, 5 on 4.5 bolt pattern. Trailer is used mostly for hauling equipment and landscaping materials.

comments.body:
For a 3500lb tandem with 2" round axles and 5 on 4.5 bolt pattern, I'd recommend the Dexter 10" electric brake kit. It's what I run on my similar trailer.

You'll need:
- 2x brake assemblies per axle (so 4 total)
- Brake controller (I like the Tekonsha P3)
- Wiring harness

The Dexter 23-105 kit is a good all-in-one option. Make sure to get the self-adjusting version - saves a lot of hassle.

Total cost is around $400-500 for everything including the controller.
I second the Dexter recommendation. Just installed the same setup on my trailer last month. Installation took about 3 hours with basic tools.

Just to add to the Dexter 23-105 recommendation — when you install the backing plates, make sure the adjuster star wheel is at the bottom on each side. The adjusters are side-specific (left and right) and if you put them on the wrong side the self-adjusting mechanism won't work. The left side adjusts when you back up and the right side... well, both adjust when reversing, but only if the star wheel is oriented correctly. Check the Dexter installation diagram that comes in the box.

One thing I'd recommend is upgrading the brake magnets from the stock ones to the ceramic magnets.
