The stock magnets in most kits are fine for normal use but if you're hauling landscaping materials and equipment regularly, the ceramic magnets give you noticeably stronger braking force. They cost about $15 more per pair and they last longer too. On a 3500lb tandem fully loaded you'll appreciate the extra stopping power.

Since your trailer currently has no brakes, you'll also need to run the wiring. Here's what worked for me on a similar setup:

- 12 gauge wire from the 7-way connector to a junction near the first axle
- Split to each brake assembly from there
- Use the trailer frame as ground but add a dedicated ground wire anyway as backup — frame-only grounds corrode over time and you'll get weak brakes
- Run all wires inside split loom and zip tie to the frame every 18 inches or so

Don't cheap out on the wiring or connections. Crimped and heat-shrunk connectors, no scotch locks.

On brake controllers — the Tekonsha P3 is great but it's about $120-150. If you want to save some money, the Tekonsha Voyager is a solid proportional controller for about $50-60 and works perfectly fine for a 3500lb tandem. Proportional controllers (both the P3 and Voyager) apply braking force based on how hard you brake in the tow vehicle, which is way better than a time-delay controller. The P3 has a nicer display and more adjustments but the Voyager gets the job done.

Don't forget you'll need a breakaway kit too. It's required by law in most states for any trailer with brakes. It's a small battery box that mounts on the tongue with a cable that attaches to your tow vehicle. If the trailer ever separates from the truck, the cable pulls a pin that activates the brakes. Runs about $40-60 and it's cheap insurance. Some brake kits include one, some don't — check before you order.

When you're bolting the backing plates to the axle flange, torque those bolts to 30-35 ft-lbs. And use blue Loctite on them. I've seen backing plates come loose from road vibration on trailers that go on rough roads regularly. Also make sure the mounting surface is clean — any rust or debris between the flange and backing plate will cause the brakes to drag or not sit flat.

I'll throw in a different perspective since you mentioned Lippert. I run Lippert brakes on one trailer and Dexter on another. Honestly they're very comparable for a 3500lb application. Lippert is usually a few bucks cheaper. The Dexter parts are easier to find at local stores and the aftermarket support is deeper. If you ever need to replace shoes, magnets, or springs down the road, Dexter parts are on the shelf at every trailer supply shop. For that reason alone I'd go Dexter.

Installed Dexter 10" electric brakes on my tandem landscaping trailer about three years ago. Same axle size as yours. Couple things I wish I'd known going in:

1. The drums need to be burnished — drive about 200 miles with light braking before you expect full stopping power. They feel weak at first.
2. Adjust the brakes manually the first time even if they're self-adjusting. The self-adjusters need a starting point.
3. Check the brake controller gain setting. Too high and the tires lock up, too low and it feels like you have no brakes. I started at about 6 on the P3 and worked up from there.

Overall very happy with the setup. Night and day difference from running with no brakes.

Since you mentioned hauling equipment and landscaping materials — that stuff shifts around. Good brakes are critical but so is having the load secured. When a 500lb mower slides forward on a hard stop it puts a lot of stress on the coupler and tongue. Just something to keep in mind. Good brakes + good tie-downs = safe towing.

Might be obvious but make sure your tow vehicle's 7-way plug is wired for electric brakes before you buy the controller. Most trucks with a factory tow package have the brake wire already run to the 7-way — it's the blue wire. If you have an aftermarket hitch or a vehicle without a tow package, you might need to run a wire from where the controller mounts to the back of the truck. Not hard but it's an extra step some folks forget about.

Confirming the $400-500 total estimate from the first answer. Here's roughly what I spent when I did mine:
- 4 Dexter brake assemblies: ~$200
- Brake controller (Voyager): $55
- Breakaway kit: $45
- Wiring, connectors, split loom: $30
- Brake drums came already on my hubs

So about $330 in my case since I went with the Voyager instead of the P3 and already had the drums. Your mileage may vary depending on whether you need new drums or hub/drum combos.

One more thing — if your 2" round axles don't already have mounting flanges welded on for brake backing plates, you'll need those too. Some bare axles come without flanges if they were set up as idler axles (no brakes). Check if there are 4-bolt flanges welded to each spindle area. If not, you might need to swap the spindles or have flanges welded on, which complicates things a bit.
